Sequestration in Scotland, explained without judgment

Sequestration is the Scottish term for bankruptcy. It is a formal process that writes off debts you have no realistic prospect of repaying, and it exists because sometimes a situation cannot be fixed by paying more slowly.

If you are reading this, you are probably frightened about your house, your car and your job. Those questions are answered further down, plainly, before anything else. And it is worth saying early that sequestration is not the only option in Scotland, and it is not the first one we would reach for.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Your home, your car, your job

These are the three questions almost everyone asks first, so here they are first.

Your home

Your share of any property you own becomes part of the estate the trustee deals with, so a home you own is at risk. That does not automatically mean it is sold. Much depends on how much equity there is, who else owns it, and whether the mortgage payments are being maintained. Keeping up mortgage payments matters, because the lender's security survives the sequestration. If you rent, sequestration does not usually affect your tenancy directly, though your landlord may treat rent arrears as a debt included in the process. Two things are worth knowing. Your trustee cannot sell a family home without the consent of your spouse, civil partner or former spouse, or the sheriff's authority, and the sheriff can refuse a sale or postpone it for up to three years. And if the trustee has taken no step against your interest in the home within three years of the sequestration, it comes back to you, but that clock only starts on time if you tell the trustee about the property within three months of the award, so tell them. This is the single most important thing to take proper advice on before applying.

Your car

A car of modest value that you need for work or caring responsibilities can often be kept. A high value vehicle is more likely to be sold, or you may be asked to pay its value into the estate. Cars on finance are treated differently again, because the vehicle may not legally be yours yet.

Your job

Most people keep their jobs. Some professions and roles have restrictions, so it is worth checking your employment contract and any professional body rules. You cannot act as a company director, or be involved in forming or managing a company, while sequestrated without the court's permission.

What sequestration actually is

Sequestration transfers your assets to a trustee, who sells what can be sold and distributes the proceeds among your creditors. In return, the debts included are written off at the end of the process, whether or not they were paid in full.

It is administered by the Accountant in Bankruptcy, the Scottish Government agency responsible for personal insolvency in Scotland. The trustee is either the Accountant in Bankruptcy or a licensed insolvency practitioner appointed to act. Where an insolvency practitioner is appointed as trustee, they take on statutory duties to your creditors as well as responsibility for administering your estate, which is why the role has to be held by someone licensed and regulated.

Sequestration is recorded on the Register of Insolvencies, which is public. It also affects your credit rating: the sequestration appears on your credit file and will make borrowing harder and more expensive for several years. For many people the credit rating damage has already been done by missed payments and defaults long before they reach this point, which is worth weighing honestly rather than treating a good credit rating as something still to protect.

This is a Scottish process under Scottish law. It is not the same as bankruptcy in England and Wales, and the alternatives are different too. A protected trust deed is the Scottish equivalent of an IVA, and the Debt Arrangement Scheme has no English counterpart at all. If you have been reading English guidance and applying it to your own position, some of it will not hold here.

The two routes into sequestration
Minimal Asset Process (MAP)

Sometimes called MAP bankruptcy, this is the simpler, cheaper route for people on a low income with few assets and no property. The application fee is £50, and it is waived if you are on a qualifying benefit or assessed as having no surplus income, which covers almost everyone eligible for MAP in the first place. The process is shorter, and there is less trustee involvement. To qualify you must owe no more than £25,000 in total, own assets worth no more than £2,000 with no single item worth more than £1,000, and own no land. A vehicle you reasonably need is left out of that total if it is worth £3,000 or less, and student loans do not count towards the £25,000. There is no minimum debt: the old £1,500 floor was removed in February 2023. You also need either an assessment showing you can pay nothing towards your debts, or six months of qualifying benefits with no other income. You cannot use MAP if you have been sequestrated in the last five years, or used MAP in the last ten. Discharge comes automatically six months after your bankruptcy is awarded, unless the Accountant in Bankruptcy takes you out of MAP first, which it can do if your assets turn out to be worth more than the limit, if you are assessed as able to contribute, or if you do not co-operate.

Full administration sequestration

The standard route, used where MAP does not apply, typically because you own property, have assets of some value, or have surplus income. A trustee is appointed to realise assets and administer the estate, and discharge is a decision taken on the trustee's report rather than something that happens by itself.

Figures correct as at July 2026. Thresholds are set by the Accountant in Bankruptcy and do change, so ask us to confirm them rather than relying on a page you found online.

You can apply for your own sequestration, and most people do. Whichever route you use, the law requires you to see an approved money adviser first. That is a statutory precondition rather than a formality, and in practice the adviser is the one who submits your application. For MAP you also need a Certificate for Sequestration from that adviser. For full administration you need the certificate, or to meet the test for apparent insolvency, or to have granted a trust deed that creditors would not let become protected. You also need to owe at least £3,000. A creditor owed above a set amount can also petition for your sequestration, but only if you are apparently insolvent as well. Owing the money is not enough on its own.

What happens during the process
  • You apply through the Accountant in Bankruptcy, or a creditor petitions the court
  • A trustee is appointed to take control of your estate
  • Assets that can be realised are identified and sold, with certain essentials protected
  • If you have surplus income, you will normally be asked to make payments under a Debtor Contribution Order, assessed from what is left after reasonable living costs
  • Creditors submit claims and are paid from whatever the trustee realises
  • You are discharged, and the included debts are written off
  • Any contribution order can continue after discharge, so the payments and the discharge are two separate things

Under MAP, discharge is automatic at six months. In a full administration sequestration it can come from twelve months onwards, on the trustee's report rather than automatically. Either way the trustee's work on the estate can carry on beyond your discharge, and contributions may continue past it.

What your creditors can and cannot do

This is usually the part that brings the most immediate relief, because the pressure people are living under comes from creditors rather than from the debt itself.

Once you are sequestrated, most creditors must stop contacting you directly and must deal with your trustee instead. They cannot continue diligence, which is the Scottish term for enforcement action such as earnings arrestment or bank arrestment, in respect of the debts included. Ongoing interest and charges on those debts stop. Creditors who want a share of whatever the trustee realises have to submit a formal claim rather than chase you for payment.

Creditors keep some rights. A secured creditor such as your mortgage lender retains its security over the property, so it can still repossess if the mortgage payments are not maintained. A creditor can object to your discharge if it believes you have not cooperated. And any creditor owed a debt that is not covered by sequestration, such as a court fine, can still pursue you for it.

Unsecured creditors, meaning credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts and most trade creditors, generally rank equally and share whatever is left after the costs of the process and any preferential claims. In many cases unsecured creditors receive very little, which is precisely why sequestration writes off the balance.

There is also a step you can take before deciding anything. A moratorium gives you six months of protection from diligence while you take advice and choose a route. It is entered on the Register of Insolvencies, and a money adviser can apply for it.

Which debts are included, and which are not

Most unsecured debt is included and written off: credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts, catalogue debt, most utility arrears, council tax arrears and, in many cases, business debts you are personally liable for. If a debt is unsecured and it existed at the date of sequestration, the working assumption is that it is included.

Some are not. Student loans, court fines, compensation orders and debts arising from fraud or breach of trust are not written off. Child maintenance is a special case: arrears that built up before the date of sequestration are written off, but maintenance falling due from that date onwards is not, and the Child Maintenance Service can still act on it. Secured debts such as your mortgage are treated differently, because the lender's security over the property survives.

If you have signed a personal guarantee for a business, the guaranteed debt is a personal debt, and it can be included. For directors and sole traders whose business and household finances have become tangled together, this is the point where the two sides of the problem have to be looked at as one. That crossover is a large part of what we do.

The alternatives, which usually deserve a look first

Sequestration is the most serious option, not the default. In Scotland there are two formal alternatives and several informal ones.

Protected trust deed

You pay a monthly contribution worked out by a statutory assessment of what you can afford, normally for 48 months from the date the deed is granted. It can run longer if you miss payments, or if you agree to keep paying beyond that, which is common where there is equity in your home. At the end your trustee applies for you to be discharged and the remaining unsecured debt is written off, though that depends on the deed having become protected and on you keeping to the terms. Your home is treated differently than in sequestration, and for homeowners this is often the more protective route.

Links: Trust deeds

Debt Arrangement Scheme (DAS)

A statutory payment programme that lets you repay the debt itself in full over a longer period, with interest and charges frozen from the day you apply and creditors of the debts in the programme barred from taking enforcement action. Complete it and the frozen interest and charges are written off; if it fails they can be added back. Your home is protected, though a programme can be approved on condition that you sell some other asset. If you can realistically clear the debt given time, this is usually the better answer.

Links: Debt Arrangement Scheme

If the debt is your company's, not yours

Directors often arrive here because a business has failed and a personal guarantee has been called in. If that is your position, the company side needs its own answer, whether that is liquidation, a CVA, or dealing with a winding up petition that has already been served. Sorting the personal position while leaving the company unresolved rarely works, because the guarantee keeps generating new liability.

Links: Insolvency practitioner | Liquidation

There are also informal arrangements, and sometimes the right answer is simply a repayment plan and some breathing space. Free debt advice is available in Scotland from Citizens Advice Scotland, StepChange and National Debtline, and a money adviser or debt adviser at any of them can issue the certificate you need to apply. We will tell you when free advice is all you need.

Where we fit

Lancefield does not act as your trustee. Only the Accountant in Bankruptcy or a licensed insolvency practitioner can do that, and we do not take those appointments.

What we do is give you a clear read on your position before anything is decided, including whether a formal process is needed at all. Because nobody here is appointed as your trustee, we have no stake in which route you take and no reason to steer you toward one. If a trust deed protects you better than sequestration, we will say so. If the Debt Arrangement Scheme is the right answer, we will say that. And if the honest answer is that you need free advice rather than us, we will tell you that too.

Where a formal appointment is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and we stay alongside you through it.

Frequently asked questions
How long does sequestration last?

It depends which route you are in. Under the Minimal Asset Process you are discharged automatically six months after your bankruptcy is awarded. In a full administration sequestration the Accountant in Bankruptcy can discharge you from twelve months onwards, but that is a decision based on your trustee's report rather than an automatic date, and it can be refused or delayed if you have not co-operated. Contributions from surplus income can continue beyond discharge, and the Accountant in Bankruptcy's guidance is that it stays on your credit file for six years.

Will everyone find out?

Sequestration is entered on the Register of Insolvencies, which is a public register. In practice, most people's friends, neighbours and colleagues never look at it. Your employer is not notified as a matter of course unless your role or profession requires it.

What if I have almost nothing?

That is what the Minimal Asset Process exists for. The £50 application fee is waived for anyone on a qualifying benefit or assessed as having no surplus income, so in practice it costs nothing; there is less trustee involvement, and discharge comes automatically at six months. The same waiver applies to the £150 fee on the full route, so do not rule that out on cost alone. It is built for people on a low income without property, and since the minimum debt requirement was removed in 2023 there is no longer any floor to fall below. We can check whether you fall inside the limits.

What happens to my benefits?

Sequestration does not stop you claiming welfare benefits. Your benefit income is taken into account when the trustee assesses whether you have surplus income to contribute, and in many cases people whose income is mainly from benefits are assessed as having nothing to pay. Benefit overpayments are treated as debts, and whether a particular overpayment is written off depends on how it arose, so it is worth listing them when you take advice.

Can I apply myself?

Most sequestrations are applied for by the debtor rather than forced by a creditor, so yes in that sense. But you cannot lodge the application yourself. Seeing an approved money adviser comes first and is required by law rather than merely advisable, and it is that adviser who submits it for you. For MAP you need a Certificate for Sequestration from them; for full administration you need the certificate or must meet the test for apparent insolvency. You do not need a solicitor.

What restrictions apply while I am sequestrated?

You cannot act as a company director or manage a company without the court's permission. You must tell a lender you are sequestrated if you are seeking credit of £2,000 or more, and for credit of any amount at all while your debts total £1,000 or more. You must cooperate fully with your trustee, including disclosing assets and any change in your circumstances. Failing to cooperate can extend the restrictions.

Does sequestration affect my partner?

Your partner's own debts and their sole assets are not included. Jointly owned assets and joint debts are affected, and if you own a home together their position needs looking at carefully. A joint bank account is likely to be frozen at the outset.

I am a director. Does this close my company?

Not automatically, but you will almost certainly stop being a director of it. Acting as a director while sequestrated is a criminal offence without the court's permission, and most companies' articles remove a director from office the moment they are prohibited from acting. Permission from the court does not put you back on the board; the company has to appoint you again. Where the company is also insolvent, the two problems are best dealt with together rather than one at a time.

Is this the same as bankruptcy in England?

It is the Scottish equivalent, but the process, the terminology and the alternatives differ. Sequestration is administered by the Accountant in Bankruptcy rather than the Insolvency Service, and the Scottish alternatives are protected trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme rather than IVAs.

We will tell you honestly whether sequestration is right, whether something less serious would protect you better, or whether you need free advice rather than us. It is free, completely confidential, and commits you to nothing.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Business restructuring

Restructuring is what a business does while it still has choices. It covers the changes that fix the underlying position: reshaping debt, improving cash flow, selling or closing the part that is losing money, and getting an honest read on whether the business works once those things are done.

It sits before insolvency, not after. That distinction is the whole point of this section, because by the time most companies speak to a restructuring specialist the useful options have already narrowed.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

The question underneath everything

Broadly there are two kinds of work here. Financial restructuring changes what the company owes and how it is funded. Operational restructuring changes how the business runs: what it sells, at what margin, and at what cost. Most companies that come to us need some of both, and treating a financial restructuring as sufficient when the operational problem is untouched is the most common way this work fails.

Every restructuring decision turns on one thing: is there a viable business under the current problem?

If there is, then the debt, the structure and the cost base are all solvable, and the work is worth doing. If there is not, then restructuring delays an outcome rather than changing it, and the honest answer is to say so early rather than spend eighteen months and a lot of money arriving at the same place.

Answering that question properly is why an independent review exists. It gives you, and any lender who is asking, an objective read on whether the business model works once the immediate pressure is removed. It is often the first piece of work we do, because everything else depends on the answer.

What restructuring covers
Turnaround

Addressing the cause rather than the symptom. Operational and financial change in a business that is underperforming but fundamentally sound: pricing, cost base, working capital, management information, and the discipline to act on it.

Links: Turnaround

Debt restructuring

Reshaping what the company owes so that repayment matches what the business can actually generate. Renegotiating terms, consolidating facilities, dealing with a lender's concerns before they become a default.

Links: Debt restructuring

Independent business review

An objective assessment of viability, usually commissioned by a lender but valuable to a director in its own right. It establishes the facts everyone then negotiates around.

Links: Independent business review

Contingency planning

Preparing a fallback before circumstances force the decision. It is the least urgent-sounding service here and frequently the most valuable, because a plan made calmly beats one made under a deadline.

Links: Contingency planning

Exit planning

Getting a business ready to be sold or wound down on your terms, over a horizon long enough to influence the outcome. Sale, succession, or an orderly solvent closure.

Links: Exit planning

Corporate simplification

Removing dormant and redundant companies from a group structure, reducing filing obligations, cost and risk. Usually executed through solvent liquidations, which is where it touches the insolvency side of the practice.

Links: Corporate simplification

How a restructuring process actually runs

Companies arrive at this expecting something abstract. In practice the restructuring process follows a fairly consistent sequence, and knowing it makes the whole thing less daunting.

  • Establish the facts. What the company actually owes, to whom, secured or unsecured, and what the cash position looks like week by week rather than month by month. A surprising number of businesses cannot answer this on day one, and nothing useful happens until they can
  • Test viability. Strip out the financing problem and ask whether the trading business generates cash. This is the independent business review question, and it determines everything that follows
  • Map the stakeholders. Lenders, HMRC, landlords, key suppliers, shareholders and employees all have different interests and different degrees of power over the outcome. A restructuring that ignores one of them tends to fail at exactly the point that stakeholder notices
  • Build the plan. What changes, in what order, funded how, over what period. The plan has to be credible to the people being asked to support it, not merely to you
  • Negotiate. Lenders and creditors are asked to agree new terms. Companies that come with evidence get better outcomes than companies that come with optimism
  • Implement and monitor. The plan runs, and it is measured against the forecast every month. Corporate restructuring fails more often through poor follow-through than poor design

Most of the value sits in the first two steps. Companies that get an honest answer on viability early either save a great deal of money or stop spending it on something that was never going to work.

The output of all this is a restructuring plan: a written document setting out the financial position, the changes proposed, the funding required and the forecast that results. Lenders and other companies in the chain will judge you on that plan, so it needs to survive scrutiny rather than merely sound encouraging. A restructuring plan built on assets nobody has valued, or on financial projections that assume the last three years were unrepresentative, will not.

Getting the stakeholders onside

Business restructuring is, in the end, a negotiation with people who have money at risk. Each of them behaves differently and each needs handling.

Lenders

A secured lender's first instinct is to protect its position, which usually means it would rather support a credible plan than enforce and recover less. What it will not tolerate is surprises, or forecasts that turn out to be optimistic. Lenders often commission an independent business review before agreeing anything, and it is better to expect that than to resist it.

HMRC

Frequently the largest unsecured creditor in an owner-managed company. HMRC will discuss Time to Pay, and is considerably more receptive before enforcement has started than after. Where tax debt is the core problem, engaging early is the single highest-value action available.

Key suppliers

A supplier that cannot be replaced has more sway than the size of its debt suggests. Identify those companies early. Some will support a restructuring for the sake of the ongoing relationship if they are told what is happening.

Shareholders

Restructuring often changes the shareholding, particularly where new money comes in. Owner-managers should understand what dilution they are accepting before agreeing to funding, not after.

Employees

Rarely consulted, frequently the people who know where the money is going. They also notice long before any announcement, and silence is generally read as worse news than the truth.

Where restructuring meets the formal procedures

There is no hard border between restructuring and insolvency. Several formal procedures are restructuring tools, and choosing one does not mean the business is finished.

A company voluntary arrangement is a restructuring of the ordinary unsecured debt, binding those creditors to a repayment plan while the company keeps trading and the directors stay in control. Secured creditors keep their security and preferential creditors keep their priority unless they agree otherwise. Administration provides a statutory moratorium, holding creditors off while a rescue or a sale is arranged, and a pre-pack administration does that with a buyer already lined up. Each requires a licensed insolvency practitioner to take an appointment, so each is a formal insolvency procedure, but the purpose of all three is preserving something rather than ending it.

On the solvent side, corporate simplification and exit planning use a members' voluntary liquidation to close down companies that have served their purpose, which is restructuring of a very different kind: tidying a group rather than rescuing one.

What decides between an informal restructuring and a formal procedure is usually whether anyone can block it. If creditors will agree to new terms voluntarily, no formal process is needed. If one creditor can block a sensible outcome that everyone else supports, a procedure that binds the minority becomes the only route. Where the dissenting creditors are ordinary unsecured ones, that is the practical case for a CVA. Where the creditor holding things up is secured or preferential, a CVA cannot bind them without their agreement, and a restructuring plan under Part 26A of the Companies Act 2006 is the procedure that can. Either option is worth understanding before it is needed rather than after.

Directors sometimes resist involving an insolvency practitioner at all, on the reasonable-sounding basis that doing so makes the situation official. In practice an insolvency practitioner advising on options has taken no appointment and nothing is formal, and their view on whether administration or a CVA would work is worth having early. The point at which you cannot avoid an insolvency practitioner is the point at which you have lost the ability to choose which one.

When restructuring is the right call

Some patterns come up repeatedly, and they are worth recognising early.

  • Profitable but out of cash. A business can be trading well and still be unable to pay its debts as they fall due. That is a working capital and funding problem, not an insolvency one, and it is very fixable
  • One loss-making part dragging the rest down. Where a group or a division is the problem, restructuring can isolate it without losing what works
  • A lender getting nervous. Covenant pressure or a facility coming up for renewal is a reason to act now, with a plan, rather than wait to be asked
  • The numbers have stopped being trustworthy. If management information is poor, nobody, including you, actually knows whether the business works. That is fixable and it is usually first
  • A change of ownership coming. Retirement, a departing shareholder, or a sale in mind, all of which go better with two years' preparation than two months'
When it is not

We would rather say this here than after taking a fee.

Restructuring will not save a business whose product or market has gone. It will not fix a company that cannot generate cash at any plausible cost base. And it will not help where the position has already deteriorated so far that creditors have taken control of the timetable, which is what a winding up petition effectively does.

Where that is the case, the options move to the insolvency practitioner side of the practice: a company voluntary arrangement if the business is viable but the debt is not, administration if protection and a sale are needed, or liquidation if the answer is closure. Knowing which side of that line you are on is exactly what the first conversation establishes.

Refinancing, and when new money is the answer

Refinancing is often the cleanest restructuring available. Where a business is fundamentally sound but the debt is the wrong shape, replacing expensive short-term borrowing with facilities that match the trading cycle can solve the problem without changing anything else.

The usual candidates are invoice finance where cash is tied up in the sales ledger, asset finance to release value from equipment, and refinancing property to spread repayment over a sensible horizon. Companies in the same industry frequently use quite different funding structures, and the mix that suits a contractor is not the one that suits a manufacturer.

Two cautions. Refinancing that simply buys time without changing the underlying economics postpones the problem and adds cost to it. And most new facilities will require personal guarantees, so a director should understand exactly what they are signing before improved cash flow makes it feel routine.

We are advisers rather than brokers. Where funding is the answer we will say so and introduce you to people who arrange it, and we will tell you plainly if we think more debt is the wrong medicine.

Selling, buying, and reshaping the group

Not all restructuring is defensive. Mergers and acquisitions are restructuring tools, and for companies in a difficult position a sale of part of the business is frequently the fastest route to stability.

Selling a profitable division to fund the rest is a legitimate and often overlooked option. So is acquiring a competitor's assets when they fail, which is how a good deal of consolidation in any industry actually happens. Both need the same groundwork: clean numbers, a defensible valuation, and enough time to run a proper process rather than a distressed one.

For groups, the work is frequently about efficiency rather than survival. Dormant companies still carry filing obligations, director duties and annual cost, even where they qualify for audit exemption. Removing them reduces cost and risk, and that is what corporate simplification does.

Where a sale cannot be arranged in the ordinary way because time has run out, a pre-pack administration can achieve one immediately. It is a legitimate route, and a sale to a connected party within the first eight weeks needs either creditor approval or an independent evaluator's report, precisely because it moves fast.

Why the timing is a legal question, not only a commercial one

Directors owe their duties to the company, and normally that means to the shareholders. Once a company is insolvent or bordering on insolvency, or an insolvent liquidation or administration becomes probable, those duties shift and creditors' interests have to be taken into account. The Supreme Court settled the point in 2022 and was clear that a distant risk of trouble is not enough to engage it: the company has to be at or near the line.

That matters here because it is the same line this whole section is about. Carrying on and hoping, once you knew or should have concluded there was no reasonable prospect of avoiding an insolvent liquidation or administration, is what wrongful trading means, and it can be met with an order to contribute personally. Taking advice, documenting what you decided and why, and acting on it is the practical answer, and it is another reason the date on which you pick up the phone matters more than the sophistication of the plan.

Why the timing matters more than the technique

The single biggest determinant of outcome in this work is when someone picks up the phone. Not the sophistication of the plan, not the size of the adviser, not the finance available. The date.

A company with six months of runway has access to funding, can negotiate with creditors from a position of choice, can sell an asset properly rather than quickly, and can plan a restructuring over a sensible horizon. The same company with six weeks of runway has almost none of that, and the same advisers will be recommending very different things.

Directors delay for understandable reasons: it feels like admitting failure, they expect a big invoice, or they think asking for advice starts something formal. None of those is true of an initial conversation, and the cost of waiting is usually far higher than the cost of asking.

Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We do not take insolvency appointments, which matters more in this section than anywhere else on the site, because it means we have no interest in whether your restructuring succeeds or fails. A firm whose income comes from formal appointments has a quiet incentive that we do not have.

We work alongside your existing accountants rather than replacing them, and we bring in licensed practitioners, lenders or solicitors where a specific piece of work needs them.

Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between restructuring and insolvency?

Restructuring is a set of voluntary changes made while the company still controls its own decisions. Insolvency is a formal statutory procedure, usually involving a licensed practitioner taking an appointment. The practical difference is control: in restructuring you still have it. Many insolvency procedures exist precisely because restructuring was left too late.

Does restructuring mean redundancies?

Sometimes, but not always, and less often than people assume. A restructuring might be entirely financial: renegotiating debt, changing facilities, or improving how working capital is managed. Where headcount is involved it is usually because a specific activity is loss-making rather than because of a general cut.

Will our lender have to know?

In most cases yes, and generally that is to your advantage. Lenders respond considerably better to a director who arrives with a plan than to one who stops communicating. A lender that discovers a problem itself will react more conservatively than one brought into the conversation early.

How long does a restructuring take?

A review to establish the position takes weeks. Implementing the changes takes months, sometimes longer where funding or a sale is involved. What it should never be is instant, and anyone promising a fast structural fix is describing something else.

Can you help if we are already in difficulty?

Yes, and the earlier the better. Even where formal insolvency turns out to be the right answer, going into it with the position properly understood produces a better outcome than arriving at it by default.

Do you work with our existing accountant?

Routinely. Your accountant knows the business and handles the compliance work; we handle the specific restructuring question. Replacing them is rarely in anyone's interest and it is not what we are there for.

CTA block

Not sure whether this is a restructuring problem or something else?

That is exactly what the first conversation is for. It is free, confidential and commits you to nothing.

Breadcrumb: Financial Advisory

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Financial advisory for business

This is corporate financial advice for companies and the people who own them. It is not personal wealth management, it is not pensions advice for individuals, and it is not a sales desk for financial products. If you have arrived looking for an adviser to manage your savings, this is the wrong page. If you run a business and need specialist financial input on a deal, a dispute, a valuation or a funding structure, this is the right one.

Financial advisory sits alongside our insolvency and restructuring work rather than under it. Much of it has nothing to do with distress at all: a founder planning a sale, a company running due diligence on an acquisition, a shareholder dispute that needs an independent expert. It is one of the three areas we advise on in our own name, and we do not refer it out.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Where this fits

Most businesses meet a firm like ours at one of two moments. The first is when something has gone wrong and they need restructuring or insolvency advice. The second is when something significant is being planned or contested, and the numbers need an independent specialist rather than an in-house view. This section is about the second.

The connection between the two is real and worth stating. The same judgement that reads a company's finances in a crisis reads them just as well before a sale, during a dispute, or when a lender wants an independent set of eyes. We work alongside your existing accountant and solicitor, and we are brought in for the specific question rather than to replace anyone.

What financial advisory covers
Corporate finance

Advice on raising money, selling a business, buying one, or valuing shares. The work runs from preparing a company for sale through to negotiating the deal and structuring how it is paid for. This is the highest-value service in the section and the one owners most often plan years ahead. Our corporate finance page covers it in full.

Links: Corporate finance

Forensic services

Independent financial investigation for disputes, litigation and suspected fraud. We quantify loss, trace funds, and produce work that stands up as expert evidence. Solicitors are the usual route in, and the forensic services output has to survive cross-examination rather than merely inform.

Links: Forensic services

Pension advisory

Corporate pension questions rather than personal ones: scheme obligations, how a pension sits inside a transaction, and how deficits are handled in a restructuring or a sale. Pension advisory here means advice to the business and its directors, not retail pension planning, and we are not authorised to give the latter.

Links: Pension advisory

Capital management

Getting the shape of a company's funding right. How much working capital the business actually needs, how the capital structure supports the plan, and where cash is tied up that should not be. Capital management is often the difference between a business that copes and one that keeps hitting the same wall.

Links: Capital management

Transaction support

Due diligence and deal support for buyers and sellers. Checking that a target is what it appears to be, or preparing your own numbers so a buyer's adviser finds nothing that stalls the deal. Transaction support is the work that decides whether a transaction completes on the terms agreed.

Links: Transaction support

Commercial arbitration

Independent input where a commercial dispute turns on financial questions. Valuation disagreements, contract disputes and shareholder fallings-out where an objective financial view helps resolve matters without a full court fight. Commercial arbitration and expert determination both sit here.

Links: Commercial arbitration

Who commissions this work

Three groups tend to bring us in, and the reason matters because it shapes the advice.

  • Owners planning something. A sale, a succession, an acquisition, or a fundraising. These are the calmest and best-prepared instructions, and the ones where good advice changes the outcome most, because there is time to act on it
  • Directors under pressure from a specific event. A dispute, an HMRC enquiry, a lender asking hard questions, a co-owner wanting out. The financial facts need establishing independently before anyone negotiates, and where the company is also under financial strain our restructuring and insolvency practitioner work runs alongside
  • Other professionals. Accountants and solicitors who need a specialist alongside them for a piece of work outside their own remit, and who want someone who will hand the client back rather than keep them

In every case the value is the same: an independent read on the numbers from people who have no product to sell and no incentive to reach a particular answer.

Why independence is the point

A lot of financial advice is attached to something the adviser is selling, whether that is a fund, a loan, or a formal appointment further down the line. Ours is not. We are paid for the advice, and the advice is the whole of it.

That matters most when the honest answer is inconvenient: that a deal is priced wrong, that a dispute is not worth fighting, that a business is worth less than its owner hoped. Advice that costs the adviser nothing to give straight is worth more than advice shaped by what happens next.

How we work with your existing advisers

We are rarely the only firm in the room, and we prefer it that way. Your accountant handles the year-round compliance and knows the business. Your solicitor handles the law. We handle the specific financial question, and we bring in licensed colleagues, valuers or lenders where a particular part of the work needs them.

For funding itself we do not act as a broker. Where a transaction needs new finance we introduce you to a finance and funding specialist we know and trust, and we say plainly when more debt is the wrong answer. Where the answer is to reshape what is already owed, that is debt restructuring, and where an owner is preparing to leave it is exit planning.

Frequently asked questions
Is this personal financial advice?

No. Everything in this section is corporate advice to businesses and their directors. We do not manage personal investments or give regulated retail financial planning advice. Where an owner needs that, we point them to an appropriate regulated adviser. If your question is about a personal debt rather than the company's, our Debt Help Scotland section is the right place, and you can always contact us to be pointed in the right direction.

Do you take the work on yourselves or refer it?

Financial advisory is one of the three areas we deliver in our own name, alongside insolvency and restructuring. We bring in specialist colleagues for specific parts of a job, but the advice is ours. It is our finance and accountancy referrals, not this, that go to third-party firms.

We already have an accountant. Why would we need you?

Because the work here sits outside most general practice remits. Valuing a business for sale, giving evidence in a dispute, or running due diligence on an acquisition are specialist jobs. We do them alongside your accountant, not instead of them.

How quickly can you get involved?

For a planned piece of work such as a sale or a review, we scope it and set a timetable that suits the deal. For a dispute or an enquiry with a deadline, we move at the pace the deadline demands. The first conversation establishes which of those you are in.

What does it cost?

It depends entirely on the work, and we agree the basis before we start rather than after. The first conversation is free and commits you to nothing.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Business finance and funding

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Why we refer instead of sell

A lot of firms that advise businesses in difficulty also earn commission arranging their finance. That arrangement shapes the advice, because a firm paid to place a loan has a reason to recommend one. We took the money out of that decision. We do not broker finance and we hold no lending panel. Where we refer you on, that referral is disclosed, and it does not affect the independence of the advice we have already given you.

What we do instead is tell you honestly whether finance is the right answer at all, and if it is, introduce you to a specialist we know and rate. Sometimes the honest advice is that more borrowing is the wrong medicine, and because we do not arrange the loan either way, we can say so plainly. That is the whole point of keeping this at arm's length.

When funding is the right answer

Used well, finance solves real problems. A profitable business can simply be short of working capital. Cash can be tied up in an unpaid sales ledger, in equipment, or in property, when it could be released and put to work. The right facility, matched to the trading cycle, fixes that without changing anything else about the business.

Used badly, finance postpones a problem and adds cost to it. Borrowing to cover a loss that keeps recurring buys a few months and a larger debt. Part of what an honest introduction gives you is someone who knows the difference and will tell you which one you are looking at. Where the underlying issue is structural rather than a cash-flow gap, the answer sits with restructuring work rather than a new facility.

The kinds of finance we can point you to

These are the facilities the specialist firms we work with arrange. Each page explains what the product is and when it fits. The introduction itself is always to a firm, never a sale by us.

By type
Invoice finance

Releasing cash tied up in unpaid invoices, so money arrives when the work is done rather than when the customer eventually pays.

Links: Invoice finance

Asset finance

Funding against equipment and vehicles, either to buy them or to release the value already sitting in them.

Links: Asset finance

Commercial mortgage

Longer-term borrowing secured on business premises, spreading repayment over a horizon that matches the asset.

Links: Commercial mortgage

Bridging finance

Short-term funding to cover a defined gap, for example between buying and selling, with a clear and realistic exit.

Links: Bridging finance

VAT loans

Spreading a VAT bill over manageable instalments instead of taking a quarterly hit to cash flow.

Links: VAT loans

Unsecured business loans

Borrowing that is not tied to a specific asset, useful for growth or a one-off need where speed matters.

Links: Unsecured business loans

By sector

Some industries fund themselves in particular ways, and a specialist who knows the sector arranges better terms than a generalist. We can introduce you to firms that work in property finance, engineering finance, hospitality finance, contractor finance, sports and entertainment finance and care home finance.

Frequently asked questions
Do you arrange the finance yourselves?

No. We are insolvency and restructuring advisers, not brokers. We introduce you to a trusted specialist firm that arranges the finance. We hold no lending panel and take no commission from lenders.

Do you get paid for the referral?

Our advice to you is not shaped by any payment from a lender. The referral disclosure below sets out the arrangement in plain terms, and it deliberately keeps our core insolvency, restructuring and financial advisory work independent of it.

What if borrowing is the wrong idea?

Then we say so. Because we do not arrange the loan, we have no reason to talk you into one. If the real answer is restructuring, or simply doing nothing yet, that is the advice you will get.

Can you help if we are already in difficulty?

Yes, and that is our core work. Where a business is under real pressure, finance is often not the first move, and we would look at the whole picture with you before anyone talks about a facility. An independent business review establishes the position, and where a formal route is needed the insolvency practitioner page explains who does what. If a personal guarantee is in play, Debt Help Scotland covers your own exposure.

That is worth a conversation before you commit to anything. It is free and confidential, and we do not arrange whatever you decide to take.

Breadcrumb: Accountancy

Eyebrow: Accountancy

Accountants in Glasgow

If you are looking for an accountant in Glasgow, it helps to be clear about what we are. Lancefield is a Glasgow insolvency and restructuring firm. We are not a general accountancy practice, and we do not want to pretend otherwise on a page you found by searching for one.

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs ongoing accountancy support, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What a Glasgow accountant actually does for you

Most businesses need an accountant for the steady, essential work that keeps them compliant and informed. In Glasgow, as anywhere else, that means much the same set of services, and it is worth knowing what you are buying before you choose a firm.

  • Year-end accounts and corporation tax for your limited company, filed with Companies House and HMRC on time
  • Bookkeeping and VAT returns, keeping the day-to-day records straight and the quarterly VAT filed correctly
  • Payroll, so staff and HMRC are paid the right amount on the right date
  • Self assessment for directors, sole traders and partners
  • Management accounts, the monthly or quarterly numbers that tell you how the business is actually doing rather than how it did last year

A good accountant does more than file the paperwork. They tell you what the numbers mean, flag a problem while it is still small, and answer the question before you have to ask it. That relationship is worth choosing carefully, which is why we only refer to a firm we would use ourselves.

Choosing an accountant in Glasgow

A few things separate an accountant who files your accounts from one who genuinely helps the business.

  • They explain, rather than just submit. You should understand your own numbers after a conversation with your accountant, not feel more confused
  • They are proactive on tax. Good advice arrives before the year end, when something can still be done, not after it when nothing can
  • They know small and owner-managed businesses. A practice built around large corporates often serves a small Glasgow company poorly, and the reverse is also true
  • They tell you when something is wrong. The most valuable accountant is the one who says the difficult thing early, which is exactly the standard we hold ourselves to
Where accountancy meets the work we do

There is a point where accountancy shades into our territory, and knowing it is useful whether you are our client or not.

When a business starts missing payments, when HMRC arrears build, or when a director begins worrying about personal guarantees, the question moves beyond routine accountancy. That is the crossover we specialise in. The problem a set of management accounts shows early might later call for a company voluntary arrangement, a formal liquidation, or, where the pressure has reached the director personally, debt help in Scotland. An unpaid tax bill that becomes a winding up petition is far easier to handle months before it is filed than in the week it lands.

Many of our clients arrive through their own accountant, who recognised the warning signs and wanted a restructuring or insolvency specialist alongside them rather than in place of them.

We work with accountants, not against them. If your accountant refers you to us, we handle the specific insolvency or restructuring question and hand you back. If you come to us directly, we keep your accountant in the loop, because they know the business and we do not intend to replace them. For businesses and their owners we also advise in our own name on financial advisory matters such as valuations, disputes and transactions.

If you want to understand how we work before picking up the phone, our about page sets out who we are and the standard we hold ourselves to. When you are ready, contact us and the first conversation is free.

Frequently asked questions
Do you provide accountancy services in Glasgow?

Not day-to-day accountancy. We are an insolvency and restructuring firm. When you need year-end accounts, tax, VAT, payroll or bookkeeping, we refer you to a trusted Glasgow accountancy firm we know well and would use ourselves.

Why refer instead of doing it yourselves?

Because we would rather do one thing properly than several things adequately. Insolvency and restructuring is where our advice carries real weight, and a specialist accountancy firm serves your routine needs better than we would.

My accountant thinks my business is in trouble. Can you help?

Yes, and that is exactly our work. Bring your accountant into the conversation if you can. We handle the insolvency practitioner or restructuring question and work alongside them rather than taking over the relationship. If the pressure is personal as well as commercial, our Debt Help Scotland section covers that side.

Are you based in Glasgow?

Yes. We are a Glasgow firm and much of our work is with businesses across the west of Scotland. The accountancy firm we refer to is local too.

Tell us what you are dealing with. If it is routine accountancy we will point you to a firm we trust. If it is the harder question of debt, cash or director risk, that is what we do. Either way the first conversation is free.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Turnaround

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Business turnaround

A turnaround is the work of fixing an underperforming company while it is still a going concern: finding what is actually causing the problem, stabilising the cash position, and changing the things that made the business lose money in the first place. It is the service that sits furthest from insolvency on this site, and the one that most often makes the rest of it unnecessary.

Most turnaround work starts late. By the time an owner accepts that the pattern is not going to correct itself, they have usually spent a year telling themselves it is a temporary dip. The businesses that recover are rarely the strongest ones. They are the ones that got help while there was still enough liquidity to act.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Is your business a turnaround, or something else?

We take no insolvency appointments, so we have nothing to gain from calling your situation worse than it is, or better. Three honest categories:

Too early

The business is profitable but under strain: growing faster than its working capital allows, or carrying a cost base that has drifted. This is ordinary management improvement and often does not need a turnaround specialist at all. What it may need is a hard look at the numbers, which is what an independent review gives you.

A turnaround

The business is losing money or barely covering its costs, cash is tight, and the causes are structural rather than one-off. There is still a viable business underneath, there are still stakeholders willing to be talked to, and there is enough liquidity to make changes before they run out. This is the page you want.

Past turnaround

The debt is beyond what the business could service even if it performed perfectly, or the market it serves has gone. Change alone will not fix that. What is needed is a company voluntary arrangement to deal with the historic debt, administration to protect and sell what is worth saving, or an orderly winding the company up. Spending six months on a turnaround here consumes the value that would have paid creditors.

Most people arrive convinced they are in the second category. A fair number are in the first or third. Establishing which is the first thing worth paying for, and it takes days rather than months.

What actually causes it

After enough of these, the causes repeat. It is almost never the reason the owner gives first.

  • Margin erosion nobody tracked. Prices held while costs rose. The business is as busy as ever and makes less on every job. This is the single most common cause we see in owner-managed businesses, and the most fixable
  • Working capital swallowed by growth. More sales, more stock, more debtors, and the cash gap widens. A profitable company can run out of money this way and frequently does
  • A cost base built for a bigger business than the one that now exists, or for a market that has moved
  • One customer, one contract or one supplier carrying too much of the risk. When it goes, there is no cushion
  • Management information that arrives too late to act on. Accounts three months in arrears mean every decision is made about a business that no longer exists
  • Debt taken on for the wrong reason, or on terms the business could only service in a good year
  • A problem the owner already knows about and has not addressed, usually because it involves a person

The diagnosis matters because the wrong one is expensive. Cutting costs in a business whose real problem is pricing makes it smaller and no more profitable, and it is the most common wasted year in this work.

The first ninety days

Turnaround work front-loads. What happens in the first three months decides whether there is a business to improve.

  • Stabilise the cash. A weekly short-term cash forecast, built properly and updated every week, replacing the monthly management accounts as the instrument you steer by. Almost every business we work with does not have one when we arrive, and every one of them keeps it afterwards
  • Establish the true position. What the business actually owes, to whom, and when. What it is actually owed and how much of that will really arrive. Where the liquidity is trapped: stock, debtors, work in progress, an overdrawn account nobody has looked at
  • Find the profit by product, customer and job. Not the overall margin. The distribution. There is nearly always a segment losing money that the average conceals, and finding it is often the whole answer
  • Buy time with the people who can grant it. HMRC, the bank, the landlord, key suppliers. Approached early with a credible plan, most will work with you. Approached after a default, most will not
  • Decide what stops. The loss-making line, the customer who never pays, the site that does not work. These decisions get harder the longer they wait and they are the ones owners most want to defer
  • Fix the reporting. Whatever the plan, it needs numbers that arrive within days rather than months. Without that, nobody can tell whether the turnaround is working

Stabilisation is not the same as recovery. It buys the room in which the actual changes can be made, and a plan that stops at stabilisation simply postpones the problem.

Getting the stakeholders to hold

A turnaround is as much a negotiation as an operational exercise, because everyone with a claim on the business can end it while you are still fixing it.

  • The bank or lender. Wants to know that someone competent has their hands on it and that the information is reliable. Lenders support turnarounds far more often than directors expect; what they will not tolerate is being surprised. If yours has commissioned an independent review, that is a signal to engage, not to retreat
  • HMRC. Usually the largest creditor in a struggling small company. Time to Pay is available and is granted on a realistic proposal, but arrears that keep building while other creditors are paid become a conduct issue later
  • Suppliers. Continuity of supply is often the thing the business cannot survive losing. Key suppliers generally prefer a customer that recovers to one that fails owing them money, and will say so if asked honestly
  • Employees. The people who will deliver the changes and the ones who see the wobble first. Uncertainty costs you the staff you can least afford to lose. What you can say may be limited, but silence is read as the worst case
  • Shareholders and family. In an owner-managed business these are often the same people, and the emotional weight of the decisions sits with them

The common thread is that early, honest contact preserves support, and late contact destroys it. That is not a moral observation. It is what we watch happen.

The plan, and making it survive

A turnaround plan is a small number of specific changes with owners, dates and a number attached to each. Anything longer than a page or two is a report rather than a plan, and reports do not change businesses.

What separates the plans that work is that someone is held to them weekly, that the financial performance is measured against the forecast rather than against last year, and that the difficult item is still on the agenda in week three. That is where an outside adviser earns their fee: not for knowing what needs doing, which the owner usually does, but for making sure it happens and for saying the thing everyone in the business is avoiding.

Where the numbers show the plan is not working, the plan changes or the route changes. A turnaround that misses its targets month after month is consuming the value that other options would have preserved, and knowing when to stop is part of the discipline.

Trading on while insolvent: the line to watch

This is the part that generic turnaround advice leaves out, and it matters more than any of the commercial work.

If the company is or becomes unable to pay its debts, a director's duties shift towards the interests of creditors. Continuing to trade past the point where insolvent liquidation or administration could no longer realistically be avoided, with the creditors worse off as a result, is wrongful trading, and it can carry personal liability.

That does not mean a turnaround is dangerous. It means a turnaround needs a documented basis: a plan that a reasonable director could believe in, contemporaneous evidence of the advice taken and the reasoning applied, and a review point at which you will stop if it is not working. Directors who do that are in a materially stronger position than those who simply pressed on, and our contingency planning page covers how to build the fallback alongside the plan.

The practical rule: take advice at the point when you first wonder whether you should, not at the point when someone tells you that you must.

When a turnaround needs something formal alongside it

Operational change fixes the future. It does not remove what the company already owes, and where the historic debt is the binding constraint, the commercial work needs a formal instrument beside it.

  • Debt restructuring where the borrowing is serviceable on different terms: reprofiled repayments, consolidated facilities, or new money on a realistic basis
  • A CVA where the debt is beyond renegotiation but the trading business is sound. It binds the whole unsecured creditor body to a repayment plan and leaves the directors in control
  • Administration, where the business needs protection from creditors while the change is made or a sale arranged
  • A pre-pack administration, where the trade is viable but the company is not, and the value would be lost in a public process

Running the commercial turnaround and the formal route in parallel is normal and often the best outcome. What does not work is doing the operational work for a year first and reaching the formal conversation with the value already spent.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your administrator or liquidator, so we have no interest in a turnaround failing and no reason to recommend a formal procedure that would generate a fee for us.

What we do is establish quickly whether there is a viable business under the problem, tell you honestly which of the three categories at the top of this page you are in, and then either do the work with you or tell you it is not needed. Where a licensed appointment is genuinely required, we bring in an insolvency practitioner we know and trust and stay alongside you through it.

We work with owner-managed businesses across Scotland, in the sectors where this comes up most: hospitality and leisure, construction and the supply chain around it. Big Four restructuring experience, applied at a scale where the owner is in the room.

Frequently asked questions
How long does a turnaround take?

Stabilisation is usually the first ninety days. Genuine recovery, meaning a business that is reliably profitable again rather than merely surviving, is more often twelve to eighteen months. Anyone promising a faster structural change is describing cost-cutting, which is not the same thing.

What does turnaround support cost?

It depends entirely on scope: a diagnostic review is a fixed fee and modest, while hands-on implementation over months is not. We scope and price it before starting, and we will tell you if the likely benefit does not justify the cost.

Will the bank find out we have taken advice?

Not from us. Advice is confidential and nothing is filed or published. In practice, though, telling a lender you have brought in specialist support usually helps rather than harms: it is evidence that the problem is being managed, which is what they want to see.

Can a turnaround work if we already owe HMRC?

Frequently, yes. HMRC arrears are the norm in this work rather than the exception, and Time to Pay is available on a realistic proposal. What causes the damage is arrears that keep growing while other creditors are paid, because that becomes a conduct question in any later insolvency.

What if it does not work?

Then you find that out with more options open than you would have had otherwise, and with a documented record of having acted responsibly. That is why the review points and the fallback plan matter. A turnaround that fails having been properly run leaves a director in a very different position from one that simply drifted.

Is this the same as an insolvency process?

No. A turnaround is a commercial exercise in an ongoing business, with no court, no appointment, no publicity and no register entry. It can run alongside a formal procedure where the historic debt needs dealing with, but by itself it is simply management change with outside help.

CTA block

Is there a viable business underneath the problem?

We take no appointments, so we have no stake in the answer. One conversation will tell you whether this is a turnaround, something smaller, or something that needs a different route.

  • Compliance: we are advisers, not brokers or lenders. Must not read as regulated credit broking. Where new money is needed we introduce, we do not arrange. No promises that lenders will agree.
