Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Debt Restructuring

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Debt restructuring

Corporate debt restructuring means changing what a company owes, or when and how it repays, so that the financial obligations match what the business can actually generate. It covers everything from reprofiling a single loan to a full renegotiation across several lenders, and it is the right answer where the trading business works but the borrowing on top of it does not. Some of it is balance sheet restructuring; most of it, in an owner-managed company, is simpler than that.

The question that decides whether debt restructuring will succeed is simple, and it is worth asking before anything else. Is this a company that can service its borrowing on different terms, or one that cannot service it at all? Restructuring solves the first. It only postpones the second, and postponing costs money that would otherwise have gone to creditors.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

When restructuring is the right answer

We take no insolvency appointments and we are not brokers, so we are not paid by the outcome. The honest test has three parts.

  • The business is viable on its own terms. Strip out the debt service and the company makes money, or would within a reasonable period. If it does not, the problem is the trade and a turnaround comes first
  • The borrowing is serviceable on some realistic profile. A longer loan term, a lower interest rate, a payment holiday, interest-only for a period, or a smaller principal after a partial repayment. If no realistic profile works, the answer is a CVA, administration or a liquidation, and the question becomes an insolvency one rather than a refinancing one
  • The lenders have a reason to say yes. A lender agrees to a restructuring plan when it expects to recover more that way than by enforcing. Your job, and ours, is to show that arithmetic honestly, with a cash flow that supports it

Where all three hold, restructuring is usually achievable and often undramatic. Where the third fails because the security covers the debt comfortably, expect a harder conversation: a lender that is fully covered has less to lose from enforcing.

The options, and what each is actually for
Reprofiling the repayments

Extending the loan term, moving to interest-only for a period, or agreeing a payment holiday. The cheapest and most common form of debt management, and the one most often agreed, because the lender keeps its principal and its security and simply waits longer. It suits a company with a temporary cash flow squeeze and a credible recovery, and it is where most debt restructuring in owner-managed businesses begins and ends.

Consolidation and refinancing

Replacing several facilities with one, or moving to a different lender on a better interest rate. Debt consolidation simplifies the covenants and often reduces the monthly cost, but consolidation does not reduce what is owed. Where refinancing is the route, we introduce you to a finance and funding specialist rather than acting as broker ourselves.

Releasing trapped working capital

Often the fastest improvement available and frequently missed. Invoice finance against the debtor book, asset finance against plant already owned, or a sale and leaseback of property. It changes the shape of the balance sheet rather than the size of the debt, and it can create the room a restructuring needs.

Debt for equity

Debt-for-equity swaps exchange some of what a lender is owed for a shareholding. A debt-for-equity swap removes borrowing permanently and is standard practice in larger restructurings, but it dilutes the owner and is rare in owner-managed businesses because the creditor rarely wants the shares. Worth knowing about; worth being realistic about.

A negotiated write-down

A creditor accepts less than the full amount to settle. It happens, usually where the alternative is demonstrably worse for them, and it needs evidence rather than argument. Informally agreed write-downs bind only the creditors who sign, which is their limitation.

A formal arrangement

Where the unsecured creditor body is too large or too fragmented to negotiate with individually, a CVA binds all of them to a repayment plan once 75% by value approve it and a majority of the unconnected creditors do not vote it down. It is the instrument for exactly the situation informal restructuring cannot reach.

HMRC, and why it is different

In most owner-managed companies HMRC is the largest creditor, and it does not behave like a bank.

Time to Pay is a genuine and widely granted arrangement, but it is a payment plan rather than a restructuring of the debt: HMRC expects the full amount, and expects you to keep filing and paying current taxes, or to come back and ask for a new bill to be added to the plan. A proposal that assumes a write-down of tax is not a proposal HMRC will engage with, and a second Time to Pay arrangement after a first one failed is a much harder conversation than the first.

What causes lasting damage is letting arrears of taxes build while other creditors are paid. Beyond the immediate risk of enforcement, it is exactly the kind of conduct an insolvency practitioner has to report on if the company later fails, and it is treated as a conduct issue rather than a commercial one.

What lenders actually agree to

We sit on both sides of these conversations, and the pattern is consistent.

  • They will extend time far more readily than they will reduce principal. Time costs them margin. A write-down costs them capital and has to be justified internally
  • They want reliable information, presented once. A short-term cash flow forecast, a realistic set of assumptions, and an explanation of what went wrong that does not blame the weather. Borrowers routinely underestimate how much credibility a well-built cash flow buys
  • They will commission their own view. An independent business review is the normal step for anything material, and it is a signal to engage rather than to panic. The review establishes the facts everyone then negotiates around
  • They want to see the equity contribute. Where owners are asking a lender to wait, lenders ask what the shareholders are putting in. Sometimes that is money; more often it is deferred remuneration, a director's loan left in place, or a personal guarantee
  • They will not restructure into a loss. If enforcing recovers more than waiting, they enforce, and the conversation turns into an insolvency one. Where a lender holds a fixed charge over property, that may mean an LPA receivership in England and Wales or enforcement of a standard security in Scotland
  • They move faster on a live default than on a warning. Approach before the covenant breaks, not after

None of that is unreasonable, and understanding it changes how the proposal is written. Most failed restructurings we see failed on presentation rather than on substance.

The restructuring process

The restructuring process is the same whether one lender is involved or five, and it runs in a set order.

  • Establish the real position. Total borrowing, interest rate and loan term on each facility, security, covenants, personal guarantees. What is secured on what, and in what order. Directors frequently do not have this in one place, and it is where the work starts
  • Build the forecast. Weekly short-term cash flow, and a longer projection showing what the business can service. It has to survive a lender's scrutiny, so the assumptions matter more than the presentation
  • Identify what is achievable. Which of the restructuring options above fit the facts, what each would deliver, and which lenders and other stakeholders need to agree to what
  • Prepare the proposal. One document, consistent across every lender, showing the position, the plan and what each creditor is being asked for. Different stories to different lenders is the fastest way to lose the room
  • Negotiate. Usually several rounds with the stakeholders in turn. Secured lenders first, since their consent frequently conditions everyone else's
  • Document it. Amended facility agreements, new security, waivers, standstill agreements. This is solicitors' work and it is not the place to economise
  • Monitor and report. Restructured facilities come with tighter reporting and covenants. Meeting them is what keeps the arrangement alive

Timescales for the restructuring process run from a few weeks for a single-lender reprofiling to several months where there are multiple secured creditors, pension obligations or a formal arrangement involved.

What it means for you as a director

Two things to be clear-eyed about.

First, personal guarantees normally survive a restructuring unless the lender expressly releases them, and lenders rarely do. That matters most on unsecured business loans, where the guarantee is often the only security the lender has. If anything, a restructuring is the moment a lender asks for more security rather than less. Establish what you have already guaranteed before you negotiate, because it changes what you should be willing to agree to. Where a guarantee is called, that becomes a personal matter and our Debt Help Scotland section covers the options.

Second, restructuring while insolvent carries the same duties as trading while insolvent. If the company is or becomes unable to pay its debts, your duties shift towards creditors as a whole, and a restructuring that a reasonable director could not have believed in is not a defence. Take advice, document the basis of the plan, and set a review point at which you stop. Our contingency planning page covers building the fallback in parallel, which is what turns a restructuring attempt into a reasoned decision rather than a gamble.

When restructuring is the wrong answer

It is worth saying plainly, because nobody else on this subject does.

  • Where the borrowing could never be repaid on any realistic profile. Debt restructuring here buys months and spends the value that would have gone to creditors, and the honest answer is insolvency advice
  • Where the trade itself has stopped working. New terms on the borrowing do not fix a business that loses money before debt service
  • Where the only new money available is expensive short-term borrowing taken to service existing debt. This is the most common route from a difficult position to an impossible one
  • Where a single creditor can and will enforce regardless. If a winding up petition is coming, the timetable is no longer yours and the winding up petition page is the more urgent read

In each of those, the better outcomes come from the formal insolvency routes: a CVA, administration, or an orderly liquidation while there is still something to distribute.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments and does not lend or broker. Nobody here earns a commission on a facility or a fee from an appointment, which means we have no interest in your restructuring being bigger, faster or more formal than it needs to be.

What we do is establish what the company can genuinely service, build the case, and put it to your lenders in a form they can say yes to. Where the honest answer is that the debt cannot be restructured into something serviceable, we say so early, while the alternatives are still worth having. Where new money is the answer, we introduce a specialist rather than arranging it ourselves.

We advise lenders and other creditors too, which is the reason we can tell you in advance what yours is likely to accept.

Frequently asked questions
What is corporate debt restructuring?

It means changing the terms of what a company owes so that repayment fits what the business generates. That can mean a longer loan term, a lower interest rate, a payment holiday, debt consolidation, debt-for-equity swaps, or a negotiated reduction. It is agreed with creditors rather than imposed, which is the difference between it and a formal insolvency procedure.

Will my lender agree?

A lender agrees when it expects to recover more by agreeing than by enforcing. That makes it an evidence question rather than a persuasion one. Reliable forecasts, an honest account of what went wrong, and a plan the numbers support are what move it. A lender that is fully covered by its security has less reason to wait, and that is worth knowing before you start.

Does restructuring damage the company's credit rating?

Renegotiated terms, missed payments and any formal arrangement are visible to credit reference agencies, and a supplier who checks the company's credit score will see it. That is a real cost and worth weighing. It is a smaller cost than a default or an insolvency procedure, which is the comparison that matters.

Can I restructure a bounce back loan or a CBILS facility?

Sometimes. Those facilities carry a government guarantee to the lender, which changes the lender's incentives and limits what it can agree to unilaterally. Pay As You Grow options exist on bounce back loans. Ask the lender what flexibility the scheme rules leave it, because the answer differs by product and by bank.

How long does it take?

A single-lender reprofiling of the loan term can be agreed in weeks. A multi-creditor debt restructuring with security to redocument runs to several months. The timetable is usually set by whichever lender is slowest to commit, and by how long it takes to produce information they trust.

What is the difference between this and a CVA?

Debt restructuring is consensual and binds only the creditors who agree to it. A CVA is a formal procedure under the insolvency legislation, and it binds every unsecured creditor once 75% by value approve it, provided more than half the unconnected creditors do not vote against. Where a handful of creditors can be negotiated with, restructure. Where there are too many, or one refuses to move, the formal route reaches further.

CTA block

Is the borrowing serviceable on different terms?

We take no appointments, and we neither broker nor arrange facilities, so the answer you get is the one the numbers support. One conversation will tell you whether a restructuring is achievable and what your lenders are likely to accept.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Exit Planning

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Optimised exit planning

Exit planning is the work of getting a business ready to leave: deciding which route out fits, then spending the time before the exit making the company worth more to whoever takes it on, or making a closure orderly rather than forced. Every owner exits eventually. The difference between a planned exit and an unplanned one is usually measured in years of preparation and a substantial share of the value.

The uncomfortable part is that most owner-managed businesses are not saleable in the form their owner imagines. Not because they are bad businesses, but because they depend on the owner, or the numbers do not evidence what the owner knows to be true, or there is no obvious buyer for that size of company in that sector. All three are fixable with enough notice. None is fixable in the last six months.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

The routes out

There are five, and the honest work is establishing which of them your business actually supports rather than which one you had in mind.

Trade sale

Selling to a competitor, a supplier, a customer or a consolidator. Usually the highest price, because a trade buyer can strip out duplicated cost and buys market share as well as profit. It is also the most intrusive process: full due diligence, warranties, and a buyer who will know everything about the business before completion.

Sale to a financial buyer

Private equity or an investment company. Realistic for businesses above a certain scale and profitability, and usually structured so that some of the price depends on future performance. Owners frequently stay on for a period, which is either the attraction or the problem depending on the owner.

Management buyout

Selling to the management team, often funded partly by the business itself over time. The price is normally lower than a trade sale but the process is faster, more private, and the business continues in familiar hands. It works where there is a management team capable of running it without you, which is the same thing that makes a trade sale easier.

Family succession

Passing the business to the next generation. The financial questions are the easy part; governance, fairness between family members who are in the business and those who are not, and whether the successor actually wants it are the hard ones. Started early it works well. Assumed rather than planned, it is how family businesses fail.

Solvent closure

Where there is no buyer, or where the business is genuinely the owner and does not survive without them, the right answer is to stop while the company is solvent, pay everyone in full, and take the reserves out as capital through an MVL. This is a legitimate and frequently optimal exit, not a failure, and it is the route the rest of the internet does not discuss.

A sixth route exists and is worth naming so nobody drifts into it: running the business until it stops. That is not an exit, and it converts a solvent closure into an insolvent one.

Why the work starts years ahead

The value of a business at exit is set long before the exit, by things that take time to change.

  • Owner dependence. If the customer relationships, the technical knowledge and the decisions all sit with you, a buyer is not buying a business, they are buying a job with your name on it. Building a management layer takes two to three years and is the single largest lever on price
  • The quality of the numbers. Buyers pay for evidenced profit, not explained profit. Clean management accounts, a defensible normalisation of the owner's remuneration and personal costs, and a couple of years of consistency are worth more than a good story
  • Customer concentration. One customer at forty per cent of revenue takes a visible chunk off the multiple, and diversifying takes years
  • Contracts and recurring revenue. Repeatable income is valued far above the same profit earned project by project. Where the business can be moved towards contracts, that shift is worth doing before the sale rather than describing during it
  • The awkward items. A property in the company that a buyer does not want, a related-party arrangement, dormant subsidiaries, a pension advisory issue, unresolved litigation. Each is a discount or a delay at due diligence, and each takes months to tidy. Corporate simplification deals with the group-structure half of that
  • Your own position. What you need from the exit, what you will do afterwards, and how long you are prepared to stay. Owners who have not answered these negotiate badly

Two to three years is the usual horizon for material improvement. A year is enough to tidy and prepare. Under six months, you are selling what you have.

What the business is actually worth

Most owner-managed businesses are valued on a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted for what a new owner would really face: your remuneration replaced with a market-rate manager, one-off items stripped out, and any personal costs removed. That adjusted figure is usually lower than the profit an owner has in mind and higher than the one their accounts show, which is why the first honest valuation conversation is often uncomfortable.

The multiple applied depends on things a buyer can see rather than things you can assert: sector, scale, growth, recurring revenue, customer spread, and how much of the business walks out with you. Two companies with the same profit can be worth very different amounts, and the gap between them is exactly what exit planning is for.

The structure matters as much as the headline. Cash at completion, deferred consideration, an earn-out tied to future performance, shares in the buyer, a period of consultancy. A high price mostly payable later, conditional on results you no longer control, is not the same as the number in the press release. Our corporate finance and transaction support pages cover the deal side.

Preparing the business
  • Build the management layer. Delegate genuinely, including the customer relationships. The test is whether the business runs for a month without you
  • Fix the reporting. Monthly management accounts that arrive within a fortnight and reconcile to the year end. Buyers discount uncertainty and this is where uncertainty shows
  • Normalise the accounts. Take the personal costs out, document the adjustments, and let a couple of clean years accumulate before you go to market
  • Sort the balance sheet. Deal with the director's loan account, the property, the dormant subsidiaries and the old assets. Anything a buyer has to ask about is a negotiating point for them
  • Secure what you are selling. Written customer contracts, employment contracts for key staff, registered intellectual property, a lease with enough term left
  • Prepare for due diligence early. Assemble the information a buyer's advisers will want before you need it. Deals fall over on delay and surprises far more often than on price

Almost all of this improves the business whether you sell or not, which is why it is worth doing even where the exit is uncertain.

Tax, and the point of getting it right early

How an exit is structured determines how it is taxed, and the decisions that matter are made before a deal is agreed rather than after. Selling shares and selling the trade and assets produce very different outcomes for the seller. Business Asset Disposal Relief has qualifying conditions that must be met for a period before the disposal, so eligibility is something to check years ahead rather than assume at completion. Where the exit is a solvent closure, the distribution comes out as capital through a liquidation and there is a separate set of rules, covered on our MVL page.

We are not tax advisers and this page is not tax advice. What we do is make sure the tax question is asked at the point when the answer can still change, and work alongside your accountant so that the structure and the tax position are decided together rather than sequentially.

When the honest answer is that there is no buyer

A meaningful share of owner-managed businesses cannot be sold at any price the owner would accept. The business is the owner, or the sector has no acquirers at that scale, or the profit does not survive replacing the owner's labour at market rate.

That is not a failure and it is not the end of the planning. It changes the objective: instead of maximising a sale price, you are maximising what the business generates between now and closure, and then closing it while it is solvent so the accumulated reserves come out efficiently. Done deliberately, that is frequently worth more than a distressed sale would have been, and it is entirely within your control.

What makes it go wrong is deciding too late. A business run past the point where it can pay its own way turns a solvent closure into an insolvent one, and the difference between an MVL and a creditors' voluntary liquidation is the whole of the owner's remaining value plus an investigation into their conduct.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments and sells no investment or wealth-management products. Nobody here earns a commission on what you do with the proceeds, and nobody becomes your liquidator.

That matters on this subject more than most, because the exit-planning field is largely populated by advisers whose interest begins after the money arrives. Ours does not. We are paid for the advice about the business, which means we can tell you the company is not saleable in its present form, or that the right exit is an orderly closure rather than the sale you were hoping for.

We work alongside your accountant and, where a sale is the route, corporate finance advisers who run the process. Where the exit is a solvent liquidation we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner to take the appointment. And where an independent review shows the business needs work before it is ready for either, we say so.

Frequently asked questions
How long before an exit should I start planning?

Two to three years for material improvement in what the business is worth, because the biggest levers all take that long: reducing owner dependence, evidencing profit, and spreading customer risk. A year is enough to tidy up and prepare properly. Below six months you are selling the business as it stands.

What is my business worth?

Usually a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted for a market-rate replacement for you and stripped of one-off and personal items. The multiple depends on sector, scale, recurring revenue, customer concentration and how much of the business depends on the owner. Any figure quoted without those adjustments is a guess.

Should I tell my staff?

Not at the beginning, and not all at once. Key management usually need to know before a sale process starts, particularly if a buyout is a possibility or if they will be asked to meet a buyer. The rest of the team normally hears at or near completion. Confidentiality agreements and a controlled sequence are part of the planning.

What if I want to stay involved?

That is a legitimate objective and it shapes which route fits. Financial buyers often want the owner to stay; trade buyers frequently do not want them for long; a management buyout can be structured with a phased handover. Deciding what you actually want before you go to market is what stops it being decided for you.

Is closing the business a failure?

No. Where there is no buyer, closing a solvent company and taking the reserves out as capital is often the best available outcome and entirely respectable. What is a failure is running past the point of solvency and losing the choice.

Do I need a corporate finance adviser as well?

For a trade sale or a private equity deal, yes, and we work with them. Exit planning is the years of preparation before the process; corporate finance is running the process itself. For a management buyout or a solvent closure the requirement is lighter, and often the accountant and ourselves are enough.

CTA block

Is the business ready for the exit you have in mind?

We take no appointments and sell no products, so we have no stake in which route you take. One conversation will tell you what the business would realistically fetch, what would move that, and how long it needs.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Independent Business Review

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Independent business review

An independent business review, universally shortened to IBR, is an objective assessment of whether a business is viable and what its realistic prospects are. It is usually commissioned by a lender, normally paid for by the borrower, and produced by a firm that reports to the lender. If yours has just asked for one, that combination is the first thing to get straight, because it explains everything about how the process feels.

The second thing to get straight is what it means. Being asked for an IBR is not the bank calling in the debt. It is the bank saying it no longer has enough information to be comfortable and wants an independent view before it decides anything. That is a moment of risk, but it is also the point at which a well-handled business gets more time rather than less.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Why your lender has asked for one

Something has changed in how the bank sees the account. Common triggers, in rough order of frequency:

  • A covenant breach, or a forecast that shows one coming
  • A facility approaching renewal where the numbers no longer support automatic rollover
  • Late or unreliable information. Management accounts that arrive months in arrears, or that do not reconcile to the statutory accounts, generate more anxiety than bad numbers delivered on time
  • A material change in performance: a loss, a big customer gone, margins visibly compressing
  • A request for more money, particularly if the last projection was missed
  • A move to the bank's business support or restructuring team, which almost always precedes a request for a review
  • Sector risk, where the lender is reviewing a whole book rather than singling you out. That is the moment a contingency planning exercise earns its keep, because you can see it coming

The trigger matters, because it tells you what the reviewer will be asked to focus on. A lender worried about a covenant wants to know about headroom and forecast reliability. One worried about a sector wants to know how exposed you are relative to peers.

What an IBR actually looks at

Scope varies with the lender's concern, but the core is consistent.

  • The current financial position, verified rather than accepted. Real cash, real debtors, real creditors, real stock, and what the balance sheet does not show
  • Short-term cash. A thirteen-week cash forecast is the standard instrument, and the reviewer will test its assumptions rather than take them
  • The integrity of the forecasts. Not whether they are optimistic, which they usually are, but whether the assumptions behind them are defensible and whether previous forecasts were met
  • The business model and market. Where the profit comes from by product, customer and contract, and whether that is durable
  • Management. Whether the team has the information, the capability and the willingness to act. Reviewers form a view on this and it carries real weight
  • The funding structure. What is owed to whom, on what security, and whether the facilities fit the business
  • Options. What could be done: turnaround measures, debt restructuring, asset sales, new equity, or a formal procedure
  • Downside. What the lender would recover in an insolvency, usually with an estimated outcome statement comparing scenarios

That last item is the one directors find hardest to see in a document about their own business. It is standard, it is in every IBR, and its presence does not mean anyone has decided anything.

Who sees it, and who pays

The lender commissions it and is the reviewer's client. The borrower almost always pays, under the facility terms that oblige the company to meet the lender's professional costs. The report goes to the lender. You will usually see it, and you should always ask to, but you are not entitled to it as of right unless the engagement says so.

That arrangement feels wrong the first time. It is standard across the industry and it is not a trap: the reviewer's value to the lender depends entirely on being independent, which means they are not simply writing what the bank wants to hear. A reviewer who produces an unbalanced report is worth nothing to the bank the next time.

What you can influence is the scope. Before it starts, ask what the terms of reference are, whether you will receive the report, and whether you will have the chance to comment on factual accuracy before it is issued. Reasonable lenders agree to all three.

How to come out of one well

This is the part no other page on the subject covers, and it makes a material difference.

  • Cooperate fully and quickly. Delay and reluctance are read as concealment, and the reviewer will say so in the report. Nothing costs a director more credibility
  • Get your own numbers straight first. If you can, produce the thirteen-week cash forecast before the reviewer asks. Arriving with it says more about management quality than anything you can assert
  • Do not present the optimistic case. Reviewers test forecasts for a living and an unrealistic one destroys trust in everything else you say. A conservative forecast that is then beaten is worth far more than an ambitious one that is missed
  • Have your own plan. A director who can set out what they intend to do, with numbers attached, changes the report. A director waiting to be told what to do also changes it
  • Bring your own adviser. You are entitled to advice on your side of this. Somebody who has written IBRs knows what the reviewer is testing and what a good answer looks like
  • Do not hide the bad item. It will be found, and being found is much worse than being told

The consistent pattern: reviewers are not looking for a perfect business. They are looking for management that understands its own position and is acting on it. That is what they report on, and it is largely within your control even when the numbers are not.

What happens afterwards

The lender takes a decision, and the realistic range is narrower than most directors fear.

  • Continued support, unchanged. Common where the review shows a viable business with a temporary problem
  • Support with conditions. Tighter covenants, more frequent reporting, a monitoring role for the reviewer, or specific actions with deadlines. This is the most common outcome
  • A restructuring of the facilities. Reprofiled repayments, a new term, sometimes additional security. Our debt restructuring page covers what lenders typically agree to
  • A requirement to raise money or sell something. New equity, an asset disposal, or a sale of the business, usually with a timetable attached
  • Withdrawal of support. The rarest outcome, and one lenders reach reluctantly because enforcing usually recovers less than waiting. Where it happens, our administration and liquidation pages set out what follows

A properly conducted IBR frequently helps the borrower, because it replaces the lender's anxiety with information. Businesses with a real problem and credible management come out of reviews with more time more often than not.

Pre-lend reviews, and commissioning one yourself

The same discipline is used at two other moments.

A pre-lend review is commissioned before a lender advances money rather than after it worries about it: the same testing of forecasts, model and management, applied to a proposal. Borrowers who go through one and are approved get better terms than they would have had, because the lender is pricing less uncertainty.

And a director can commission a review for their own purposes, which is the version we most often recommend. Where you suspect a problem but are not sure of its size, an independent assessment gives you the facts before your lender asks for them, on your terms and with the report addressed to you. It is also the natural first step if you are considering an exit, since it establishes what a buyer's adviser will find. Our exit planning page picks that up.

Where we fit

We do this work from both sides, and we are explicit about which side we are on in any engagement.

For lenders and other creditors, we conduct reviews: independent, evidenced and delivered on a timetable, with a clear view on viability and options rather than a description of the position. The wider restructuring section sets out what happens next in each direction.

For directors, we advise on the other side of the table. What the reviewer will test, how to prepare, what to have ready, how to respond to a draft, and what to do with the outcome. Because we take no insolvency appointments, we have no interest in the review concluding that a formal procedure is needed.

We do not act for both parties on the same engagement, and we say at the outset which role we are in.

Frequently asked questions
Does an IBR mean the bank is calling in our facility?

No. It means the bank wants an independent view before deciding anything. Withdrawal of support is the least common outcome, because enforcing typically recovers less than continuing to lend to a business that recovers. The review is the step before a decision, not the decision.

Do we have to pay for it?

Almost always, under the facility terms that require the borrower to meet the lender's professional costs. It is worth asking for a fee estimate and a defined scope before it starts, and reasonable lenders will provide both.

Do we get to see the report?

Usually, but ask at the outset rather than at the end. The reviewer's client is the lender, so disclosure to you is a matter for the engagement terms. You should also ask for the chance to comment on factual accuracy before it is issued, which is normal and which most lenders agree to.

Can we choose who does it?

Typically the lender selects from firms it knows, though it will often accept a suggestion. What you can influence more usefully is the scope and the timetable.

How long does it take?

For an owner-managed business, usually two to four weeks from instruction to draft, depending on the state of the information. Poor management information is the single biggest cause of delay, and delay costs credibility as well as money.

Should we get our own advice?

Yes. The reviewer is not your adviser and cannot be. Having someone on your side who has written these reports changes how well you prepare and how the report reads, and it costs a fraction of the review itself. Contact us before the reviewer arrives rather than after the draft lands.

CTA block

Has your lender asked for a review?

We conduct these for lenders and we advise directors going through them, and we tell you at the outset which side we are on. One conversation will tell you what the reviewer will test and how to be ready for it.

Verified 2026-08-22. The tax claims are the ones verified in full on the MVL page; the Companies Act claims were verified directly and three of them were wrong:

1. "Annual accounts for every entity, every year, regardless of dormancy" is not right. CA 2006 ss.394A and 448A exempt a dormant subsidiary, and it is a group exemption, so it applies to precisely the reader this page addresses. The commercial argument survives because the exemption is bought with a parent guarantee of the subsidiary's liabilities.

2. The late-filing penalty falls on the company, not the directors. s.453 makes the company liable to the civil penalty; s.451 makes each director's default a criminal offence. What lands on a name is a conviction, not the penalty. As drafted the sentence would have been picked apart by any accountant.

3. "A single transaction breaks dormancy" is not the statutory test. s.1169(3) expressly disregards several transactions, including the confirmation statement fee.

Also strengthened: administrative restoration is unavailable after a voluntary strike-off, so the court is categorically the only route back; and the Crown representative for Scottish property is the KLTR, not the Bona Vacantia Division.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Corporate Simplification

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Corporate simplification

Corporate simplification is the removal of dormant companies, redundant entities and duplicated ones from a group structure. Most organisations accumulate them without deciding to: an acquisition brings three subsidiaries with it, a trading name gets its own company, a joint venture ends but the entity does not, a property is held separately for reasons nobody can now recall. Each one carries filing obligations, professional fees, directors' duties and a small amount of risk, indefinitely, in return for nothing.

The work is straightforward and the benefit to the organisation is durable: lower costs, simpler corporate governance, and a group structure a lender or a buyer can follow. What makes it worth doing properly rather than quickly is the choice of how each company is closed, because the wrong route on a company holding reserves is expensive in a way that is difficult to reverse.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What each dormant company actually costs you

Owners consistently underestimate this, because no single item is large.

  • Compliance costs. A confirmation statement for every entity, every year, whether or not it does anything, and accounts too unless the entity qualifies as an exempt dormant subsidiary. That exemption is bought by the parent guaranteeing the subsidiary's liabilities, which is rarely free. Then the finance team's time and the accountancy fee on top
  • Directors' duties. Every company needs directors, and those directors carry statutory duties to a company they have probably not thought about since 2019. That is a corporate governance exposure as much as an administrative one. Filing defaults attract a civil penalty against the company and a criminal offence against every director in default, and it is the conviction rather than the penalty that lands on the public record against a name
  • Risk that does not expire. Old trading liabilities, dilapidations on a lease nobody cancelled, warranties given on a disposal, a guarantee the group forgot it gave. A dormant company is not a closed one, claims can be brought against it, and if one of them cannot be met the entity is heading for a creditors' voluntary liquidation rather than a tidy closure
  • Audit and consolidation drag. More entities means more group reporting, more intercompany reconciliation, and more work for the finance team at every year end
  • Deal friction. In due diligence on a sale, a buyer's advisers examine every company in the group. Each dormant entity is a set of questions, a warranty and a potential retention. This is where the real cost lands, and it is why the tidy-up belongs in exit planning rather than after it
  • Trapped value. Reserves sitting in a subsidiary that could be in the shareholders' hands

Individually, small. Across fifteen entities over ten years, a material and entirely avoidable running cost for the business.

The decision that matters: strike-off or solvent liquidation

There are two ways to close a solvent company, and choosing between them is the whole of this exercise for any entity holding money.

Strike-off

An application to Companies House to dissolve the company. Cheap, simple, and the right answer for a genuinely empty entity. Its limit is tax: a distribution before strike-off is treated as capital only up to £25,000 in total, and only if the company is actually dissolved within two years and its debts and receivables have been settled. A pound over, or a dissolution that does not happen in time, and the whole amount is taxed as income, not just the excess, retrospectively if need be. A creditor can also object during the two-month Gazette period, and the registrar will not strike the company off while a valid objection stands.

Members' voluntary liquidation

A formal solvent liquidation conducted by a licensed insolvency practitioner. It costs more and takes longer, and in return the whole distribution is treated as capital however large it is, subject to the anti-phoenixing rule that recharacterises it as income where the shareholder carries on a similar trade within two years and tax avoidance was a main purpose, the company's affairs are formally closed off with a liquidator's final account, and creditors are dealt with properly rather than left to object. Our MVL page covers it in full.

The practical rule across a group: strike off the genuinely empty entities, and put anything holding reserves above the threshold through an MVL. Our liquidation page sets out how the solvent and insolvent routes differ. Getting that wrong on a single subsidiary can cost more than the whole simplification project. Note also that the twelve-month statutory test for solvency applies to each company separately, so each entity is assessed on its own position rather than the group's.

How the work runs
  • Map the group structure. Every entity, its status, its accounts, what it owns and owes, who its directors are, and whether it is actually dormant or merely quiet. The management team is regularly surprised by what this turns up
  • Decide what each company is for. Anything with a business purpose stays. Every other entity is a candidate, and the burden is on keeping it rather than closing it
  • Do the diligence before closing. Intercompany balances, guarantees given, leases, contracts with change-of-control or dissolution clauses, pension participation, VAT group membership, registered intellectual property, and any bank account or asset still in that company's name. This diligence is the whole of the risk, and it is where a rushed project goes wrong
  • Deal with the assets. Transfer intellectual property, property and contracts to the entity that should hold them, settle intercompany balances, and distribute or transfer cash. Intra-group transfers have tax consequences and this is where your accountant earns their fee
  • Choose the route per entity. Strike-off or MVL, decided on the numbers rather than by default
  • Execute and close. Strike-off applications, or an MVL run by a licensed practitioner. A strike-off cannot be applied for if the company has traded, changed its name or disposed of trading property in the previous three months, or while any insolvency or scheme process is live, so that three-month clock starts when the entity actually goes quiet rather than when you decide to close it. Then final tax returns, deregistrations, and closing the bank accounts
  • Tidy what remains. Fewer entities, correct names, a structure chart someone can read

For a group of five to fifteen companies the whole exercise typically runs six to twelve months, governed less by the work than by tax clearances and the wait for dissolution, which follows three months after the liquidator's final account is registered. It is a project the finance function can run alongside its normal work rather than a service that takes the business over.

What to check before you close anything

Dissolution is difficult to undo and the assets of a dissolved company can pass to the Crown as ownerless property, so the diligence matters more than the closing.

  • Assets still in the company. A bank account, a small shareholding, a registered trade mark, a domain name, a property title never transferred. These are the ones that surface afterwards
  • Guarantees and cross-guarantees. Group borrowing frequently makes every company a guarantor. Closing one can breach the facility
  • Leases and dilapidations. A lease held by a dormant company is a live liability until it is assigned or surrendered
  • Employment history. Old employees, TUPE history, and any pension scheme the entity participated in
  • Litigation or claims, threatened or possible, including warranties given on an earlier sale
  • Whether it is really dormant. Dormant means no significant accounting transaction in the year, meaning one that has to go into the accounting records, and a single one is enough to break it. The confirmation statement fee and a handful of other registrar fees are specifically disregarded, which is why entities get wrongly assumed dormant in both directions. Where an entity turns out to be insolvent rather than dormant, the insolvency practitioner page explains what changes

A company can be restored to the register after dissolution, but it is a court process. The cheaper administrative route exists only where the registrar struck the company off, not where you applied to strike it off yourself, so for a voluntary strike-off the court is the only way back. It costs considerably more than the check that would have avoided it.

Why it is worth doing before a sale

On any transaction, due diligence works through every company in the group. Dormant companies generate enquiries, and enquiries generate warranties, indemnities, retentions and delay. A group structure with four clean companies is a materially easier deal than the same business held through fourteen, and the difference shows up in the timetable, the legal fees and occasionally the price.

It is also work that cannot be done at the last minute. An MVL takes months, and a buyer will not wait for a tidy-up to complete. Two years before an intended exit is the right time, which is why this sits alongside exit planning in the same restructuring section. If you are not sure the group is ready, an independent review establishes the position first.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Where a solvent liquidation is the right route we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner to take the appointment, and we stay alongside you and your accountant through the project.

What we add is the decision-making rather than the filing: which entities can go, what diligence has to be done before each one does, and whether a strike-off or an MVL is right for each company on its own numbers. It is a service your accountant and your management team run with us rather than hand over. It is unglamorous work with a clear return, and it is the point where our restructuring and insolvency sides meet, since a solvent liquidation is an insolvency procedure used for an entirely positive purpose.

Frequently asked questions
What is corporate simplification?

Reducing the number of companies in a group by closing the dormant companies and redundant entities, having first moved any assets and dealt with any liabilities they hold. The aim is lower costs, less administration and less risk for the organisation, and a group structure that is easier to explain to a lender or a buyer.

Should we strike off or liquidate?

Strike off a genuinely empty company. Use an MVL where the company holds reserves above £25,000, because up to that figure a pre-strike-off distribution is treated as capital and above it the entire amount is taxed as income. Decide per entity, on its own numbers.

How long does it take?

Six to twelve months for a group of five to fifteen companies. Strike-offs complete in a few months; an MVL runs longer because of HMRC clearance and the period before dissolution. Preparation, moving assets and settling intercompany balances, is usually the longest part.

Can we reverse it if we close the wrong company?

A dissolved company can be restored to the register, but where you applied for the strike-off yourself the administrative route is not available and it has to be a court application, and in the general case within six years of dissolution. Assets left in the company at dissolution pass to the Crown as ownerless property, dealt with in Scotland by the King's and Lord Treasurer's Remembrancer. Which is why the checking stage matters far more than the closing stage.

Does this need an insolvency practitioner?

Only for the MVLs. A strike-off is an application the directors make. Where an entity holds reserves worth doing an MVL for, only a licensed insolvency practitioner can act as liquidator, and we introduce one.

Is this only for large groups?

No. The most common case we see is an owner-managed business with three to six companies accumulated over the years, one of them holding cash nobody has taken out. The arithmetic works at that scale as well as it does for a large organisation, and the corporate governance benefit is proportionally greater because the same small management team carries every directorship.

CTA block

How many companies are you filing for that do nothing?

We take no appointments, so we have no interest in which route each entity takes. One conversation will tell you which companies can go, what has to happen first, and whether a strike-off or a liquidation is right for each.

Breadcrumb: Restructuring › Contingency Planning

Eyebrow: Restructuring

Contingency planning

A contingency plan is the answer to a question most directors avoid asking: what do we do if this does not work? If the refinancing is declined, if the contract is not renewed, if the biggest customer goes elsewhere or goes under. Not a forecast, and not a prediction that any of it will happen. A worked-through answer, prepared while there is still time to choose between options rather than take the only one left.

It is the least urgent-sounding service we offer and, measured by what it saves, frequently the most valuable. Everything else on this site is something you do once a problem has arrived. This is the one you do before.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Why the timing decides the outcome

The uncomfortable arithmetic of financial distress is that your options narrow as your position weakens, and they narrow faster than most directors expect.

A company with six months of runway can sell a division, refinance, negotiate with a landlord, restructure its debt, run a proper sale process, or decide to close in an orderly way and pay its creditors. The same company with six weeks can do almost none of that. The buyer knows you are forced. The lender has already made its decision. The sale that would have realised full value becomes a fire sale, and a solvent closure becomes an insolvent one.

Nothing about the business changed in between. Only the time did. That is the entire case for doing this work early, and it is why our restructuring page argues that timing matters more than technique.

When to build one

The trigger is not distress. It is a foreseeable event with a real chance of going the wrong way, and a consequence you have not worked through.

  • A refinancing or facility renewal that is not certain. The single most common one. If the answer is no, what happens on the Monday after?
  • A major contract, tender or customer up for renewal, where losing it would take the business below the line
  • A lender that has started asking different questions, moved you to a different team, or commissioned an independent review
  • A large, uncertain liability: an HMRC enquiry, a dispute, a dilapidations claim, a warranty exposure from an earlier sale
  • A sector or supply chain under visible strain, where you can see what is coming towards you before it arrives
  • A shareholder or partner dispute that could force a sale or a split
  • A personal deadline, such as a guarantee falling due, retirement, or ill health

If any of those is on your horizon and you have not written down what you would do, the plan is worth an afternoon.

What a contingency plan actually contains

It is a short, practical document, not a consultancy report. Ours generally cover six things.

  • The trigger points. What specific event or number means the fallback is now live. A cash balance, a date, a decision from a third party. Written down in advance, because the hardest part of any plan is admitting the moment has arrived
  • The real cash position, forward. A short-term cash forecast that survives contact with reality, showing the point at which the company runs out of room. Most plans fail here, on optimistic debtor collection
  • The options, priced and ranked. Sale, refinancing, a turnaround programme, a company voluntary arrangement, administration, a pre-pack administration, or an orderly winding the company up. What each would realistically achieve, what it costs, how long it takes, and what has to be true for it to work
  • The preparation each option needs. Some routes require weeks of groundwork: a buyer identified, a valuation done, funding lined up, information ready for a purchaser's adviser. Doing that work in advance is what makes the option real rather than theoretical
  • Your personal exposure, mapped. Every personal guarantee, the director's loan account, anything you have secured on your own property. This is the part directors most often discover too late, and it frequently changes which option they choose
  • Who does what, and who is told. Advisers, lenders, key staff, and the order in which they hear anything

The output is usually a handful of pages. Its value is not the document. It is that the thinking is done, so that the day it is needed you are executing a decision rather than making one.

What it is not

Two things this page is regularly confused with, and neither is what we do here.

It is not business continuity planning

Continuity and disaster-recovery planning deals with fires, floods, cyber incidents and IT failure: how the business keeps operating through a disruption. Useful, and someone else's speciality. This page is about financial contingency, where the risk is solvency rather than operations.

It is not a decision to do anything

Building a plan commits you to nothing. Most of the plans we write are never executed, because the refinancing lands or the contract renews. That is a good outcome and the work still earned its place: you spent the intervening months making decisions with the downside understood rather than guessed at.

Directors' duties, and why a plan protects you

Once a company is unable to pay its debts, or close to it, a director's duties shift towards the interests of creditors, and the decisions taken in that period are the ones examined later if things do not recover. Wrongful trading is not about a company failing. It is about what you knew, when you knew it, and what you did next.

A director who identified the risk early, took advice, documented the options and acted on a plan is in a materially stronger position than one who pressed on and hoped. That holds whether or not the plan was ever needed. The paper trail a contingency plan creates is one of the better protections a director can give themselves, and it costs a fraction of what defending the alternative costs.

How we run it

It is deliberately light. A first conversation to understand the business and what is coming. A short piece of work on the numbers and the options, usually one to three weeks depending on complexity and how good the information is. Then a document, a conversation about it, and a review point tied to whatever the trigger event is.

Where the review shows the business needs attention now rather than a plan for later, we say so, and the work becomes a turnaround or a debt restructuring conversation instead. Where it shows the company is fine, we say that too, and you have spent very little to find out.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your administrator or your liquidator, which means we have no financial interest in your contingency plan ever being executed, and no reason to steer you towards the formal option that would generate a fee for the firm.

That is the whole reason this service can be honest. An adviser who takes appointments and tells you to prepare for administration is describing work they might later be paid for. We are not, so when we tell you the fallback should be a solvent sale, or that you do not need a plan at all, you can take it at face value.

It is also why accountants and solicitors send us clients at this stage rather than later: they know the client will come back to them, not be absorbed into a process.

Frequently asked questions
Is it not premature to plan for something that may not happen?

That is the objection, and it is the wrong way round. The plan costs little and commits you to nothing. The alternative is discovering your options at the point when most of them have expired. Directors almost never regret having done this; they regret the months they spent deciding whether to.

Does taking advice make insolvency more likely?

No. It makes it less likely, because problems addressed early are more often solved without a formal procedure at all. What advice does is remove the excuse of not knowing, which is why some directors avoid it. The regime is not aimed at directors who acted on what they learned.

Who needs to know we are doing this?

Nobody, unless you decide otherwise. This is confidential advisory work. It is not filed, published or notified anywhere, and there is no register of companies that have taken advice.

How long does it take?

Usually one to three weeks from the first conversation, depending on the size of the business and the state of the management information. Where a trigger event is days away rather than months, we work to that instead and cut the scope to what is decision-useful.

What does it cost?

It is a fixed fee agreed before we start, scoped to the size of the question. It is by a wide margin the cheapest piece of work on this site, and the only one bought before it is needed.

What if the plan says the business cannot be saved?

Then you have found that out while you still have choices about how it ends, which is a materially better position than finding out when a creditor forces the timing. An orderly solvent closure and a compulsory winding up are very different outcomes for a director, and the difference between them is usually months of notice.

CTA block

Is something coming that you have not planned for?

We take no appointments, so we have no stake in whether your fallback is ever used. One conversation will tell you whether a plan is worth building and what it would need to cover.

Breadcrumb: Financial Advisory › Corporate Finance

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Corporate finance

Corporate finance is the advice around the transactions that change who owns a business, what it is worth and how it is funded: mergers and acquisitions, selling a company, buying one, valuing shares, raising capital, or reshaping the capital structure so that the people running the business are the people who own it. For most owners it is the largest financial event of their working life, and it happens once.

That asymmetry is the whole reason advisers exist in this market, and it is why this sits inside our restructuring and advisory practice rather than alongside a lender. The buyer across the table has done twenty deals. Their advisers do nothing else. The seller has done none, and is negotiating on terms they are seeing for the first time, in a document written by someone else's solicitor.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What we advise on
Selling a business

Preparing the company for sale, identifying and approaching buyers, running a competitive process where the market supports one, and negotiating the deal through to completion. The preparation is where most of the value is won, which is why it belongs alongside exit planning rather than starting when the business goes to market.

Mergers and acquisitions

Buying a company or a trade, or merging two: assessing whether the target is worth what is being asked, structuring the transaction and its funding, and managing the process through to completion. Most acquisitions by owner-managed businesses are trade purchases rather than mergers, but the discipline is the same. The financial due diligence itself sits on our transaction support page.

Management buyouts and buy-ins

Structuring a purchase by the management team, including how much of the price the business itself can fund out of future profits, what the funders will require, and how the equity is split between the team. Frequently the best outcome where a trade sale would break up something worth keeping.

Valuations

What a business or a shareholding is actually worth, and on what basis. For a transaction, a share transfer, a shareholder agreement, tax purposes, or simply so an owner knows. Where the value is disputed rather than negotiated, that is forensic work and our forensic services page covers it.

Capital raising

Working out what capital structure the business needs and what it can support: debt, equity, or a mix, and on what terms. Capital investment from a private equity house comes with governance conditions as well as money, and those terms deserve as much attention as the valuation. We advise on the structure and introduce funders. We are not brokers and we do not arrange the facility, which our finance and funding page explains.

Shareholder reorganisations

Buying out a departing shareholder, bringing in a new one, resolving a deadlock, or reshaping a group so the ownership matches the intention. These transactions rarely make headlines and frequently do more for shareholder value than a sale would. Often the quiet transaction that prevents a dispute later.

What a business is worth, and why the number moves

Most private companies are valued on a multiple of sustainable earnings, adjusted to show what a new owner would actually inherit: the owner's remuneration replaced at market rate, personal costs removed, and one-off items stripped out. The multiple then depends on things a buyer can verify rather than things a seller asserts.

  • Scale. Larger companies attract higher multiples for the same profit, because they carry less risk and reach more buyers, including private equity firms that will not look below a certain size
  • Recurring revenue. Contracted or repeat income is worth substantially more than the same profit earned job by job
  • Customer concentration. One customer at a large share of revenue is the most common single reason a multiple is marked down
  • Owner dependence. If the business needs you, the buyer is acquiring a problem alongside the profit
  • Growth and market position. Demonstrated, not projected. Buyers discount forecasts heavily and pay for track record
  • Quality of information. Reliable monthly accounts and a clean audit trail reduce perceived risk, and perceived risk is what the multiple prices

Two companies with identical profits routinely sell for very different amounts. The gap is not luck. It is the preparation, which is why the conversation is worth having years before the transaction rather than at the point of sale.

Structure: the difference between the price and the money

This is the part owners understand least and regret most, and it is more important than the headline number.

  • Cash at completion. The only part that is certain. Every other element depends on something happening afterwards
  • Deferred consideration. A fixed amount paid later. Its value depends entirely on the buyer still being able to pay it, so who the buyer is matters as much as what they promise
  • Earn-out. A payment contingent on the business hitting targets after the sale, when you may no longer control the decisions that determine whether it does. Earn-outs are where sellers most often lose money they had counted as theirs. If you accept one, the mechanics of how performance is measured and what the buyer may not do to the business matter more than the headline figure
  • Shares in the buyer. Value that depends on somebody else's company, usually with restrictions on when you can sell
  • Warranties and indemnities. Promises about the business that, if wrong, let the buyer claim money back. The cap, the time limits and the disclosure exercise decide your real exposure after the deal
  • Retentions and escrow. Money held back against warranty claims, sometimes for years

A headline price with half of it deferred, conditional and warranty-exposed is not the same offer as a lower price paid in cash. Comparing offers properly means valuing the certainty, not just the total, and it is the single most useful thing an adviser does.

How a deal actually runs
  • Preparation. Financial information assembled and normalised, a financial forecast a buyer will believe, the equity story written, and the obvious problems fixed before a buyer finds them
  • Approach. A targeted list of credible buyers rather than the widest possible net. Confidentiality agreements before anything meaningful is shared
  • Initial offers. Indicative and non-binding, usually subject to due diligence. This is the point at which a seller has the most negotiating power, and it is where structure should be agreed rather than left
  • Heads of terms. The commercial deal in outline, including exclusivity. Once exclusivity is granted, the balance of power shifts decisively to the buyer, so what is agreed here matters more than its non-binding status suggests
  • Due diligence. The buyer's advisers examine everything. Surprises here cost price or kill deals, which is why preparation earns its keep
  • Documentation. Share purchase agreement, disclosure letter, ancillary documents. Solicitors' work, with the adviser keeping the commercial deal intact through the drafting
  • Completion, and afterwards. Funds flow, and any post-completion accounts, earn-out periods and warranty periods begin

Three to nine months from decision to completion is typical for an owner-managed business, and the timetable is usually set by due diligence and by how ready the information was.

When not to do a deal

We are paid for advice rather than by completion, so this section can exist.

  • When the business is not ready and a year of preparation would change the price by more than the delay costs
  • When the market is wrong for that business and waiting is genuinely better than accepting a discount
  • When the structure transfers the risk to you. A high headline price mostly in earn-out, from a buyer whose ability to pay depends on the business continuing to perform without you
  • When the buyer cannot fund it. Private equity buyers and trade acquirers alike need their capital confirmed, and establishing this early avoids months of due diligence on a transaction that was never going to complete
  • When there is no buyer at any acceptable price. For some owner-managed businesses the honest answer is an orderly solvent closure through an MVL, and that is a legitimate outcome rather than a failure
  • When the business needs fixing rather than selling. A struggling company sold in distress realises a fraction of its value, and a turnaround or an independent review is the right route first
Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We are not a broker, we do not arrange finance or deal in investments, and we take no insolvency appointments. Where a transaction needs funding we introduce specialists; where it needs a licensed appointment, we bring one in. On the accountancy and tax side we work with your own accountant rather than replacing them.

What we bring that a pure corporate finance house does not is the other end of the story. We spend the rest of our time on businesses in difficulty, including businesses that got into difficulty because of how a deal was structured: an earn-out that failed, an acquisition funded with debt the business could not service, warranties that turned into claims. That experience shapes how we advise on structure, and it is why our advice tends to be more conservative about deferred consideration than a fee-on-completion adviser's would be.

We work alongside your accountant and your solicitor rather than replacing either, and we hand the client back. Where the funding structure itself is the question rather than the transaction, our capital management page covers it, and the wider financial advisory section sets out how the pieces fit together.

Frequently asked questions
What does a corporate finance adviser actually do?

Corporate finance services cover preparing the business and its information, identifying and approaching the right counterparties, negotiating price and structure, and managing the transaction through due diligence to completion. The value is concentrated in preparation and in structure, which is where the difference between the headline price and the money received is decided.

What is my company worth?

Usually a multiple of adjusted sustainable earnings, where the adjustment replaces the owner with a market-rate manager and strips out personal and one-off items. The multiple depends on scale, recurring revenue, customer concentration, owner dependence and the quality of the numbers. Any valuation quoted without those adjustments is a guess.

How long does selling a business take?

Three to nine months from decision to completion for a typical owner-managed business, plus whatever preparation is needed beforehand. Due diligence is the usual bottleneck, and the better prepared the information, the shorter it is.

Should I accept an earn-out?

Sometimes, but treat it as the risky part of the price rather than part of the price. Look at who controls the decisions that determine whether the targets are met, how performance is measured, what the buyer is prevented from doing to the business, and what happens if you leave. Value the certain money and the contingent money separately.

Do I need a corporate finance adviser as well as my accountant?

For a sale or an acquisition of any size, yes, and the two do different jobs. Your accountancy adviser knows the business and handles the tax and the numbers. The corporate finance experts run the process and negotiate the commercial deal. On a small management buyout the requirement is lighter and the accountant plus ourselves is often enough.

Can you help raise the money?

We advise on what structure the business needs and can support, and we introduce funders we know. We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities and we take no commission from lenders, which is the reason we can tell you when more debt is the wrong answer.

CTA block

Thinking about a transaction?

We are paid for advice, not on completion, so we have no stake in a deal happening. One conversation will tell you what the business would realistically fetch, what structure to expect, and whether now is the moment.
