Forensic accounting and forensic services

Forensic accounting is the application of accountancy and investigation to questions that will be decided by a court, a tribunal, an arbitrator or a negotiated settlement. It covers three things: finding out what happened to the money, quantifying what someone has lost, and presenting both in a form that survives challenge from the other side.

The distinguishing feature is not technique. It is audience. Ordinary accountancy work has to be right; forensic accounting has to be right and also demonstrable, by someone who did not want it to be true, months later, under cross-examination. That constraint shapes everything about how the work is done.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What we are instructed to do
Fraud and financial crime investigation

A fraud investigation establishes whether money has been taken, how, by whom and how much. Employee theft, false invoicing, procurement fraud, bribery and corruption, misappropriation by a director or partner, and the concealment that usually accompanies financial crime. The output is evidence for a disciplinary, a civil claim, an insurance claim or a police report, and it has to be gathered in a way that keeps all of those options open.

Expert witness and quantum

Quantifying loss in a dispute and giving evidence on it. Loss of profits from a breach of contract, business interruption, the value of what was destroyed or withheld. Reports prepared to the standards courts require, with the reasoning exposed so it can be tested rather than asserted.

Valuation in dispute

Where the value of a company or a shareholding is contested: a shareholder dispute, a divorce, an unfair prejudice petition, or a buyout where the parties cannot agree the number. Different from the valuation work on our corporate finance page, because the audience is a judge rather than a buyer.

Professional negligence

Assessing whether financial advice or accountancy work fell below the standard required, and what that professional negligence cost the client. Instructed by claimants and defendants alike, and the work has to be equally rigorous either way.

Insurance claims

Preparing or reviewing insurance claims where the loss is financial: business interruption, fidelity and crime cover, and disputes about the measure of indemnity. Insurers commission work on insurance claims as often as policyholders do.

Asset tracing and recovery

Following funds and identifying where value has gone. Frequently instructed alongside an administration or a liquidation, where money has left a company before it failed, and often the point at which our forensic and insolvency work meet.

The expert's duty, and why it decides whether the report is useful

This is the part that separates evidence from advocacy, and the sales-led pages on this subject leave it out.

The duty an expert owes runs to the court, and it outranks any duty to whoever is paying. In practice that means independence, a report kept within the limits of the expert's own expertise, the facts and assumptions set out where they can be seen, and, critically, an acknowledgement of anything that qualifies the opinion or points the other way. An expert who omits the inconvenient point is not helping the client; they are creating an opening for the other side and putting their whole report at risk.

So the honest version of what a good forensic accountant offers a solicitor is this: an opinion that is genuinely defensible, reached without being told what it should be, and delivered with the weaknesses identified early enough to be dealt with. That is what an instructing solicitor is buying, and it is not the same as agreement. Where our analysis does not support the client's case, we say so at the outset, when it is still useful, rather than discovering it in the witness box.

In Scotland that duty comes from the case law rather than a rule of court. The Supreme Court in Kennedy v Cordia (Services) LLP adopted the Ikarian Reefer duties for Scottish civil cases, and went further than the English rules do: it treated independence and impartiality as a question of admissibility rather than of weight. A Scottish court can refuse to hear a report that does not meet them.

For that reason we distinguish clearly between advisory work, where we assist a party, and expert work, where we owe the duty to the court. Both are legitimate. Confusing them is what gets reports excluded.

How a forensic investigation runs
  • Scope it properly. The single biggest cause of wasted forensic cost is an open-ended instruction. What question is being answered, for what forum, by when, and what is the proportionate depth given what is at stake
  • Secure the evidence. Accountancy records, bank statements, the accounting system's audit trail, emails, contracts. Preservation matters from day one, particularly where an employee is still in post and has access
  • Establish the baseline. What the records show, and how reliable they are. In fraud work, the pattern of what is missing frequently carries more information than what is present
  • Analyse. Reconstructing transactions, tracing funds through accounts, testing the numbers against the documents and the documents against each other. Where the matter involves bribery or corruption, the payment trail and the approval trail are examined separately
  • Quantify. Building the loss calculation on stated assumptions, with sensitivities, so that a change in one assumption does not collapse the whole figure
  • Report. In the form the forum requires, with the reasoning visible
  • Support through to conclusion. Meetings of experts, responding to the other side's report, and giving evidence if it goes that far

Matters frequently settle. A well-constructed report is often what causes them to, because it converts an argument into a number both sides can see the basis of, which is why forensic accounting is as much a dispute resolution tool as a litigation one.

In the Scottish courts

Most of the forensic accounting content online describes English procedure, and the practical differences matter if your case is in Scotland.

Proceedings run in the Court of Session or the sheriff court, with a Commercial Court in the Court of Session and a commercial procedure in some sheriff courts for disputes of a commercial or business nature. The vocabulary is different: pursuer and defender rather than claimant and defendant, a proof rather than a trial, and documents lodged as productions. The evidence is that of a skilled witness, which the Rules of Court call a report of a skilled person, though everyone says expert in practice. Recovery of documents runs through commission and diligence rather than the English disclosure regime, and the statutory power is available before proceedings are even raised, which is worth knowing early. The timetable in a commercial action is actively managed by the judge.

None of that changes the accounting. It changes how the work is packaged, when it has to be ready, and who it is addressed to. We are Glasgow-based and this is the system we work in.

Where forensic work meets insolvency

This is our unusual angle, and it comes from the practice rather than the marketing.

A large share of financial wrongdoing surfaces when a company fails, because that is when someone independent looks properly at the records for the first time. Our insolvency practitioner page explains who does that looking and why they are obliged to. Money paid to connected parties, assets transferred before the collapse, a director's loan account that grew without explanation, or trading that continued long after it should have stopped. Where a government body such as the Insolvency Service is already investigating, an independent analysis is worth having early. In Scotland the relevant challenges are gratuitous alienations and unfair preferences, and the equivalent claims elsewhere are transactions at an undervalue and preferences.

We work on both sides of that: instructed by an insolvency practitioner to run the forensic investigation and quantify what was lost, and instructed by directors who need an independent analysis of transactions being questioned. Because we take no insolvency appointments ourselves, we can act in either direction without a conflict, which a firm that also takes appointments frequently cannot. Our insolvency practitioner and liquidation pages cover the procedures that generate this work.

What it costs, and keeping it proportionate

A forensic investigation is charged on time, because its scope is genuinely unknowable at the outset. What is controllable is the shape of it: a defined first phase with a decision point at the end, rather than an open instruction.

We will tell you early where the cost of proving something is likely to exceed what proving it is worth. That happens more often than the industry admits, particularly in smaller frauds where the money has already been spent and the perpetrator has nothing to recover from. A short scoping exercise that concludes the claim is not worth pursuing has saved the client a great deal, and we would rather deliver that answer than bill for the alternative.

Where we fit

Lancefield is an independent advisory firm. We perform no audits, sell no financial products, and take no insolvency appointments, so there is no other engagement waiting behind the forensic instruction and nothing our conclusion could be shaped by. Nor do we sell compliance or anti-fraud systems, which is a common second engagement behind a fraud investigation elsewhere.

Solicitors are the usual route in, and we work the way instructing solicitors need: scoped, on time, with the difficulties raised early rather than late. The wider financial advisory section sets out the rest of what we do. Where the matter is heading for arbitration or an expert determination rather than court, our commercial arbitration page covers that route. Where the question is about a transaction rather than a dispute, transaction support is the right page.

Frequently asked questions
What is forensic accounting?

Accounting and investigation applied to a question that will be tested by a court, tribunal, arbitrator or negotiation. It covers investigating what happened to money, quantifying financial loss, and presenting the analysis so that it stands up to challenge. The distinguishing feature is that the work has to be demonstrable, not merely correct.

What does a forensic accountant do that an auditor does not?

An audit gives reasonable assurance that the accounts as a whole are free from material misstatement, whether caused by fraud or by error, working from samples and to materiality thresholds. The auditing standard itself recognises that fraud concealed by forgery, unrecorded transactions, misrepresentation to the auditor or collusion carries a higher and unavoidable risk of going undetected. A forensic accountant investigates a specific question without a materiality threshold, follows individual transactions wherever they lead, and produces evidence rather than an opinion on the accounts as a whole. That is a difference in design, not a criticism of the accountancy profession.

Can you act as an expert witness?

Yes, and it is a distinct role from advising a party. As an expert the overriding duty is to the court rather than to whoever is paying, which means the report has to set out its assumptions, acknowledge what qualifies the opinion, and stay within our expertise. We are explicit at the outset about which role we are being instructed in.

We suspect an employee is stealing. What should we do first?

Preserve the evidence and contact someone before confronting anyone. Secure the accounting records and system logs, restrict access carefully, and do not alert the individual before you have what you need. Employment law, criminal reporting and any insurance claim all have their own requirements, and the order in which you act affects all three.

How much does a forensic investigation cost?

It is charged on time, because the scope cannot honestly be fixed before anyone looks. What we do is agree a defined first phase with a cost and a decision point, so you learn what you are dealing with before committing to the full investigation.

Will you tell us if our case is weak?

Yes, at the point when it is still useful. An expert who only tells a client what they want to hear produces a report the other side takes apart, which is worse than no report. Where the analysis does not support the case, saying so early is the most valuable thing we can do.

CTA block

Need an independent view of the numbers?

We audit nothing and take no appointments, so there is nothing behind the instruction shaping the answer. One conversation will tell you whether the question can be answered, what it would take, and whether it is worth answering.

  • Compliance: not FCA authorised, no insolvency appointments, no fee contingent on completion. We do the financial workstream only, and the page must not imply we do the legal one.

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Transaction support and due diligence

Due diligence is the investigation a buyer runs before committing money, and the preparation a seller does before letting anyone look. It answers one question in detail: is this company what it appears to be? The price adjustments, the warranties and the money held back at completion all follow from what that investigation finds. Larger firms sell the same work as transaction services.

We do the financial workstream, for the buyer and for the seller, on owner-managed deals across Scotland. It sits inside our financial advisory practice. We charge for the work rather than the deal, so when the numbers do not support the offer we say so. Much of our other work is with a company in difficulty because of an acquisition nobody examined.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What due diligence actually is

An audit tests whether a set of accounts is fairly stated. Due diligence asks something else: what would a new owner of this company inherit? It is an investigation rather than a compliance exercise, and it produces findings rather than an opinion. Whether the transaction is a merger, a trade purchase or a management buyout, the question is the same.

Scope is agreed at the start and deliberately narrow. Nobody examines everything. A proportionate financial due diligence review concentrates on the few places where the value could be materially wrong, and says what was left alone.

Buy-side: is the company what it appears to be?

You are making an investment decision on evidence that is entirely historic. Buy-side work takes the numbers a seller has presented and establishes which of them survive into the first Monday after completion. Most of the financial risk sits in the first four items.

  • Quality of earnings. Reported profit restated as sustainable trading profit: one-off gains out, the owner's pay at a market rate, personal costs removed, policy changes unwound. The normalised EBITDA this review produces is what the multiple applies to
  • Revenue quality. Where income comes from, how much is contracted or repeating, customer concentration, and whether any was recognised early
  • Working capital. How much cash the business needs at its normal level of trade. Understate it and the buyer funds the gap weeks after completion
  • Debt-like items. Unpaid tax and time to pay arrangements, overdue creditors used as finance, deferred consideration from an earlier deal, dilapidations, pension deficits, accrued holiday
  • Tax exposures. Historic PAYE and VAT treatment, the employment status of contractors, open HMRC enquiries, and anything a later inspection could unpick
  • Forecast credibility. Whether the assumptions trace back to something that has already happened, and whether the synergies behind the offer belong to the target or to the buyer
  • Operational reality. Systems, capacity and the few people the trading depends on, which is where the operational cost of year one hides

Two findings recur above all others on owner-managed deals: working capital understated, and profit that depends on an owner working for less than the job is worth. Neither is dishonest. Both move the number.

Vendor due diligence: examined before the buyer arrives

Vendor due diligence is the same investigation run on your own company, commissioned by the seller before the market sees anything. The point is that the buyer's adviser finds nothing that stalls the deal.

What kills owner-managed deals is rarely the price. It is delay and surprise. A buyer who finds in week six what the seller could have explained in week one does not simply adjust the offer. Every unexplained item is then treated as a financial risk.

  • Awkward things get fixed while there is time. Related-party balances, a property nobody wants, dormant subsidiaries, an unresolved employment matter. corporate simplification handles the group-structure half
  • The numbers get told once. A normalised earnings position the seller can defend, with the adjustments already made and evidenced
  • Competitive tension survives. With more than one bidder, late information is what lets a buyer reopen terms after the others have gone home
  • The owner keeps running the business. Deals fail because trading dips while the seller answers data requests

Vendor work belongs with exit planning. Treat it as an investment in the sale rather than a cost, and start it well before the memorandum goes out.

Financial, legal, commercial and tax: who does which

Due diligence is spoken about as one job. It is at least four, run by different people at once, and knowing which is which stops you paying twice.

  • Financial due diligence. Earnings, working capital, debt-like items, cash and tax exposure. Done by accountants, and it is our part
  • Legal. Title to the shares, contracts, property, employment, litigation, and the change of control clauses a new owner triggers by buying the company. Done by solicitors, and in Scotland by a Scottish firm: the title system and the rules for ending a commercial lease are not the English ones
  • Commercial due diligence. The market, the customers, the competition, and whether the growth in the forecast is available to anybody at all. Usually a specialist firm, and the workstream most often skipped
  • Tax. Historic exposure, plus the structure of the deal. Run alongside the financial work, because each keeps finding the other's problems
  • Operational and IT. Systems, capacity, key people, and the operational investment a buyer faces in year one. On smaller deals it folds into the commercial and financial scope
  • ESG due diligence. Environmental, social and governance exposure. Standard where private equity or institutional investors sit behind the deal. On a small acquisition, ESG due diligence is a section rather than a workstream

Somebody must own the whole list, because the gaps between workstreams are where things get missed. On a merger that is the corporate finance lead, and our corporate finance page covers the role.

How a due diligence review runs
  • Scoping. What the review is for, what it will test, what it will not, what it costs and on what terms. In writing, before anything starts
  • Information request. One specific list, sent early. The pace of the whole review is set here
  • Analysis. The numbers rebuilt from the underlying records rather than lifted from the accounts, and management answering questions in a session rather than by email
  • Interim findings. Anything that could change the price or stop the deal is raised the day it is found. A review that saves bad news for the final report has failed
  • Report. Findings quantified where they can be, each with a recommendation attached: adjust, warrant, indemnify, hold back, or reconsider
  • Support to completion. Findings have to survive the drafting, so we stay involved while the deal is active
What the findings do to the deal

Findings are worth only what is done with them. A report that sits in a folder while the transaction completes on the terms originally offered has cost money for nothing. Six things a finding can become, and choosing between them is where the negotiation happens.

  • A price adjustment. A finding that changes sustainable earnings is multiplied by whatever multiple the deal was struck on, so a modest error in profit becomes a large one in the consideration. In a merger it moves the share exchange ratio instead
  • A completion mechanism. How the consideration is trued up afterwards: completion accounts measuring cash, debt and working capital on the day, or a locked box fixing the balance sheet at an earlier date
  • A warranty. A statement by the seller that something is true, with a claim if it is not. Warranties cover the unknown, and taking one instead of an adjustment for a problem already found is a poor trade for a buyer
  • An indemnity. A pound for pound promise covering one identified exposure, usually a tax one. For the problems the investigation found but could not size
  • A retention. Part of the consideration held back against claims, sometimes for years. The only protection that does not depend on finding the seller afterwards
  • A condition, or no deal. Some findings cannot be priced. A key contract with a change of control clause and a customer who will not confirm they are staying is a reason to pause

Disclosure runs alongside it. The seller discloses against the warranties, and anything properly disclosed generally cannot then be claimed for. Good transaction services work stays with the commercial terms through the drafting rather than stopping at the report.

When due diligence is not worth doing

We are paid for the work rather than for the deal, which is what lets this section exist.

  • When the cost is out of proportion to the investment at risk. On a small asset purchase with no history, no employees and no liabilities coming across, the financial risk is small and a full review buys comfort rather than information
  • When value sits in assets rather than earnings. If it is property or plant, a valuation and a solicitor matter more than an earnings review
  • When you already know. A management buyout team that has run the company for a decade does not need a stranger to explain its own working capital cycle
  • When nobody has written the scope. Open-ended instructions produce long reports and large fees. Our recommendation is usually to narrow the terms of the work to the value genuinely at risk
  • When the company needs fixing rather than buying. A distressed target is a different exercise, and an independent review answers the question better

On a smaller transaction the right scope is a short review of earnings, cash and tax, delivered in days rather than weeks. And if the seller will not release the information, that is the finding.

Where we fit

Lancefield advises. We take no insolvency appointments, we are not FCA authorised, we do not arrange finance, and no part of our fee depends on a deal completing. Where funding is needed we introduce a trusted specialist firm rather than broking it, which our capital management and finance and funding pages set out.

What we bring to transaction services that a pure deals team does not is the other end of the story. Much of our work is with a business under operational and financial pressure, sometimes because of an acquisition: debt the trading could not service, working capital that belonged to somebody else, an earn-out built on a forecast nobody tested. Where a target is genuinely distressed and the route is a purchase out of administration, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust, because nobody here takes the appointment.

We work with your own accountant and your solicitor rather than replacing either. Where a finding turns into a dispute rather than a negotiation, that is forensic services. Where the real question is whether to sell the business at all, restructuring and, for a solvent closure, an MVL are honest alternatives.

Frequently asked questions
What are due diligence services?

The investigations run before a deal completes: financial, legal, commercial and tax, with operational, IT and ESG work added on larger transactions. Financial due diligence, our part, tests earnings, working capital, debt-like items and the tax exposure a buyer inherits with the company. Larger firms sell due diligence services as transaction services.

How long does financial due diligence take?

Two to six weeks from a complete information pack is typical on an owner-managed acquisition, and the timetable is set by how ready the seller's records are. Private equity or bank funding behind the deal makes the review longer, because several workstreams report into one deadline.

What due diligence is needed for a merger or acquisition?

Financial, legal and tax on any deal of substance. Commercial due diligence wherever the value depends on growth rather than on what the business already earns. Operational and ESG due diligence scale with size. On M&A transactions between similar companies, the commercial workstream decides whether the synergies were real.

What is a red flag report?

A report listing only the issues that could change the offer or stop the deal, with no descriptive background. It costs less and arrives faster, which suits an early stage or a competitive process, and on a first look our recommendation is often exactly that.

Who pays for vendor due diligence?

The seller does, and the report is then released to bidders on agreed terms. It is normal on private equity exits. On a smaller business, getting the numbers into a defensible state before anybody asks delivers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

If due diligence was thorough, do I still need warranties?

Yes. Investigation deals with what can be found and warranties with what cannot. Covering a known problem with a warranty instead of a deduction is how a buyer ends up litigating something they could have taken off the consideration during the negotiation.

Is due diligence different in Scotland?

The financial work is the same. The legal work is not. Title to property, standard securities and the rules for ending a commercial lease follow Scots law, and a purchase of Scottish land or buildings attracts Land and Buildings Transaction Tax rather than Stamp Duty Land Tax.

Looking at a deal?

One conversation will tell you what a proportionate scope looks like, roughly what it should cost, and what it is likely to find. We have no stake in the transaction happening.

Breadcrumb: Financial Advisory › Pension Advisory

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Pension advisory

This page is about pensions as a company problem: what an employer still owes when cash is short, what a scheme does to a restructuring or a sale, and where it ranks when a business fails. Lancefield is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, and we give no personal pension advice, no investment advice and no retirement planning advice to individuals.

Most of the volume behind pension advisory is people asking about their own money, and the section below says where to get that advice. If pensions have become the hardest item on your company's balance sheet, this is the right page, and it sits inside our financial advisory work.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

If the pension you are worried about is your own

We will say this plainly, once. Decisions about a personal pension plan, whether to transfer benefits out of one scheme into another, when to draw a pension pot and whether to buy an annuity, are regulated advice. How the State Pension fits with the rest of your retirement belongs in the same conversation with a regulated adviser. Giving it without authorisation is a criminal offence, so we do not give it, and nothing here concerns your own pension savings.

  • Free guidance. MoneyHelper publishes guidance on its website, and Pension Wise is its free appointment service for people aged 50 and over with a defined contribution pension
  • A regulated financial adviser. The Financial Conduct Authority register lists every firm authorised to give pension advice, and its website is where you check one
  • Your own record. A State Pension forecast comes from the GOV.UK website

Everything below this line is about the company.

Auto-enrolment when the money is tight

Automatic enrolment duties under the Pensions Act 2008 do not pause because a business is struggling. The company still enrols eligible staff, still owes the employer contributions it promised, and still has to hand over the employee contributions it deducted from wages.

The deducted money is where directors get into real trouble. It is not the company's money to use, even for a fortnight. It has to reach the scheme by the statutory deadline in the following month, and a trustee who does not receive it has to report the failure to the Pensions Regulator once it looks materially significant, so the Regulator usually hears about arrears without being told.

  • Enforcement escalates. A compliance notice, then a fixed penalty, then penalties accruing daily until it is put right
  • Inducing staff to opt out is prohibited. Persuading a worker to leave so the employer saves money is its own breach
  • It follows the director. Money deducted from wages and not passed on turns up in a conduct report

When the pension payment is the one that gets skipped, the problem is not the scheme, and an independent review will say how fast the company can catch up.

Defined benefit schemes and the real size of the deficit

A legacy final salary scheme is not a trade creditor. The figure in the accounts is an accounting measure. The figure that decides a restructuring, a sale or an insolvency is what it would cost to buy the members' benefits from an insurer, and it is usually much bigger. That becomes a statutory debt on the employer when the scheme winds up or the employer fails.

  • The trustees are an organised creditor. They have their own actuary and covenant adviser, and they negotiate with employers for a living
  • Money leaving the company gets examined. Dividends and intra-group payments made while a scheme is in deficit invite questions years later
  • The Pension Protection Fund sits behind the scheme. If the employer fails, the scheme may enter PPF assessment and members may end up with less than they were promised at retirement

So a company that looks saleable on its trading numbers can turn out not to be, and the scheme belongs in the restructuring conversation from the first week rather than the last.

The Pensions Regulator, transactions and sales

The Pensions Regulator's powers reach past the company that employs the members. Where a transaction leaves a defined benefit scheme worse off, it can require another group company, or a connected person, to make good the loss. There are also criminal offences aimed at conduct that avoids an employer debt or risks accrued benefits.

That changes how a deal is run rather than whether it can be run. Certain corporate events have to be notified, and clearance can be sought in advance, which binds the regulator only on the facts you actually disclose, but puts the transaction in front of it first. Design a sale or a corporate simplification and involve the scheme afterwards and it goes badly, so the pensions workstream runs alongside the financial due diligence in our transaction support and corporate finance work.

On a sale, staff who move with the business keep most of their employment rights, but occupational pension rights are treated separately and the buyer's obligation is a minimum one. Whether they transfer at all depends on the type of proceedings. In a pre-pack administration the scheme is usually left with the insolvent employer while the trade continues in the buyer's hands. That is lawful, and it is the transaction the regulator examines hardest, so the evidence on price has to exist at the time. Our administration page covers the process.

Where a scheme ranks when a company fails

One scheme produces two claims, and they rank very differently.

  • Employee money deducted from pay is preferential. What was taken from wages in the months before the insolvency ranks ahead of floating charge holders and ordinary unsecured creditors, provided the scheme is an occupational one. Unpaid employer contributions are not. Since contracting-out ended they rank with the ordinary unsecured creditors
  • The scheme's own deficit claim is not. That statutory debt ranks with the trade creditors, which on a large scheme means the trustees control the creditors' vote
  • The National Insurance Fund can fill part of the gap. Certain unpaid amounts are met from the fund on employees' behalf
  • A qualifying insolvency event starts PPF assessment. The scheme is then run with a view to whether the Pension Protection Fund takes it on

The ranking is GB-wide. The procedure around it is not: notices go in the Edinburgh Gazette, and a winding up goes to the Court of Session or to the sheriff court where paid-up share capital is £120,000 or less. If you have arrived from a winding up petition, the pension position is one to establish in the first week.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator or your administrator, so there is no process we need to happen, and where a formal appointment is required we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust. We are not FCA authorised, we do not arrange finance or deal in investments, and we do not act for scheme trustees.

Our work is corporate advice: what the pensions position does to the company's options, and who needs to be in the room. For actuarial and covenant work we bring in a trusted specialist firm. For anything personal, a regulated financial adviser. We work alongside your accountancy and legal advisers, and you can contact us first.

Frequently asked questions
Can you advise me about my own pension?

No. We are not FCA authorised, so that advice is not ours to give: not whether to move a scheme, and not whether to buy an annuity. We do not advise on State Pension timing either. Use MoneyHelper for free guidance, or a regulated financial adviser you have checked on the FCA register.

Can a company stop paying into the pension scheme to save cash?

Not the money already deducted from wages, which belongs to the members. The employer's own payments are a legal obligation too, and stopping them is a breach the scheme has to report. If that payment is the only thing keeping the month afloat, contingency planning is the next step.

What happens to a defined benefit scheme if the employer goes into administration?

A qualifying insolvency event puts it into a Pension Protection Fund assessment period. If the scheme cannot secure benefits at or above PPF levels, the PPF takes it on and pays compensation, which for some members is less than they were promised at retirement.

Does a scheme deficit stop me selling the business?

It changes the transaction rather than stopping it. Buyers price the risk, the trustees have a say, and the Pensions Regulator has to see the scheme was treated properly. The position needs to be understood before the business goes to market, which is part of exit planning.

Is any of this different in Scotland?

The rules are GB-wide, so the duties, the ranking and the Pensions Regulator's powers are the same. Procedure differs: the Edinburgh Gazette, the sheriff court or the Court of Session, and gratuitous alienations and unfair preferences where an English adviser would say transactions at an undervalue. If a director has given a personal guarantee too, Debt Help Scotland covers that side.

CTA block

Is the pension scheme the thing holding everything up?

One conversation will tell you what the scheme does to your options, who needs to be in the room, and what has to happen before anyone approaches a buyer or a lender. We take no appointments, so there is no answer we need this to have.

Breadcrumb: Financial Advisory › Capital Management

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Capital management

Capital management is making sure a business has the money it needs, in the form it needs, when it needs it. Working capital management is the short cycle: cash tied up in stock, in work in progress and in customers who have not paid, set against the credit your suppliers give you. Capital structure is the long one: how much of the business is funded by borrowing, how much by its owners, and whether the mix carries the plan.

Most owners meet the subject through one unpleasant discovery. The accounts say the year went well and the bank balance says otherwise. The money is inside the business, in a form that will not pay Friday's wages.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

A profitable company can run out of money

A business wins a bigger order than it has handled before. It buys materials, pays people to do the work, delivers and invoices. Revenue is recorded the day the invoice goes out, so the profit and loss account looks excellent. The customer pays in sixty days. The supplier wants paying in thirty, HMRC wants the VAT on an invoice nobody has settled, unless the business is on cash accounting, and the payroll runs regardless. Growth widens the gap: every order consumes money before it produces any. Overtrading is the old word for it, and it is still a common route to going into administration for a company with a full order book.

Profit and cash answer different questions. Profit says whether a period of trading was worthwhile. Cash says whether you can meet what falls due this week. The statutory cash flow test for insolvency is whether a company can pay its debts as they fall due, whatever the year looked like on paper. Profitability measures performance. Liquidity measures survival.

The cash conversion cycle

This is the number of days between money leaving the business and coming back for the same piece of work, and the most useful single figure in working capital management.

  • Stock days. How long goods sit before they sell, your money on the shelf
  • Work in progress. Time between doing the work and being entitled to bill for it, often the biggest block of trapped cash
  • Debtor days. How long customers take to pay. Not the terms you agreed, the days they take
  • Creditor days. How long you take to pay suppliers, the one part of the cycle that funds you
  • The cycle itself. Stock plus work in progress plus debtor days, less creditor days: the days you fund yourself

A business running a cycle of seventy days carries seventy days of cost before it is paid. Take a fortnight off that and cash is released permanently, with no lender involved.

Where the cash is trapped
  • Late invoicing. Work finished on the fourth, billed at month end, paid sixty days after that
  • No credit control. Terms exist on the invoice and nowhere else, and customers pay whoever asks first
  • Unbilled work in progress. Jobs part done and part billed, with a milestone nobody agreed at the outset
  • Equipment bought from the current account. A ten year asset paid for out of this month's cash, which is what asset finance exists to prevent
  • VAT and PAYE used as an overdraft. The most dangerous of them: it works for two quarters and then stops all at once, and it is usually the point at which a VAT loans conversation starts

Some of that is process, fixable within weeks. Some is structural: if your customers pay in ninety days and will not move, chasing changes nothing, and invoice finance may be the answer. We will also say when a facility is only interest on a problem better process would fix.

How much working capital the business needs

This should be a number rather than a feeling. A week by week cash flow across the next quarter shows the peak requirement rather than the average, and the peak is what matters: a business that averages comfortable and drops below zero for four days in October has a problem in October. An overdraft repayable on demand is not committed money, and liquidity a lender can withdraw in a phone call is not liquidity you can plan around.

Where the numbers need testing from outside, that is what an independent review is for, and lenders often ask for one.

Does the capital structure support the plan?

The second half of capital management is the shape of the funding itself. A business can be solvent today and funded in a way that will not survive its own plan.

  • The mix. How much debt sits against owners' capital. Gearing comfortable at current trading can be uncomfortable at forecast trading
  • The maturity. Short term money funding long term assets is the classic error. The overdraft that bought the machine is repayable on demand. The machine is not
  • The conditions. Covenants are tested on dates somebody else chose. Knowing which one you would breach first is worth more than knowing your rate
  • The personal exposure. Directors' loans, guarantees and security over the family home turn a company decision into a household one

Where the structure has stopped fitting the business, the answer is often debt restructuring: reprofiling repayments, replacing the wrong facility, or agreeing terms with lenders before a covenant test forces it. Where the trading is the problem, turnaround is the route, and contingency planning is for the owner who wants the fallback mapped before needing it.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes the liquidator or administrator of a company we have advised, so recommending a formal process never pays us better than fixing the business. Where one is genuinely needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust.

We are not FCA authorised, and we do not arrange finance, broker facilities or take commission from any lender. Where a facility is right we introduce a trusted specialist firm, which our finance and funding section explains. Capital management sits inside our wider financial advisory work, alongside corporate finance, because how a business is funded and what it is worth are the same question at different moments.

Frequently asked questions
What is capital management?

Capital management covers the working capital a business needs day to day and the capital structure that funds it over the longer term. It answers how much cash the business needs, where the cash it has has gone, and whether the funding fits the plan.

Can a profitable company really run out of money?

Yes, and it is one of the commoner ways a sound business fails. Profit is recorded when you invoice. Cash arrives when the customer pays. Growth widens the gap, because every order consumes money before it returns any.

What is the cash conversion cycle?

Stock days plus work in progress plus debtor days, less creditor days. It is the number of days a business funds itself between paying for work and being paid for it, and the first thing to examine when liquidity is tight.

Is more borrowing the answer?

Sometimes, and often not. Borrowing works when the business is sound and cash arrives later than it leaves. It is wrong when the business is losing money: the loan buys months and adds a creditor. We earn nothing either way.

Do you arrange the funding?

No. We are not FCA authorised and we do not broker facilities. Where we refer you on, that referral is disclosed and does not affect the independence of our advice. Where a facility is right we introduce a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool.

CTA block

Cash problem or profit problem?

The answer changes what you do next, and the two are easy to confuse from the inside. One conversation with your last accounts and current bank position usually settles it.

Breadcrumb: Financial Advisory › Commercial Arbitration

Eyebrow: Financial Advisory

Commercial arbitration and expert determination

Most commercial disputes are an argument about money wearing a legal costume. The contract settles who is entitled to what, and the fight is about the number. Commercial arbitration decides that argument privately, in front of arbitrators the parties choose themselves, and ends in an award that binds both sides.

We are not arbitrators and we are not solicitors. What we supply is the financial expertise inside the process: the valuation, the loss calculation, and evidence that holds up when the other side's expert pulls at it. Your solicitor runs the case. We answer the money question inside it, as we do in our forensic services work.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Arbitration, expert determination, mediation or court

These four are not interchangeable, and choosing wrong is expensive. The useful question is whether your disagreement is about the law or about a number.

  • Litigation. Public and adversarial, decided by a judge in the Court of Session or the sheriff court, on an open record your customers and bank can read
  • Commercial arbitration. Private, governed by the arbitration agreement in your contract and decided by arbitrators appointed for their expertise. The arbitral award is final and enforceable, and the grounds of appeal are narrow
  • Expert determination. One expert decides the point using their own knowledge, usually on paper and in weeks not months. No hearing, no arbitral tribunal, very little room to challenge. Share valuation and earn-out clauses often name it in advance
  • Mediation. Nobody decides anything. A mediator helps the parties reach their own settlement, and it earns its place while the relationship still has value

Where the disagreement is really about valuation or quantum, expert determination is often quicker and cheaper than arbitration. Where it turns on what the contract means, you want a lawyer deciding it. Settling that distinction when the clause is drafted saves more than any other choice in dispute resolution.

Scotland has its own arbitration regime

Almost everything written about commercial arbitration in the UK describes the English position. Arbitration seated in Scotland runs under the Arbitration (Scotland) Act 2010, not the Arbitration Act 1996 that applies in England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The 2010 Act carries the Scottish Arbitration Rules, some mandatory, some applying only until the parties agree otherwise.

The seat decides which regime governs you, and a seat is a legal address rather than a venue. If the dispute resolution clause in your contract names London, the arbitration is seated in England: the Arbitration Act 1996 governs the procedure and the English court supervises it, usually the Commercial Court, even where every hearing is in Glasgow and the contract itself is governed by Scots law. Scottish businesses sign up to a London seat more often than they realise, because the template came from London.

Two features of the Scottish Arbitration Rules are worth knowing. Confidentiality is written in as a default, where in England it rests on case law. So is the right to appeal to the court on a point of legal error, which the parties can contract out of.

The financial questions these disputes turn on
Valuation disagreements

What a company, a shareholding or a division is worth when the parties cannot agree. Maintainable earnings, minority discounts, directors' loan accounts, and the gap between what a formula produces and what the business would fetch. On a sale rather than a dispute, corporate finance is the page you want.

Shareholder and partnership fallings-out

Exit provisions, the buyout price, disputed drawings, and whether the accounts the price is calculated from can be relied on at all. These start as valuation arguments and become forensic ones. Owners planning an orderly separation should start at exit planning.

Contract and loss claims

Loss of profits from a breach, disputed variations, unpaid milestones, and the counterfactual: what would have happened had the contract been performed. That counterfactual is where claims of this kind are won and lost.

Completion accounts and earn-outs

Arguments after a deal about working capital, accounting policy and whether an earn-out target was met. The share purchase agreement usually sends these to expert determination, and that clause sets what the expert may consider. Our transaction support page covers the deal side.

International arbitration and enforcement

International arbitration exists mainly because of enforcement. A court judgment is hard to enforce against assets held abroad, while an arbitral award travels: the New York Convention obliges the courts of the states signed up to it to recognise an arbitral award made in another signatory state. That treaty is why cross-border contracts choose arbitration at all.

International commercial arbitration usually runs under the rules of an arbitral institution such as the LCIA in London, with ad hoc arbitration under the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules as the alternative. Whichever the arbitration agreement names, the financial evidence is built the same way, although currency, tax and the applicable law can move the figure more than the facts do.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments, sells no financial products and audits nothing, so there is no second engagement waiting behind the opinion we give. Where a formal appointment is needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust.

Disputes and distress turn up together more often than either side expects. If the counterparty is failing, the value of winning changes, and liquidation sets out what happens to a claim then. If the dispute is what threatens your own business, start with restructuring. The rest of this section sits on the financial advisory hub, and you can reach us through contact us.

Frequently asked questions
What is commercial arbitration?

A private process in which the parties to a commercial contract agree that a dispute between them is decided by arbitrators instead of by a court. The arbitral proceedings are private, and in Scotland confidential unless the parties agree otherwise, and they end in an award enforceable through the court like a decree.

Is arbitration cheaper than going to court?

Not always. The parties pay the arbitrators and the venue, so a small claim can cost more than it would in court. What arbitration buys is privacy, a decision maker who knows the sector, and a timetable the parties control.

Our contract says the seat is London. Does that matter?

It decides the procedural law. A London seat means the Arbitration Act 1996 and English law procedure apply, with the English court supervising, in practice usually the Commercial Court in London, even where the businesses and the evidence are entirely Scottish.

Can an arbitration award be enforced overseas?

Usually, and more easily than a court judgment. The New York Convention requires the courts of every state signed up to that treaty to recognise an arbitral award made elsewhere, apart from a limited set of grounds for refusal. It is the strongest argument for international arbitration where your counterparty's assets sit abroad.

Do we have to name an arbitral institution in the contract?

No. A contract can name an arbitral institution such as the LCIA, whose rules then administer the case for a fee, or provide for ad hoc arbitration that the parties and the arbitrators run themselves. Institutional rules cost more and remove a lot of argument about procedure.

Can you act as the arbitrator or as the deciding expert?

No. We are not arbitrators and we do not take appointments as the expert who decides. We are instructed by one party, or jointly by both, to produce the financial analysis and give evidence on it. Keeping those roles separate is what makes the evidence usable.

CTA block

Is the argument really about a number?

If it is, the route matters as much as the case you make, and both are easier to fix before positions harden. One conversation will tell you what the money question is and what it would take to answer.

Breadcrumb: Debt Help Scotland › Trust Deeds

Eyebrow: Debt Help Scotland

Protected trust deeds

In Scotland, and nowhere else in the UK, you can deal with unmanageable debt by granting a trust deed. You transfer your estate to a trustee, who realises what can be realised, takes contributions from your disposable income for an agreed period, and distributes the proceeds among your creditors. At the end of it the balance of the debts covered by the deed is written off. Where it becomes protected, and most do, the creditors bound by it can no longer pursue you or take diligence against you.

Protected trust deeds are a real and useful remedy, and also the debt solution most heavily marketed to people in Scotland, because arranging one earns a fee. Both things are true at once. The purpose of this page is to explain what it actually does, and to be honest about the two situations in which something else would serve you better.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Is a trust deed actually the right answer for you?

We arrange nothing. Nobody here becomes your trustee, we take no fee from a trust deed, and we are not paid by anyone who does. That is why this section comes first rather than last.

It may suit you if

You have unsecured debts of at least £5,000, which is the statutory minimum, typically credit cards, loans and overdrafts, and you genuinely cannot repay them in a reasonable time. You have disposable income you could make contributions from each month, and your circumstances are stable enough to keep those payments up for the full term. You want the creditor pressure to stop, and you accept that some of what you own may have to be realised to pay them.

Something else may suit you better

If you could repay the debt in full given time and protection from interest, the Debt Arrangement Scheme offers a Debt Payment Programme that does exactly that and writes nothing off, which means it does not touch your assets in the same way. If you have almost no disposable income and few assets, sequestration may be quicker and cleaner, and you would be discharged sooner. And if the debt is a company debt rather than yours, the answer may be on the insolvency practitioner side entirely.

If you have been recommended a protected trust deed by someone who would be paid to arrange it, and nobody mentioned a Debt Payment Programme, ask why. It is a fair question and any reasonable source of debt advice will have a reasonable answer. If a creditor is already taking action against you, ask about a moratorium too, because that buys time to get proper debt advice before you commit to anything.

How a trust deed becomes protected

This is the part that matters, and it is the part the marketing tends to skip.

Signing a trust deed does not by itself stop creditors taking action. What it creates initially is an ordinary trust deed, and that binds nobody except the creditors who sign up to it. The trustee registers it in the Register of Insolvencies and must send the paperwork to every known creditor within seven days. Creditors then have five weeks from registration to object. The deed becomes protected unless objections come in from a majority of them in number, or from creditors holding at least a third of the debt by value. Once protected, it binds every creditor covered by it, including those who never replied, and they can no longer take diligence against you for those debts. One narrow exception is worth knowing: a creditor who was never notified, or who objected in time, keeps a limited right to ask the court for your sequestration instead, and the court will only grant it if that is genuinely in the creditors' best interests.

If too many object, the deed does not become protected. It can still run as an ordinary trust deed with whoever signed up, but everyone else is free to continue their action against you, including going to court, and in practice a failed protection means reconsidering the whole approach.

The trustee must be a licensed insolvency practitioner, and the arrangement is supervised by the Accountant in Bankruptcy, Scotland's insolvency regulator, which also maintains the public Register of Insolvencies where the deed is recorded. Note one consequence of signing: while the trust deed subsists you cannot apply for your own sequestration, so it is a decision that closes a door as well as opening one.

What happens to your home

This is the first question almost everyone asks, and the honest answer is that it depends on your equity, not on the trust deed itself.

Your interest in your home forms part of the estate conveyed to the trustee. Your mortgage itself sits outside the trust deed and you keep paying it as normal, but the equity above the mortgage is what the trustee looks at. Where there is little or none, it is common for arrangements to be made that let you keep the property, sometimes by a third party paying the value of your interest, and sometimes because the equity is not worth realising. Where there is significant equity, the trustee has a duty to creditors to realise it, and that can mean the property has to be sold or the equity bought out. Where an agreement is reached to keep it, the payments for the equity typically run on after the four-year period rather than being found at the start. There is also a formal route, agreed before the deed is granted, that keeps the house outside the estate altogether where the lender agrees not to claim, and it requires a proper valuation by a chartered surveyor first.

What you should not do is sign anything before this has been worked through with a valuation and a redemption figure in front of you. An arrangement that looks affordable monthly can still end with the sale of a house, and finding that out in year three is not the same as knowing it in month one. If keeping the property is your priority, say so at the outset, because it may change which option is right.

The rest of what it affects
  • Your credit rating. The trust deed is recorded in the Register of Insolvencies, which is public and searchable, and credit reference agencies pick it up, so it appears on your credit file. The effect on your credit rating lasts years beyond the end of the arrangement, and it is one of the reasons a Debt Payment Programme suits some people better
  • Your vehicle. A car of modest value that you need for work is often retained; a valuable one is an asset like any other. Where the vehicle is on hire purchase it does not belong to you in the first place, and the agreement has to be dealt with separately
  • Your job. For most people, nothing changes. A minority of professions and roles have restrictions or notification requirements, and certain positions become difficult. Check your contract and any professional body rules before you sign, not after
  • Being a company director. A trust deed does not itself disqualify you, which surprises people. Sequestration is different: it is a criminal offence for an undischarged bankrupt to act as a director or take part in running a company without the court's permission. What a trust deed may do is trigger a term in the company's own articles of association, which under the standard Model Articles remove a director automatically where a composition is made with their creditors generally, or breach a shareholders' agreement, a lending covenant or an employment contract. Read the articles first
  • Windfalls during the term. An inheritance, a redundancy payment, a lottery win or a compensation award received while the deed runs is generally claimed for the creditors
  • New credit. The trust deed will restrict you from taking on credit during the arrangement, including credit cards, and any change in your income has to be reported
The trustee, the term and the money

The trustee is not your adviser. Their duty is to the creditors as a body, and their job is to realise what can be realised and distribute it. That is not a criticism, it is the design of the thing, and it is precisely why having someone independent explain the options to you beforehand matters.

You make contributions from your disposable income for the agreed term, which for most protected trust deeds is four years. The payments are set from a proper assessment of what you actually have left after reasonable living costs, including your mortgage or rent, using the Common Financial Statement, which is the statutory assessment tool, rather than a figure someone thinks you can manage. Social security benefits cannot be counted towards a contribution. If your circumstances change materially, the contributions can be reviewed in either direction, and you are discharged at the end.

A few debts survive the discharge whatever happens: student loans, court fines and penalties, compensation orders, aliment, and anything you incurred through fraud or breach of trust. A secured lender also keeps its rights over the security. Everything else covered by the deed is written off at the end.

The trustee's fees and outlays come out of the money collected, before the creditors are paid. That is normal and it is disclosed, but it is worth understanding: a proportion of what you pay in each month funds the administration rather than reducing your debt. Ask for the fee basis in writing before you sign.

What happens if you cannot keep it up

This is the risk the marketing does not lead with, and it is the reason the affordability assessment at the start matters so much.

If you stop paying, the trustee will first look at whether the contributions can be varied. Where the payments genuinely cannot be sustained, the trust deed can fail, though since 2024 there is a middle path: where circumstances have changed and there is no realistic prospect of resuming, the trustee can apply for an early discharge instead of letting the deed collapse. A failed trust deed is the worst of both worlds: the money you have paid in is gone, a good deal of it into fees, the debts revive to the extent they have not been paid, and your creditors are free to pursue you again. The trustee may also petition for your sequestration.

So the affordability figure at the outset should be conservative and should assume that some months will be worse than the one you are in now. An arrangement that only works if nothing goes wrong for four years is not an arrangement, it is a hope.

Trust deed, sequestration or DAS
Trust deed

Voluntary, four years for most people, and you are discharged from the remaining debt at the end. Your assets, including any equity in your home above the mortgage, are available to the trustee. Suits someone with real disposable income and debt they cannot clear in a sensible time.

Sequestration

Scotland's bankruptcy. Usually shorter, often cheaper to enter, and administered by a trustee who may be the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Being made bankrupt carries a wider public record and more restrictions while it lasts, and you are discharged sooner. For someone with minimal income and few assets it is frequently the more honest answer.

Debt Arrangement Scheme

A Debt Payment Programme that freezes interest and charges and stops creditor action while you repay in full over a longer period. Nothing is written off, which is why providers promote it least, and nothing is realised, which is why it is often the right answer for someone with equity in a home and a mortgage they want to keep.

The choice between them turns on three things: how much disposable income you really have, how much equity sits in your assets after the mortgage, and whether repaying the debt in full over a longer period is realistic. Anyone recommending one without having established all three is guessing.

If the debt came from a business

This is where most debt advice stops and where a large share of our work begins.

If you are a company director who signed a personal guarantee, or a sole trader, or a partner in a firm, you have two problems that have to be solved together. The company or the firm has its own position, and you have yours, and the order in which they are dealt with changes the outcome. Settling the personal side before the business position is resolved can leave you having paid for a liability that would have reduced. Dealing with the business first without understanding your guarantee exposure can leave you facing a claim you had not planned for.

Our creditors' voluntary liquidation and partnership liquidation pages cover the business side. What matters here is that the two are looked at as one problem by one adviser, which is the thing a debt-advice firm and an insolvency firm each do half of.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no appointments and arranges no trust deeds. Nobody here becomes your trustee, we receive no fee or commission from anyone who does, and there is no product at the end of this conversation.

What we do is establish the whole picture, including the business side if there is one, and tell you which of the routes actually fits your numbers, including the ones that pay nobody anything. Where a formal arrangement is the right answer we introduce you to an appropriately qualified person to advise on and administer it, and we stay alongside you.

That is the difference between advice and a sales process, and on this subject it is worth insisting on.

Frequently asked questions
What is a protected trust deed?

A voluntary arrangement, available only in Scotland, in which you convey your estate to a trustee and make payments from your disposable income for an agreed period, usually four years. Once protected it binds all the creditors it covers, they cannot pursue you or take diligence for those debts, and you are discharged from the remaining debt at the end.

Will I lose my house?

It depends on the equity above your mortgage rather than on the trust deed itself. Where there is little or none, arrangements are often made that let you keep the property. Where there is significant equity, the trustee has a duty to realise it for the creditors, and that may mean a sale or a buyout. Get a valuation and a redemption figure before you sign, not after.

Will my employer find out?

There is no general obligation to tell an employer, and for most people nothing changes. The Register of Insolvencies is public, so it is discoverable. Some professions and some roles have their own rules, and certain contracts and professional bodies require disclosure, so check yours before you sign. One thing worth knowing: if payments due from your wages are missed on two consecutive occasions, the trustee can instruct your employer directly to deduct them. Keeping the payments up is what keeps this private.

Can I be a company director during a trust deed?

A trust deed does not itself disqualify you from acting as a director. Sequestration is a different matter, because an undischarged bankrupt commits an offence by acting as a director or taking part in running a company without the court's permission. What a trust deed can do is trigger a clause in the company's own articles of association, which usually remove a director automatically on a composition with creditors generally, or breach a shareholders' agreement or a contract of employment. The answer is in your own documents rather than in insolvency law.

What happens if my circumstances change?

Tell the trustee early. Contributions can be reviewed up or down where circumstances change materially. What causes real damage is stopping payments without telling anyone, because a failed trust deed leaves the money paid in gone, the debts revived and the creditors free to act again.

Is a trust deed better than sequestration?

Not inherently. Protected trust deeds are better for some people and worse for others. Someone with real disposable income and assets worth protecting is often better off in a trust deed; someone with minimal income and few assets is frequently better off sequestrated and discharged sooner. The comparison has to be done on your numbers, ideally with independent debt advice rather than a provider's.

Does a trust deed cover my business debts?

It covers debts for which you are personally liable, which includes a personal guarantee you have given and the debts of a sole trade or a partnership. It does not deal with a limited company's own debts, which sit with the company. Where both exist, they need to be looked at together.

Who regulates trust deeds?

The trustee must be one of the licensed insolvency practitioners authorised to act, and the Accountant in Bankruptcy supervises the regime and maintains the Register of Insolvencies in which the trust deed is recorded.

CTA block

Has someone recommended a trust deed?

We arrange nothing and take no fee from any of these routes, so the answer you get is the one your numbers support. One conversation will tell you whether a trust deed, sequestration or the Debt Arrangement Scheme actually fits.
