Eyebrow: Debt Help Scotland

The Debt Arrangement Scheme

The Debt Arrangement Scheme, always shortened to DAS, is the Scottish Government's statutory way for Scottish residents to repay debt over a longer period without any of it being written off. You agree a Debt Payment Programme, you make a single affordable monthly payment, that money goes to a payment distributor who divides it among your creditors, and while the payment plan runs the interest and charges are frozen and your creditors cannot take diligence against you.

It is the least promoted form of debt management in Scotland and, for a particular kind of person, the best one. Nothing is written off, so it earns a provider considerably less than a Scottish trust deed does. Nothing is realised either, which is exactly why it suits someone with equity in a home they want to keep.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What a debt payment programme actually does
  • It freezes interest and charges. From the day the application goes in, not from approval, interest and charges stop being payable, and once the programme completes they cease to be owed at all. For someone whose balances have been rising despite paying every month, this alone changes the arithmetic completely
  • It stops diligence. Creditors covered by the programme cannot use earnings arrestment, bank arrestment or attachment against you, and cannot petition for your sequestration for those debts
  • It consolidates everything into one payment plan. A single monthly payment to a payment distributor, who divides it among your creditors, instead of managing a dozen separate arrangements with credit cards, loans and catalogues
  • It repays in full. The debt you owe on the day you apply is paid, over a longer period. The interest and charges that would otherwise have piled up are the only thing extinguished, and that is the trade for everything above. There is one long-stop: after twelve years, where seventy per cent of the original debt has been paid, the balance can be composed and discharged
  • It does not touch the home you live in. There is no trustee and nothing is conveyed to anybody. A programme can carry a condition that you realise an asset, but the regulations expressly except the house or mobile home you live in, and since 2018 it can only be brought in at all if you choose to include it

That last point is the one that decides it for a great many people, and it is the difference that gets least airtime.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It suits you if

You have a reliable monthly surplus, you could clear the debt in full given enough time and no more interest, and you have something worth protecting: equity in a home, or simply a strong preference for keeping your credit rating from taking the harder hit a formal insolvency brings. It also suits people whose profession or employment makes an insolvency awkward.

It does not suit you if

The debt is so large relative to your income that repaying it in full would take an unreasonable period. There is a point past which a programme becomes a life sentence rather than a solution, and at that point a trust deed or sequestration, which do write debt off, is the more honest answer. It also does not suit someone whose income is too irregular to commit to a monthly figure.

The honest test is arithmetic. Take the total debt, divide it by what you can genuinely afford each month, and look at the number of years that produces. If the answer is a period you can live with, DAS is very likely your answer. If it is not, it is not, and no amount of preferring it will change that.

Why you may not have been told about it

Worth saying directly, because it explains a pattern people notice.

A Scottish trust deed generates a fee for the firm that arranges and administers it. Sequestration generates a fee too. A Debt Payment Programme is administered by an approved money adviser, and where those advisors sit in the free advice sector, as many do, there is no commercial fee at all. The result is entirely predictable: the option that pays least is mentioned least.

That is not an accusation of dishonesty against anyone. It is a structural observation about how debt advice is paid for in the United Kingdom, and it is why the Financial Conduct Authority banned debt packagers from taking referral fees altogether in 2023, having found the fees paid for trust deeds and IVAs were far higher than for anything else. It is also why our position on this page is what it is: we arrange nothing, and we have nothing to gain from which route you take.

How you get one
  • Speak to an approved money adviser. Only an approved money adviser can submit a DAS application. Most of these debt advisers sit in local authorities, Citizens Advice Bureaux and other free-to-client services, and we can point you to one
  • Ask about the moratorium. Applying for a moratorium gives you six months' protection from diligence while you get advice and put the application together, and you can use it once in any twelve months. It is the thing to do first if a creditor is already moving against you
  • Build the financial statement. Income, reasonable living costs including your mortgage or rent, and what genuinely remains. This information is the whole application, and an over-optimistic figure here is what causes payment plans to fail later
  • The application goes to the DAS Administrator. That role sits with the Accountant in Bankruptcy
  • Creditors are notified and may object. A creditor who does not respond within twenty-one days is deemed to consent. Where creditors holding nine tenths by value consent, the programme is approved automatically. Where they do not, the DAS Administrator decides whether it is fair and reasonable, against prescribed criteria, and can approve it over an objection
  • The Debt Payment Plan starts. You make one monthly payment to a payment distributor, who distributes it to your creditors, and the interest and charges stop

The application itself is free to you, and a money adviser cannot charge an individual a fee for this work at all. There is a fee within the scheme, taken from what is distributed: twenty per cent to the payments distributor and two per cent to the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Creditors receive seventy-eight pence in the pound rather than you paying anything extra.

Your home, and why this is the section that matters

Under a Debt Payment Programme nothing is conveyed to a trustee, because there is no trustee. Your home is not part of any estate and nobody has a duty to creditors to realise it. The Administrator does look at any equity in land you own when deciding whether a programme is fair and reasonable, but the regulations expressly except the property you live in from being realised. You keep paying your mortgage as normal, outside the programme, and the DAS deals with the unsecured debt: credit cards, loans, overdrafts and the like. Mortgage arrears themselves are treated differently and should be raised with the adviser separately.

Compare that with a Scottish trust deed, where your interest in the property forms part of the estate conveyed to the trustee, and significant equity has to be realised for the creditors, potentially by a sale. For a homeowner with equity, that difference is frequently worth more than everything else on this page combined.

This is the single most common reason we tell someone to go and look at DAS. If you own a home with equity in it and you have been recommended a trust deed, get a second view before you sign anything.

What can go wrong
  • Missing payments. A programme can be revoked where arrears reach the equivalent of two months' payments. If it is revoked, the protection ends, the interest and charges that had been suspended become payable again back to the date you applied, the revocation itself counts as apparent insolvency, and you are back where you began with time lost
  • An over-optimistic budget. The commonest cause of the above. The figure should assume that some months will be worse than this one
  • A change in income. Payment plans can be varied where circumstances change, and a variation is far better than silence. Tell your debt adviser early
  • A creditor who will not engage. The fair and reasonable test exists precisely for this, and an objection does not automatically defeat an application
  • The debt was never going to be repayable. Where the arithmetic at the outset was wrong, a programme delays a decision rather than solving anything
  • Taking on new credit. Unlike a trust deed, the credit restriction here is in the regulations rather than in an agreement, with narrow exceptions for things like emergency repairs and trade credit in the ordinary course of business
DAS, trust deed or sequestration
Debt Arrangement Scheme

Repay in full over longer. Interest and charges frozen, diligence stopped, no trustee, no assets realised, no insolvency, and a softer effect on your credit rating. Suits a reliable monthly payment and assets worth protecting.

Trust deed

A formal insolvency. Contribute for a set term, usually four years, then the balance is written off. Your estate including any equity in your home is conveyed to a trustee. Suits someone who cannot repay in full in a sensible period.

Sequestration

Scotland's bankruptcy. Usually the shortest route and often the cheapest to enter, with the widest public record and the most restrictions during it. Frequently the right answer for someone with minimal income and few assets.

All three stop creditor action. The differences that decide between them are whether debt is written off, whether your assets are realised, and how long you are committed for. Any recommendation made without weighing all three is not a recommendation, it is a default.

If the debt came from a business

DAS is for individuals habitually resident in Scotland, and it covers debts for which you are personally liable. A director who has given a personal guarantee, a sole trader and a partner in a firm can all use it for their own liabilities, and business debts such as HMRC arrears in a sole trade can be included where the liability is personal.

There is also a separate route for the firm itself, known as Business DAS. A partnership, a trust or an unincorporated body can have its own programme, provided a money adviser certifies that it can pay within five years and is still trading. A sole trader is an individual and uses ordinary DAS. Where you are a partner, a debt can go into your programme or the firm's, but not both.

What DAS does not do is deal with a limited company's own debts, which stay with the company and need the routes on our insolvency practitioner side. Where both exist, the sequence matters: settling your personal position before the company's is resolved can mean paying for a liability that would have reduced. That joined-up view is the thing neither a money adviser nor an insolvency firm usually provides on its own, and it is the reason this section of the site exists.

Where we fit

Lancefield does not administer debt payment programmes and takes no fee from any debt remedy. We are not the approved money adviser who submits your application, and we will tell you who is.

What we do is establish the whole position, including the business side where there is one, work through the arithmetic honestly, and tell you which of the three routes your numbers actually support. Where that is DAS, we point you at an approved money adviser and you pay us nothing further. Where it is a trust deed or sequestration, we say so just as plainly.

Having no product to sell is the whole of what we offer on this page.

Frequently asked questions
What is the Debt Arrangement Scheme?

Scotland's statutory debt management scheme, run by the Scottish Government through the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Student loans are excluded from it by the regulations. You agree a Debt Payment Plan, make one affordable monthly payment that a payment distributor divides among your creditors, and while it runs the interest and charges are frozen and creditors cannot take diligence against you. You repay the debt in full over a longer period; nothing is written off.

Is DAS a form of insolvency?

No, and that is one of its main attractions. There is no trustee, nothing is conveyed to anybody, and it is not a sequestration or a trust deed. It is a statutory payment arrangement.

Will I lose my house?

No. There is no trustee and nothing is conveyed to anybody, and the regulations expressly except a house or mobile home you occupy as your main residence from being realised. Since 2018 it can only be included at all if you choose to include it. You continue paying your mortgage as normal outside the programme. This is the main reason DAS suits homeowners with equity better than a trust deed does.

Does it stop interest and charges?

Yes, that is the core of it. The freeze runs from the date of application rather than approval, and once the programme completes the suspended interest and charges cease to be owed altogether. For many people that is the difference between an arrangement that works and one that never finishes.

Can my creditors refuse?

A creditor can object, but an objection does not automatically defeat the application. Where creditors holding nine tenths of the debt by value agree, it is approved automatically. Otherwise the DAS Administrator decides whether the programme is fair and reasonable against prescribed criteria, and can approve it over an objection. A creditor who simply does not reply within twenty-one days is treated as consenting.

How long does a programme last?

As long as it takes to repay the debt at the agreed rate, so it depends on the balance and what you can afford. There is no statutory maximum for an individual, though the Administrator has to be satisfied the period is fair and reasonable, and after twelve years a composition can close out the remainder. The trade is that nothing is written off, so the period runs longer than a trust deed's fixed term.

Does it appear on my credit file?

Yes. The programme is recorded on the DAS Register, which is public, and credit reference agencies pick it up, so your credit rating is affected. The effect is generally regarded as less severe than a trust deed or sequestration, but it is real and it lasts.

Who can apply for me?

Only an approved money adviser can submit a DAS application. Most such advisors are in local authorities, Citizens Advice Bureaux and other free services. We are not one, and we will point you to one.

Been told a trust deed is your only option?

We administer nothing and take no fee from any of these routes. One conversation will tell you whether repaying in full under DAS is realistic, or whether something that writes debt off is the honest answer.

Jurisdiction note. Everything on this page is Scottish. Personal insolvency is devolved and the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016 governs it, so the Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 and the office of official receiver have no application here. Corporate insolvency law is largely GB-wide, but Scottish procedure runs under SSI 2018/347 for winding up and SI 2018/1082 for administration and company voluntary arrangements, and the AiB has no part in corporate appointments. The Accountant in Bankruptcy, explained

The Accountant in Bankruptcy is the public body that runs personal insolvency in Scotland. It awards bankruptcy, acts as trustee in a large share of cases and supervises the trustee in the rest, keeps the public register of Scottish insolvencies, and runs the statutory repayment scheme. Most people meet the name on an envelope, and the letter inside rarely explains what the organisation is.

This page covers what the AiB is, what it does, when it becomes your trustee, what it publishes about you, and how to deal with it. It is written for the person told to send an application there, and for the director whose company trouble has turned personal too.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What the Accountant in Bankruptcy is

The AiB, as it is shortened in its own letters and almost everywhere else, is a Scottish Government executive agency: inside government, but at arm's length from ministers, with its own chief executive and its own statutory duties. Most of those duties come from the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. The Accountant in Bankruptcy is also a person, a statutory office holder appointed by Scottish Ministers, whose staff work out of Kilwinning in Ayrshire.

It holds two roles that pull against each other. It regulates, overseeing every trustee other than itself and taking complaints about how that trustee has behaved. It also administers cases itself, and in a great many of them it is the trustee. One body can therefore be your case handler, your trustee and the referee at once.

What the AiB actually does
  • Awards bankruptcy. Apply for your own bankruptcy and the AiB decides, not a court. Creditors wanting you made bankrupt against your will petition the sheriff court
  • Acts as trustee. In a debtor application the AiB becomes trustee over your estate unless a licensed insolvency practitioner is named and agrees to act
  • Supervises every other trustee. An insolvency practitioner acting as trustee in a Scottish bankruptcy, or under a protected trust deed, accounts to the AiB for the case
  • Runs the Debt Arrangement Scheme. As DAS Administrator it approves each debt payment programme and oversees the money moving through it
  • Keeps the Register of Insolvencies. The public record of Scottish personal insolvency cases, and of Scottish liquidations and receiverships
  • Grants moratoriums. A short application buys a period during which most enforcement against you must stop while you take advice
  • Publishes the numbers. The quarterly Scottish Statutory Debt Solutions Statistics, and the Notes for Guidance that trustees and money advisers work from

Two of those matter far more than the rest: whether the AiB is your trustee, and what reaches the register.

When the AiB is your trustee

A trustee takes control of your estate, sells what can be sold, deals with creditors' claims and pays out what there is. Somebody does that job in every bankruptcy, and here it falls to the AiB by default.

The AiB acts as trustee wherever nobody else is appointed. In a debtor application you may name an insolvency practitioner willing to act, and that person becomes your trustee instead. It is also trustee in every Minimal Asset Process bankruptcy, and it picks up any case where a trustee resigns, dies or is removed without replacement.

Your trustee is not your adviser and is not acting for you. The duties are owed to creditors, and they take in how the debt arose, what assets you have not mentioned and whether you have income to spare. Being straight from the first form is the most useful thing you can do.

Creditors then claim through the appointment rather than chasing you. They deal with the trustee rather than with you, and they cannot continue diligence, the Scottish word for enforcement such as an earnings arrestment or a bank arrestment. Creditors keep some rights: a secured lender still holds its security over your home, and creditors can object to your discharge.

Where you have surplus income, it is assessed and you are asked for a monthly payment, set by statutory calculation rather than by negotiation. That payment runs for a fixed period. No contribution can be taken from social security benefits, and where your income comes solely from benefits the contribution is fixed at zero.

The Register of Insolvencies

The AiB keeps that register, and it is genuinely public: anyone with an internet connection can search it, free, without saying who they are or why. This is the part most people find hardest, and it is better faced now than discovered later.

An entry names you, gives an address, and records the date of the award, the trustee's name and contact details, and the date you are discharged. It does not name your creditors. A trust deed appears once the trustee registers notice of it, and Scottish liquidations and receiverships appear too, which is how creditors check a customer.

Very few people are ever looked up. Credit reference agencies do check, and so do some lenders and some employers in regulated roles. The larger effect is on your credit rating: a bankruptcy sits on your credit file for years counted from the award rather than from your discharge. For most people the credit rating damage arrived long before, with the defaults that led here.

Your bank account is a separate question. Bankruptcy does not close a bank account by itself, but banks often freeze or close one on learning of it, particularly where the same bank is owed money. Opening a basic bank account elsewhere first, with wages and benefits paid into it, saves trouble later.

How the AiB differs from the Insolvency Service

The Insolvency Service is a UK government agency, an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade, whose personal insolvency work covers England and Wales, and its official receivers act there. It has no role in Scottish personal insolvency, and the AiB has none south of the border. The nearest thing to an IVA in England is a protected trust deed here, and the statutory repayment scheme has no English counterpart.

Some differences are structural. In England and Wales a debtor's bankruptcy application goes to an adjudicator; here it goes to the AiB, and there is no official receiver because the AiB does that work itself. Nor does the AiB license insolvency practitioners: professional bodies authorise them across Great Britain, and the AiB supervises how they run Scottish cases.

Corporate insolvency runs the other way round. Liquidation and administration are largely GB-wide law, so a Scottish company closing follows broadly the same statute as an English one, and the AiB appoints nobody to a company. A director facing a failed business and a personal shortfall deals with two systems in the same month.

Dealing with the AiB
  • Everything runs on your case reference. Quote it on every letter, form and call
  • Most dealings are with the trustee, not a switchboard. Where an insolvency practitioner holds the appointment, the AiB supervises rather than handles the case
  • Answer the forms fully and on time. A half complete statement of assets and liabilities invites more questions
  • Report changes as they happen. A new job, a drop in income, a move or an inheritance all have to be disclosed, and any payment can be reassessed either way
  • Ask for a review if a decision looks wrong. Many AiB decisions can be reviewed on request, with an appeal to the sheriff from the review, and the time limits are short
  • Complaints have their own route. The AiB runs a complaints procedure, and what it does not resolve can go to the Scottish Public Services Ombudsman

One thing causes most of the frustration we hear about: the AiB administers the process, it does not advise you on whether the process suits you. Its staff cannot say whether a trust deed would protect your home better than bankruptcy would. The law requires an approved money adviser before any debtor application in any event, and free advice is available from Citizens Advice Scotland, StepChange and National Debtline.

Where the AiB fits among your options

Most people who reach this page are working out which of three formal routes applies. The AiB touches all three.

Bankruptcy, or sequestration

The formal name is sequestration, though bankruptcy is the ordinary Scottish word and the AiB uses both. Assets are realised, creditors receive what there is, and the balance is written off. The AiB is either your trustee or the supervisor of the practitioner who is, and under the Minimal Asset Process it is always the trustee.

Protected trust deed

A voluntary arrangement with your creditors, run by an insolvency practitioner and supervised by the AiB rather than administered by it. You pay a contribution for a set period and the remaining unsecured balance is written off at the end, provided the deed became protected and you kept to its terms. Our page on trust deeds explains how protection is obtained.

Debt Arrangement Scheme

A statutory repayment programme: you repay the debt in full over a longer period, interest and charges frozen, creditors unable to enforce, and nothing written off because nothing needs to be. The AiB approves it as DAS Administrator. See Debt Arrangement Scheme.

If the debt is your company's rather than yours, the AiB is not the body you need. A winding up petition already served, a director-led CVL, or a partnership insolvency where partners carry personal liability are corporate questions first. The rest of Debt Help Scotland covers the personal side, and the two are best dealt with together.

Where we fit

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your trustee, and we have nothing to gain from you entering any particular process, which is the reason the advice can be straight.

We read your position before anything is filed and tell you which route fits, or that none of them does yet. Where a formal appointment is genuinely needed we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust. If free advice is all you need, we will say so. Get in touch when you are ready.

Frequently asked questions
Is the Accountant in Bankruptcy the same as the Insolvency Service?

No. The AiB handles personal insolvency here. The Insolvency Service is a UK government agency whose personal insolvency work covers England and Wales, and its official receivers have no function north of the border. The process, the terms and the alternatives all differ, so English guidance will mislead you.

How do I apply for bankruptcy?

You see an approved money adviser first, which the law requires rather than recommends, and that adviser lodges the application for you. A Minimal Asset Process bankruptcy is the shorter route for people on a low income with almost nothing to realise; full administration bankruptcy covers everyone else. The Minimal Asset Process carries limits on what you can owe and own, and those limits change, so check them rather than assuming. The AiB decides the application either way.

What happens to my home?

Your share of a property you own forms part of the estate the trustee deals with, so a home you own is at risk, though a sale is not automatic. Equity, joint ownership and whether the mortgage is kept up all bear on it, and a secured lender keeps its security either way. A trust deed treats a home differently, which is why homeowners should take advice first.

What happens to my creditors?

They deal with the trustee instead of with you. Creditors submit claims, interest and charges on the included debts stop, and enforcement for those debts stops. Creditors share whatever is realised after the costs of the process and any preferential claims, which in many cases is very little. That is the point of the process rather than a flaw in it, and creditors know it going in.

Will my bankruptcy appear on a public register?

Yes, on the Register of Insolvencies, which anybody can search free of charge. The entry shows your name, an address, the date of the award, the trustee's details and the date of your discharge, but not the names of your creditors. Your employer is not told as a matter of routine unless your role or profession requires it.

Can the AiB stop creditors chasing me before I apply?

It can, for a while. A moratorium application to the AiB gives protection from most diligence while you decide what to do, and it can be used once in a rolling period. It does not reduce the debt, but it buys room to take proper advice rather than signing up to the first thing offered.

CTA block

Not sure whether the AiB should be hearing from you at all?

We will read your position, tell you which route actually fits, and say so plainly if the answer is free advice rather than us. It costs nothing and commits you to nothing.

Breadcrumb: Home

Eyebrow: Clarity when it matters most

Independent insolvency and restructuring advice in Glasgow

If money worries are keeping you awake, you can talk to us. One confidential conversation is enough to start, and it commits you to nothing. We advise company directors, sole traders, partners and individuals across the UK and Ireland, and the first thing we do is establish where you actually stand rather than what someone wants to sell you.

Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator or trustee, which means there is no procedure we earn anything from recommending. That single structural choice is why we can tell you a formal process is the wrong answer, and it is the reason accountants and solicitors send us their clients.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

You are not the first person to leave it too long

Most people who contact us have been carrying it alone for a long time before they say anything. People tend to wait between six and eighteen months before asking for help, and some struggle on for years. The reasons are always the same: it did not feel serious enough yet, asking might make it official, and there was a persistent hope that the next contract would fix it.

What actually happens in that period is that the options narrow. A business with six months of runway can sell a division, refinance, negotiate, restructure its debt or close in an orderly way and pay its creditors. The same business with six weeks can do almost none of that. Nothing about it changed except the time available.

So the single most useful thing on this page is this: getting advice does not commit you to anything, and it does not start a process. It tells you what your options are while you still have them.

What we do
Insolvency

The formal procedures and, more often, whether you actually need one. Liquidation in its three forms, administration, a company voluntary arrangement, and what to do the day a winding up petition arrives.

Restructuring

Fixing a business before it becomes an insolvency question. Turnaround, debt restructuring, an independent review when a lender asks for one, and exit planning for owners on the way out.

Debt Help Scotland

Personal debt under Scots law, which works differently from England. Sequestration, protected trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme, explained by people who are not paid to sell you one.

Financial Advisory

Corporate finance, forensic accounting and expert evidence, transaction support, pensions and capital. Independent advice on the numbers, with nothing attached to the answer.

Finance and Funding

We are not brokers and arrange nothing. Where funding is genuinely the answer we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we say plainly when more borrowing is the wrong move.

Accountancy

Ongoing accountancy is not what we do. We refer it to a firm we would use ourselves, and keep our own work to the specialism.

Who we help
  • Company directors under creditor pressure, particularly those who signed a personal guarantee and have realised it is a second problem rather than a footnote
  • Sole traders and partners, who carry business debt personally and for whom the business and personal questions are genuinely one question
  • Individuals with debt that has stopped being manageable, who want to understand the Scottish options before committing to any of them
  • Accountants and solicitors who need a specialist for a client they intend to keep, and who want that client handed back
  • Lenders and creditors who need an independent read on a borrower before deciding what to do

In business terms that usually means companies from around £50,000 of turnover up to about £20 million: the range where the owner is still in the room and the decisions are personal as well as commercial. Hospitality and leisure, construction and the supply chain behind both come through the door more than any other sector.

Who you would be speaking to

Lancefield is led by Phil Dunn, who has spent over twenty years in restructuring and recovery across three of the Big Four accounting firms. He works as a consultant rather than as a licensed insolvency practitioner, and does not take formal appointments. Where a licensed practitioner, a solicitor, a valuer or a funder is needed, he brings in the right one and stays alongside you.

That is a deliberate model rather than a limitation. It means the person assessing your position has no appointment waiting at the end of the assessment. Our about page sets out the background and the principles in full.

How it starts
  • A confidential conversation. Free, no obligation, and nothing is filed or registered anywhere as a result of it
  • A diagnostic review. The whole picture, business and personal together, so nothing surfaces late
  • Your options, in plain English. Every realistic route with its consequences attached, including the ones that earn us nothing
  • Support if you want it. We handle the mechanics, deal with creditors and HMRC, and bring in a licensed practitioner where the law requires one
  • We stay involved. Through implementation and afterwards, rather than stopping at the advice

If nothing needs to happen yet, we will tell you that too, and contingency planning is how you prepare for the decision without making it today.

Why independence is the whole point

This market has a trust problem and it is not a secret inside the profession. A great deal of advice comes from people paid out of the procedure they are recommending, whether through the appointment itself or a product carrying a commission. The question of whether you need that procedure ends up being answered by someone with a stake in the answer.

We took the appointments out of the model so the advice could be straight. It costs us the fee income a licensed practice earns from formal work, and it buys the ability to say the sentence that matters most often: you do not need this yet.

Frequently asked questions
Does contacting you start a formal process?

No. A conversation is a conversation. Nothing is filed, registered or notified to anyone, there is no public record of having taken advice, and no creditor learns anything. You decide what happens next, at your own pace.

Are you insolvency practitioners?

No, and we are careful with the term: only a licence holder can act as an insolvency practitioner, and doing so without a licence is a criminal offence. We are independent advisers. Where a formal appointment is required by law, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust, and we stay alongside you through it.

What does the first conversation cost?

Nothing, and it commits you to nothing. Any work beyond it is scoped and priced before it starts, so you always know what you are agreeing to.

Is it too early to call?

Almost certainly not. The commonest regret we hear is having waited, and the options available at six months of runway are very different from those at six weeks. Early advice is the cheapest advice there is.

Do you only work in Glasgow?

We are a Glasgow firm and much of our work is across the west of Scotland, but we advise across the UK and Ireland. The jurisdictions genuinely differ, particularly on personal insolvency, and getting that right is part of the job.

I am an accountant with a client in difficulty. What happens to the relationship?

It stays yours. We handle the specialist question and hand the client back. A good proportion of our work arrives from accountants and solicitors, and it continues arriving because we do not absorb their clients.

CTA block

One conversation will tell you where you stand.

We take no appointments, so nothing we recommend earns us a fee for carrying it out. Tell us what you are dealing with and we will tell you what your options actually are.

About Lancefield Advisory

Lancefield Advisory is an insolvency and restructuring advisory firm in Glasgow. We advise company directors, sole traders, partners and individuals under financial pressure who want to know where they actually stand before committing to anything.

The firm was built around one structural choice, and it explains most of what follows. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator or trustee, so there is no outcome we have an interest in steering you towards.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Why the firm exists

The insolvency and debt advice market has a trust problem, and it is no secret inside the profession. Much of the advice comes from people paid out of the procedure they recommend, whether from the appointment itself or from a product carrying a commission. So the question of whether you need that procedure gets answered by someone with a stake in the answer.

The pattern is familiar. Liquidation proposed where a turnaround was still possible, or a director pushed towards a default answer before anyone has looked at what they signed personally. The harm is rarely a shortage of options. It is the absence of an unbiased read on them while there is still time to use them.

Lancefield was set up as the counterweight. We look at the whole position, business and personal together, and say what we think.

Phil Dunn

Lancefield Advisory is led by Phil Dunn, who has spent over twenty years in restructuring and recovery, gained across three of the Big Four accounting firms. That is two decades at the difficult end of this work: lenders who have run out of patience, HMRC arrears that have been rolling for a year or more, and directors who signed a personal guarantee and have not slept properly since.

Phil works as a consultant rather than as a licensed insolvency practitioner, and the distinction is deliberate rather than incidental. He is not licensed to take formal appointments and does not seek them. What he does is establish where a business or an individual actually stands, then bring in the right licensed specialist for whichever part of the problem needs one. On any given case that might be an insolvency practitioner, a solicitor, a valuer, a tax adviser or a funder. His job is to work out what is genuinely required and assemble it, not to be all of it.

He describes his own role as a trusted adviser rather than a technician, and the test he applies to it is a practical one: whether a professional contact sends him a second client after the first. Most of his work arrives that way.

Who sends us work, and why

A large share of what we do comes from other professionals rather than directly from the businesses themselves, and the reasons are worth stating because they explain how we work.

  • Accountants who cannot carry out restructuring or debt work themselves, whether for independence reasons, because the work sits outside their practice, or because the client relationship is too valuable to risk on unfamiliar ground
  • Solicitors approached by a client for corporate debt advice, who need a financial specialist alongside them rather than a firm that will absorb the client
  • Lenders and funders who need an independent read on a borrower's position before deciding what to do about it
  • Directors and individuals who found us directly, usually late at night, usually after months of not asking anyone

What the professional referrers want is the same thing in each case: a specialist who will handle a sensitive situation properly, keep them informed, and hand the client back. That is the whole basis of the relationship and it is why the independent business review and advisory work sits where it does, deliberately separate from taking appointments.

Who we work with

Distressed small and medium-sized businesses, sole traders, partners and private individuals. In practice that means companies from around £50,000 of turnover up to roughly £20 million, which is the range where the owner is still in the room and the decisions are personal as well as commercial.

We advise across every sector, though three come through the door more than the rest: hospitality and leisure, construction, and the supply chain behind both. That concentration is useful to a client, because it means we can usually tell you in a first conversation whether what you are seeing is ordinary for your sector or a sign of something structural. Our hospitality finance and contractor finance pages set out what we see in each.

Geographically we are a Glasgow firm, and we have people across Scotland, England and Ireland. The jurisdictions genuinely differ, which matters more than most advisers admit. Personal insolvency in Scotland runs on its own statute with its own regulator, and a firm working from English precedent will get parts of it wrong. Our Debt Help Scotland section covers sequestration, trust deeds and the Debt Arrangement Scheme as they actually work here.

What a good outcome looks like

There is a persistent misconception about why businesses fail and what happens when they get into difficulty, and it costs people time they cannot afford. Insolvency is treated as a single event with one meaning, when the reality is a range of outcomes that differ enormously.

The part that gets least attention is the positive side of a restructuring process: jobs kept, suppliers paid, a landlord dealt with properly, a business that continues in some form rather than stopping. Those outcomes are frequently available and frequently missed, because the people who could have taken them did not know they were there.

So the most satisfying work here is rarely the dramatic kind. It is the case where someone asked early enough that the good options were still on the table.

Why we take no appointments

Certain roles in a formal insolvency can only be held by a licensed insolvency practitioner: liquidator, administrator, nominee and supervisor of a company voluntary arrangement, and in Scotland trustee under a trust deed for creditors, or trustee in a sequestration where the Accountant in Bankruptcy is not acting. Lancefield holds none and does not seek them.

Where a formal appointment genuinely is needed, we bring in a licensed practitioner we know and trust, and stay alongside you rather than handing you over at the door. The same applies to the other specialisms a difficult case pulls in: valuers, solicitors, tax advisers, funders. Phil's job is to work out what is actually required and assemble it, not to be all of it.

Because nobody here takes the appointment, we earn nothing from one happening, which leaves us free to say when a formal procedure is the wrong answer. Most firms in this market are not in a position to write that sentence.

What we believe

Six principles run through the work. They were written down before this website was, and they decide the awkward cases.

  • Integrity first. The advice has to be right for the client, including when it is uncomfortable or less profitable for us
  • Clarity over complexity. Confusion does real damage here, and plain explanation is most of what restores control
  • People before profit. Vulnerable situations call for restraint, not a sales process
  • Results through realism. Honest outcomes rather than false hope, and no promises about what a procedure will achieve
  • Follow-through. Responsibility does not end when the advice is given, it runs through to resolution
  • Specialism over breadth. We do not try to do everything. Where a specialist firm will serve you better, we refer, and we stand behind who we refer to

That last one is why our finance and funding and accountancy pages point to a trusted specialist firm rather than pretend the work happens in house. Not a panel. Not a broker pool.

The Clarity Path

People hesitate because they think asking a question starts something they cannot stop. It does not. You keep control of the pace.

  • Confidential consultation. A first conversation to understand the situation and any deadlines already running against you. Free, and it commits you to nothing
  • Diagnostic review. The full picture, business and personal at once, so nothing surfaces late. Where a lender or board needs it in writing, that becomes an independent review
  • Clear, unbiased options. Every realistic route in plain English with its consequences attached, from turnaround and debt restructuring through to liquidation where that is where things stand
  • Supported implementation. If action is needed we handle the mechanics, deal with creditors and HMRC, and bring in a licensed practitioner where the law requires one
  • Ongoing support. We stay involved after the decision, through recovery and onto steadier ground

Acting before you are forced to is what most changes the options left, which is what contingency planning is for.

One practical point about how we work. Seeking advice about debt is stressful, and for a lot of people an email form is the wrong way to start. We try to be easy to reach and we still do a great deal of this face to face, because a fair number of clients prefer it to a screen. Whichever you want is fine, and you can contact us either way.

Where we work, and what we cover

We are at 48 West George Street in Glasgow, and work across the UK and Ireland, so where the business sits is rarely the obstacle people expect. The jurisdictions do differ, though. Personal insolvency in Scotland has its own statute and its own regulator, and a firm working from English precedent will get parts of it wrong. Our Debt Help Scotland section covers those routes properly.

The work divides into four areas: restructuring, what a business does while it still has choices; insolvency, the formal procedures including administration; Debt Help Scotland, the personal side, frequently the same problem wearing different clothes; and financial advisory, covering valuation, forensic and transaction work.

Some prefer to sit across a table, others the phone. Either works, so contact us.

Frequently asked questions
Are you insolvency practitioners?

No. We are advisers. Formal appointments such as liquidator, administrator or trustee are restricted to licence holders, with one Scottish exception: the Accountant in Bankruptcy acts as trustee in most sequestrations. Lancefield takes none of them. Advice is not restricted in the same way, though advice about personal debt is separately regulated, which is worth knowing when you work out who you are speaking to.

Does the first conversation cost anything?

No. The first consultation is free, confidential and commits you to nothing. You can take what you learn and never speak to us again.

Will contacting you start a process I cannot stop?

No. Nothing becomes formal until you decide to start it, and that decision stays yours. The belief that asking for advice triggers consequences is why many directors wait until their options have narrowed.

Do you work alongside my accountant or solicitor?

Routinely, and a good number of our enquiries arrive that way. We work with a client's existing advisers rather than replacing them.

Do you only work in Scotland?

No. The Insolvency Act 1986 covers Great Britain, but Scotland has its own court rules, its own challengeable-transaction regime and an entirely separate personal insolvency system. Ireland is different again. If your position straddles a border, say so early. We write about those differences in Insights, because most guidance a Scottish director finds online is written for England.

What is the Discretion Guarantee?

Every conversation is completely confidential, from the first call onwards, whether or not you become a client. We state it as a promise rather than leave it as an assumption.

CTA block

Want an honest read on where you stand?

One conversation is usually enough to tell you whether this is as serious as it feels. It is free, and you will get a straight answer.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Every conversation is 100% confidential, always. That is our Discretion Guarantee.

Breadcrumb: Contact

Eyebrow: Contact

Speak to us, in confidence

Most people who get in touch have been turning it over for weeks, some for months. The first conversation costs nothing and commits you to nothing. No engagement letter, no procedure started, no letters going out to anyone.

It helps to know who you are speaking to. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator or trustee, so there is no procedure we are paid to sell you.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

How to reach us

Lancefield Advisory, 48 West George Street, Glasgow G2 1BP.

[DEV: telephone and email are still unconfirmed and must not be invented. All three details, once confirmed, must match the Google Business Profile entry exactly, character for character. The company registration details for the footer are also still outstanding. An email address is not optional once the site is live: the Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations 2002 reg.6(1) require the provider's name, the geographic address and an electronic mail address to be given, so this has to be resolved before launch rather than after it.]

The form comes straight to us. A sentence or two is enough: who you are, what the business does, and what has brought you here.

How quickly we reply

We aim to come back to you the same working day, and to pick up anything that lands over a weekend on Monday morning. If a winding up petition has been served, or another clock is already running, say so in the first line.

What the first conversation covers

Around half an hour, by phone, video, or in person in Glasgow. We ask what has happened and where the pressure is coming from, then tell you where you stand.

  • What is actually wrong. Distress and insolvency are different states, and the difference decides what is still open to you. Where that is unclear, an independent review settles it
  • Which routes are realistic. Turnaround work, debt restructuring, a company voluntary arrangement, or an orderly winding the company up. Each carries consequences and we go through them
  • Where you stand personally. A signed personal guarantee makes the company problem and your own finances one problem in two halves. Debt Help Scotland covers that side

Where a formal appointment genuinely is needed, we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we know and trust. That is an introduction, not a sale.

What to have ready

Nothing. You do not need figures or a tidy explanation, and plenty of first calls happen with someone who has not opened the post in a fortnight. If you have recent management accounts, a rough list of who is owed what, and the detail of any guarantees you signed, we get specific faster.

What we do with what you tell us

It stays with us. We will not approach your bank, your lender, HMRC or your accountant unless you ask us to, or unless the law requires it, and nothing becomes formal unless you decide to start something. If you would rather we left no voicemail, say so.

If you feel awkward about calling

Almost everyone does. Directors tend to open by apologising, as though two hard years were a character flaw. Businesses run into trouble for ordinary reasons and we are not going to be shocked by yours. The people who leave it longest have the least room left to move, which is the only real cost of waiting. That is the argument for contingency planning.

For accountants and solicitors

If you have a client in difficulty, contact us directly rather than through the form. We take no appointments and do no compliance work, so we are not competing for your relationship. Your client stays yours. We give a second opinion, an options review, or the conversation you would rather not be the one to have. Much of our restructuring and financial advisory work starts this way.

Frequently asked questions
Is the first conversation really free?

Yes, with no obligation attached. If we think you need nothing from us, we will say so.

Does contacting you start anything formal?

No. Nothing becomes official until you choose to begin a procedure.

Do I need to be in Glasgow?

No. We work across Scotland, and most first conversations happen by phone or video.

Can I ask about a personal debt problem rather than a company one?

Yes. Directors frequently have both at once, and our advice on Scottish bankruptcy and trust deeds sits on that side.

What if I already have an accountant?

Good. We work alongside your existing accountant rather than replacing them.

CTA block

Ready to say it out loud?

One conversation, free, and entirely your decision what happens after it. Most people tell us the waiting was the worst part.

Every conversation is 100% confidential, always. That is our Discretion Guarantee.

Breadcrumb: Insights

Eyebrow: Insights

Plain writing on the decisions directors actually face

This is where we publish what we learn advising Scottish businesses in difficulty. Every piece starts with a question a director or an adviser has put to us, and answers it plainly.

We do not run commentary on the week's news. Quarterly statistics and court rulings are covered well elsewhere and rarely change what you should do on Monday morning. What is harder to find is a straight account of how a process runs in Scotland, what it means for you personally, and what the alternatives were before anyone reached for a formal appointment.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What you will find here

Three kinds of writing, all of it drawn from live work rather than from a textbook.

  • How a process actually runs. Step by step accounts of liquidation, administration and what follows a winding up petition, with Scottish procedure stated correctly rather than borrowed from English practice
  • The decisions before the process. Where turnaround work, debt restructuring or an independent review still leaves options open, and how to tell when it does not
  • The personal side. Personal guarantees, director exposure, and the point at which a company problem becomes a sequestration or trust deeds question, which our Debt Help Scotland section covers in full

Because we take no insolvency appointments, we can write about when a formal procedure is the wrong answer. A firm whose fee depends on that procedure happening cannot really write that piece.

Who it is written for

Owners and directors of Scottish businesses first. Accountants and solicitors second, because they are usually asked the question before we are, and something they can forward to a client is more use than a brochure.

If your position is urgent, do not wait for us to write about it. The insolvency and restructuring sections cover the main routes today, and you can contact us for a confidential conversation.

Planned, not yet published

Nothing below has been written yet. These are the pieces we intend to publish first.

  • What a personal guarantee really means once the company closes
  • Choosing an insolvency practitioner: the three questions worth asking
  • Acting early: what contingency planning buys a director

Frequently asked questions
How often will you publish?

When there is something worth saying. We would rather post four useful pieces a year than a monthly filler.

Who writes these?

Named people at Lancefield, with a byline and a short biography on every post. If you cannot see who wrote something, you cannot judge whether they know the subject.

Is any of this advice for my situation?

No. General writing cannot account for your numbers, your security or your guarantees. Use it to ask better questions, then have the conversation.

Do you cover personal debt as well as company matters?

Yes, because for many of our clients they are one problem. Personal insolvency in Scotland runs on sequestration, which is what bankruptcy is called here, and on protected trust deeds. There is no IVA in Scotland.

Can I suggest something for you to write about?

Please do. Questions from directors, and from the accountants who refer them, are where most of these pieces start.

CTA block

Would a straight answer be more use than an article?

Most people who land here have one specific problem and limited time. A short call will tell you more than any page can.

Eyebrow: Creditor Services

Creditors' guides to insolvency practitioners' fees

If a company or person that owes you money has entered a formal insolvency procedure, you have a financial interest in what the office holder is paid, because it comes from the same estate your dividend does. The profession publishes a guide to fees for each procedure, and this page points you to the right one. Our fee estimates page explains how that figure is set, and details of our work covers what the office holder has to report to you.

One thing first. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here acts as liquidator, administrator or trustee, so we hold no estate and have no remuneration of our own to publish. These guides govern the licensed insolvency practitioner we bring in, and any other office holder you deal with.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What SIP 9 asks of an office holder

SIP 9 is the Statement of Insolvency Practice on payments from an estate. The Scottish version took effect on 1 April 2021 and covers proceedings under the Insolvency Act 1986 and the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. A members' voluntary liquidation is caught only if those paying the fees ask for the disclosures, and a moratorium under Part A1 of the Insolvency Act 1986 sits outside it too.

Anyone asked to approve a payment should be given enough to form a view: what work is planned and why, what it should cost, and afterwards what was done and what it came to. The office holder should also point creditors to information about their rights, in the first communication and in every later report. These guides are that information.

How the fee is calculated

Remuneration is fixed on one of three bases: a percentage of the value of the property realised or dealt with, the work reasonably undertaken by the office holder and staff, which everyone calls time cost, or a set amount. Bases can be combined across different parts of the work.

For a percentage or a set amount, the office holder should explain why it fairly reflects the work and which costs it covers. For time cost, you should see charge out rates by grade of staff. Expenses are approved separately, and any paid to an associate need approving like the fee itself.

How fees are fixed in Scotland

Scotland has its own corporate insolvency rules, so a guide written for England and Wales will send you the wrong way. In an administration, the creditors' committee fixes outlays and remuneration. Where there is no committee, the creditors do it by decision procedure. If they fail to, the claim goes to the court, which must determine it.

In a creditors' voluntary liquidation, or a court winding up that began with a winding up petition, the liquidator submits accounts and a claim after each accounting period, and the liquidation committee may audit them and must issue a determination fixing the amount. Where no committee exists, that falls to the court.

Two rights follow. In a liquidation a creditor may appeal a committee determination to the court within 14 days, having first given the liquidator notice. And in either procedure creditors representing a quarter of the debt by value may apply for an order reducing outlays or remuneration as excessive, within eight weeks of the end of the accounting period where the case is an administration.

Finding the guide for your procedure

There is a separate guide for each procedure, with Scottish versions where the law differs. Use the one matching your appointment.

  • Liquidation. Covers liquidation in each form, creditor led, court led and solvent
  • Administration. Including a sale agreed before appointment, a pre-pack administration, which carries further disclosure under SIP 16
  • Company voluntary arrangement. In a company voluntary arrangement the nominee's and supervisor's fees usually go to creditors with the proposal
  • Receivership. Receivership over a Scottish company runs under Part 3 of the Insolvency Act 1986 and under the same 2018 winding up and receivership rules. A LPA receivership is an English appointment and can be made only over property in England and Wales
  • Personal insolvency. A trustee's fees fall under the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016. In a sequestration the commissioners, or the Accountant in Bankruptcy where there are none, fix the outlays and remuneration for each accounting period. Under a protected trust deed the trustee takes a prescribed fixed fee and a percentage fee, and the fixed fee can only be increased with the approval of a majority in value of the creditors or of the Accountant in Bankruptcy
  • Partnerships. Where the debtor is a firm rather than a company, see partnership liquidation

If a practitioner we introduced is handling the appointment and the fee information does not read right, tell us. We are not paid from that estate, so we have no stake in the answer. Get in touch whenever you want.

Frequently asked questions
Does Lancefield have fees to disclose here?

No, which is the point of the page. We take no appointments, so there is no estate we could be paid from and no remuneration of ours for creditors to approve.

Who approves an insolvency practitioner's fees?

It depends on the procedure. In a Scottish administration: the creditors' committee, or the creditors by decision procedure where there is none, or the court if they do not determine it. In a liquidation: the committee, or the court where none exists.

What if I think the fees are too high?

Ask the office holder for the narrative behind the figures first, because a good many objections resolve there. After that there are two routes: in a liquidation, an appeal to the court within 14 days, and in either procedure an application for a reduction by creditors holding a quarter of the debt by value.

What is the difference between remuneration and outlays?

Remuneration pays for the office holder's own work. Outlays are everything else paid from the estate that is not a distribution, from advertising in the Edinburgh Gazette to solicitors' costs.

Do the English guides apply in Scotland?

Not for the mechanics. The principles are shared, but who fixes the fee, the time limits and the court route all differ here. Use the Scottish version.

I am a creditor, and also a director of a company under pressure.

Common enough, particularly when a large customer fails. The bad debt is one problem and your own company's solvency another, and they are best looked at together. Our Debt Help Scotland section covers the personal side.

Send it over and we will tell you plainly what it means and whether it is worth pressing. It is free, confidential, and commits you to nothing.

Framing brief: why this page is written this way

  • Page job: Compliance and trust. It discharges the transparency expectation behind SIP 9 without pretending to an appointment we do not hold, and it gives a creditor the vocabulary to read the fee document they were actually sent.
  • Searcher state: Not searching. Arriving from the footer, or from a link we sent them, usually with a fee document open in another window and a suspicion that the number is high.
  • Competitor framing: Insolvency firms publish a fees and expenses page that reproduces the England and Wales rules almost verbatim, links to the R3 creditors' guide, and stops. Few get the Scottish position right, and none of them can comment on their own fee independently.
  • Mirror: the SIP 9 structure, the category 1 and category 2 split, the bases of remuneration, the challenge route.
  • Differentiate: we state the Scottish position properly, and we are the only firm writing on this subject with no fee of our own sitting in the estate.
  • Compliance: high. The page must never suggest Lancefield holds appointments, sets fees, or is regulated as an office holder. It must not read as a fee estimate.

Corrections made at verification:

1. The estimate is not a statutory cap in Scotland. The first draft said an office holder here cannot exceed the fees estimate without further approval. That mechanism is Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 r.18.30 and has no counterpart in either Scottish instrument. In Scotland the discipline comes from two other places: SIP 9 (Scotland), a professional standard rather than a rule, and the after the event determination of outlays and remuneration for each accounting period by the committee or the court. The section now says so, and its heading changed accordingly.

2. Committee, not creditors, in a Scottish liquidation. The draft had creditors approving liquidator remuneration by decision procedure, which is the England and Wales position. Under r.7.11 the liquidation committee determines, and where no committee exists it goes to the court, not to the general body of creditors.

3. Expenses of a challenge differ by procedure. In a liquidation the expenses of a r.7.15 application fall on the applicant unless the court orders otherwise; in an administration the court may order them paid as an expense of the administration. The page does not state either, because the distinction needs more space than it earns here and getting it half right would be worse than leaving it out.

Jurisdiction note: this is one of the areas where copying an English page produces something wrong rather than merely imprecise. The Insolvency (England and Wales) Rules 2016 do not apply. Scottish administration and CVA remuneration runs under the Insolvency (Scotland) (Company Voluntary Arrangements and Administration) Rules 2018, SI 2018/1082. Scottish liquidation and receivership remuneration runs under the Insolvency (Scotland) (Receivership and Winding up) Rules 2018, SSI 2018/347. SIP 9 has its own Scottish version, effective 1 April 2021, and that is the version described above. Personal insolvency is governed separately again, by the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016.

Deliberately not stated: no fee figure, hourly rate, percentage or range appears anywhere on this page, because we hold no appointments and quoting market rates would read as a benchmark we are in no position to set. We have not said that fee estimates are routinely exceeded, or that any group of office holders overcharges, because we have no evidence for either and both would be smears on a regulated profession. We have not reproduced the priority ranking for expenses, remuneration and creditor classes, which belongs on the liquidation page where it can be given properly. We have not named R3, ICAS or any other body as a recommended source, per the external link policy. We have not said how often a liquidation committee is formed in smaller Scottish cases, though practitioners will tell you it frequently is not, because no published figure supports it.

Fee estimates and the basis of remuneration

In a formal insolvency you will be sent a document setting out what the office holder expects to charge. It is worth reading properly. The fee comes out of the estate, the same pot that would otherwise be shared among creditors.

This page covers what it should contain, who approves the fee, and how it can be challenged.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

[DEV: footer link only. Keep it out of the main navigation and at sitemap priority 0.3 or below.]

Why there is no Lancefield estimate here

We take no insolvency appointments. Nobody here becomes your liquidator, administrator, receiver or trustee, so there is no estate we are paid from and no fee of ours to estimate. The estimate that matters comes from the licensed insolvency practitioner holding the appointment, and it should reach you before you are asked to approve anything.

That is easier to do honestly when none of your own income depends on appointments.

What you should be told before a fee is approved

The standard is Statement of Insolvency Practice 9 (Scotland). It covers a creditors' voluntary liquidation, an administration, a pre-pack administration and a company voluntary arrangement alike, though solvent members' voluntary liquidation work sits outside it. Anyone approving a fee needs enough to judge whether it is reasonable:

  • The work proposed. What is intended, and why each part of it is necessary
  • What it will cost. And whether it benefits creditors or is simply required by statute
  • The rates. Where time is charged, rates by grade of staff and the time unit used
  • The likely return. What creditors can expect to receive
  • The expenses. What comes out of the estate on top of the fee, and any work sent outside
The three bases, and what the estimate binds

Remuneration is fixed on one of three bases, or a combination: a percentage of the value of the property realised or dealt with, the work reasonably undertaken, or a set amount. Different bases can apply to different parts of the work, which is common where a company later moves into company liquidation.

An estimate is not a suggestion. In England and Wales an office holder cannot draw more than the total in it without further approval. Scotland reaches the same protection differently: outlays and remuneration are determined after the event, period by period, against what was estimated.

Outlays, expenses and disbursements

Scottish rules say outlays for what is spent from the estate other than the fee itself. SIP 9 says expenses, and treats disbursements as a subset: payments the office holder meets first and is reimbursed for later.

  • Category 1. Payments to a person providing the service concerned who is not an associate of the office holder, such as advertising, insurance or storage. No prior approval needed
  • Category 2. Payments to an associate, or any payment carrying a shared or allocated element. These need approval before payment, in the same way the fee does

A charge calculated as a percentage of the remuneration, an administration fee on top of it, and overheads belonging inside the charge out rates are all disallowed.

Who approves the fee, and how to challenge it

In a Scottish liquidation the liquidator claims for each accounting period and the liquidation committee determines what is payable, or the court where no committee exists. In an administration the creditors' committee determines it, or the creditors by decision procedure where there is no committee, or the court if the creditors do not.

If you disagree there are two routes. A committee determination in a liquidation can be appealed to the court within 14 days by the liquidator, or by any creditor or contributory who has first given the liquidator notice of an intention to appeal. Separately, creditors representing at least 25 per cent in value can apply to have outlays or remuneration reduced as, in all the circumstances, excessive, with an eight week deadline in an administration.

Before either, ask. A request for more information is meant to be handled fairly and in proportion to the case, and one good question often does more than an application.

Frequently asked questions
Does Lancefield publish its own fee estimate?

No. Estimates come from office holders, who are paid from the estate. We take no appointments and draw nothing from any estate. Our own fees are agreed in advance, in writing.

Are the rules the same as in England and Wales?

No. Corporate insolvency law is largely shared across Great Britain, the procedural rules are not. Scottish administrations run under one 2018 instrument and Scottish liquidations under another, and they differ on how remuneration is fixed and challenged.

Can I see how the time was spent?

You can ask. Time is recorded in units of no more than six minutes for each grade of staff. Ask by work area rather than as one total, because an odd figure usually explains itself.

Does any of this apply to personal debt?

The principles carry across, the machinery differs. Trustee remuneration in a sequestration or under a protected trust deed runs through the Bankruptcy (Scotland) Act 2016, overseen by the Accountant in Bankruptcy. Our Debt Help Scotland section covers it.

A creditor has petitioned. Does this page still help?

Only partly. Once a winding up petition is live the timetable is the problem and the fee sits well down the list. Deal with that first, then creditor guides, and if you would rather talk it through, get in touch.

CTA block

Not sure whether a fee you have been sent is reasonable?

We will read it with you and say plainly what we think, with nothing of our own riding on the answer. It commits you to nothing.
