Details of our work

When an office holder asks creditors to approve what they are paid, or reports on what has happened since the last time, the professional standards require more than a figure. They require a narrative: an explanation of the work actually done, why it was necessary, what it achieved, and what remains. This page explains what that narrative should contain and how to read one.

One thing to be clear about first, because it shapes everything else here. Lancefield takes no insolvency appointments. Nobody here acts as liquidator, administrator or trustee, so we hold no estate, we draw no remuneration from one, and we have no narrative of our own to publish. What follows describes the obligations of the licensed insolvency practitioner we introduce where a formal appointment is needed, and of any other office holder you are dealing with.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What you should receive, and when

An office holder reports to creditors at intervals through the case, and again at the end. The reports are cumulative: each one covers the period since the last, so read together they should account for the whole of the appointment.

  • An account of the period. What was done, by whom, and what it produced. Not a list of activities, but an explanation of what the estate got for the time spent
  • What has been realised. Assets recovered and money received, against what was expected at the outset
  • What has been paid out. Costs, expenses, and any distributions, with the office holder's remuneration shown separately
  • What remains. Outstanding matters, why they are outstanding, and what the office holder expects to achieve
  • Progress against the estimate. Where an estimate of remuneration was given, how the actual position compares to it. Our fee estimates page explains that in Scotland the estimate is not a cap: outlays and remuneration are determined after each accounting period by the committee, the creditors or the court
  • The creditors' position. What has been distributed, or an honest statement of the prospects of a distribution

Where the case has moved from one procedure to another, for instance an administration ending in a creditors' voluntary liquidation, the reporting picks up in the new procedure and the earlier office holder accounts for their own period.

How to tell a useful report from a boilerplate one

This is the practical part, and it is the reason a page like this is worth writing properly.

  • Does it explain, or does it list? "Correspondence with creditors, 14 hours" is an activity. "Dealt with 60 creditor claims, of which 11 were disputed and required adjudication" is an explanation. The second tells you what the estate bought
  • Does the time relate to the outcome? Significant time on an asset that realised very little should carry a reason. Sometimes there is a good one, such as a claim that had to be pursued to establish it was worthless
  • Are the difficulties named? Cases go wrong. A report that describes only progress, in a case that has plainly stalled, is not telling you the useful part
  • Does it compare to the estimate? A narrative that never mentions the original estimate is avoiding the question a creditor most wants answered
  • Can you tell what happens next, and when? A report that ends without a next step or a timescale has not finished its job

None of that means an office holder who writes a thin report is doing a poor job. It means you cannot tell from the document, which is precisely what the standard exists to prevent.

If the report does not answer your question

You are entitled to ask. A creditor can request further information about the office holder's remuneration and expenses, and about the work behind them. In Scotland the professional standard is that the office holder considers the request on its merits and answers fairly, in proportion to the case, rather than within a fixed statutory period. In a company voluntary arrangement charged on time there is a harder right: a written statement of the hours spent and the rates charged must be provided free of charge within a set period.

Beyond that, where the remuneration and outlays have been fixed by the committee or the creditors, creditors representing at least a quarter of the debt by value can apply to the court to have them reduced as excessive. That is a serious step and rarely the first one, but the availability of it is what gives the earlier request its weight. Where you believe the process itself has been misused rather than merely poorly reported, complain to the office holder first, and if their answer does not satisfy you the complaint route runs through the Insolvency Service's complaints gateway, which passes it to the office holder's professional body.

In our experience most unsatisfactory reports are the product of a busy case rather than an evasive office holder, and a direct question resolves them. If it does not, contact us and we will tell you whether what you are being told is reasonable.

Our own fees are a different thing

Worth separating, because creditors and directors both conflate the two.

Where Lancefield advises a company on restructuring or an individual on their own position, our fee is agreed with that client directly, before the work starts, and it is paid by them. It is not office-holder remuneration, it does not come out of an insolvent estate, and it is not subject to approval by creditors, because we are not an office holder and there is no estate involved.

If you are a creditor looking at a report and wondering which fees are which: the office holder's remuneration is the amount determined by the committee, or where there is none by the creditors or the court, and drawn from the estate. Anything we were paid for advising the company before the appointment is a pre-appointment cost like any other professional fee, and the office holder will treat it as such.

Frequently asked questions
What is the narrative of work done?

The written explanation an office holder gives creditors of the work carried out, why it was necessary, what it achieved and what remains. It accompanies the figures so that creditors can judge whether the time charged produced value, rather than simply being told the total.

How often should I receive a report?

At intervals set by the rules for the procedure, and again at the end of the case. The reports are cumulative, so together they should account for the whole appointment. If you have not received one when you expected it, ask.

Can I ask for more detail?

Yes. A creditor can request further information about the remuneration, the expenses and the work behind them. In Scotland the office holder should consider the request on its merits and answer fairly and in proportion to the case. In a company voluntary arrangement charged on time, a written statement of hours and rates must be supplied free of charge within a set period.

What if I think the fees are too high?

Raise it with the office holder first, in writing, and ask for the detail. If that does not resolve it, creditors representing at least a quarter of the debt by value can apply to the court on the ground that the remuneration or outlays are excessive. The fee estimates page covers how remuneration is approved in the first place.

Does Lancefield publish one of these?

No, and it could not. We take no insolvency appointments, so we never hold an estate or draw remuneration from one. This page explains the obligations of the office holders we introduce and of any other you are dealing with.

CTA block

Looking at a report and not sure what it tells you?

We hold no appointments, so we have no stake in how any office holder's work is judged. One conversation will tell you whether what you are reading is adequate and what to ask for next.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Invoice Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Invoice finance

Invoice finance turns unpaid sales invoices into cash now. A provider advances most of an invoice's value within a day or two of you raising it, then releases the balance, less its charges, once the customer pays.

Lancefield does not provide this facility and does not arrange it. What we do is tell you whether it is the right move at all, which is a different question from which provider to use.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Factoring and discounting are not the same thing

They differ in the one respect owners care about: who speaks to your customers.

  • Invoice factoring. The provider collects. It runs your sales ledger and chases payment, so customers know a third party is involved. For a business with no credit control, that is often a relief
  • Invoice discounting. You collect. The facility sits behind the scenes and your customers need never know, which is why the undisclosed version is sold as confidential invoice discounting. Providers want stronger systems and figures first, since the chasing is left to you

Scots law transfers a debt differently from English law. Since April 2025 a Scottish assignation can be completed either by intimating it to your customer or by registering it, so a Scottish ledger may be documented its own way. Ask how yours is handled.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You sell to other businesses on credit terms, bill for work already delivered, and have a spread of solid customers. It is at its best when growth is the problem: every new order eats cash before it produces any. capital management covers the mechanics.

It is the wrong move if

You sell to consumers, bill in stages before work is done, lean on one customer for most of your turnover, or work under a contract barring assignment of the debt. Each of those will narrow or close it. And if the business loses money on every job, this only releases cash faster. Equipment and vehicles belong with asset finance.

The warning nobody gives you

This is the fastest way to release trapped working capital in a business under pressure. It is also the facility most likely to be withdrawn as that pressure worsens. The provider sees your ledger weekly, so it spots the slide before your bank does. Credit notes rise, debts age, a customer fails, and the terms tighten. The cash taken back is cash you have spent.

So the timing matters more than the rate. Put in while trading is stable, it is a useful tool. Reached for in the last quarter before a crisis, it often brings the crisis forward, and one pulled at the wrong moment is a well-worn route to going into administration. Near that point, talk about turnaround or a restructuring plan first, and start with contingency planning.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. For finance we introduce you to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is look at the ledger with you and say whether the problem is the timing of the cash or the shape of the business, which is a different question from which product to buy.

Where the honest answer is that the business needs fixing rather than funding, that is turnaround work. Where the existing borrowing needs reshaping rather than adding to, it is debt restructuring. And where a personal guarantee has already been called, our Debt Help Scotland section covers your own position.

Frequently asked questions
Do you arrange the finance yourselves?

No. We are not brokers, and not FCA authorised to arrange finance. We introduce you to a trusted specialist firm, and that introduction does not change the advice we have already given you.

Can we get it if the company is already struggling?

Sometimes, and that is when to be most careful. A facility taken on at that stage can be cut back at the point you most need it.

Will our customers find out?

With factoring, yes, because the provider does the collecting. With confidential invoice discounting, usually not. Ask any provider to confirm in writing which you are being offered.

CTA block

Releasing cash, or postponing a problem?

We will look at the ledger with you and say which one it is, and we neither broker nor arrange the facility, so the answer is not ours to sell. More options sit on the finance and funding page, or contact us direct.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Every conversation is 100% confidential, always. That is our Discretion Guarantee.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Asset Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Asset finance

Asset finance is borrowing against things rather than against a balance sheet. It covers buying equipment on hire purchase or a lease, and refinancing assets the business already owns to release cash, which is usually called sale and leaseback or asset based lending.

It is one of the more accessible forms of business funding, because the lender's security is the asset itself rather than your trading history. That is also the thing to understand before signing: the lender's position is protected in a way an unsecured lender's is not.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What it actually covers

Two directions. Forward-looking, it funds an acquisition: a machine, a fleet, a fit-out, spread over the asset's working life rather than paid for out of one quarter's cash. Backward-looking, it releases capital tied up in assets you have already bought and paid for, which can be the fastest source of working capital available to a business under pressure. Hire purchase ends with you owning the asset; a lease generally does not, and the difference matters for both your accounts and what happens on an insolvency.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You need equipment to grow or to replace something failing, and paying cash for it would leave the business short. Or you own unencumbered plant and need working capital faster than a bank facility could be arranged. The asset has a real second-hand value, which is what makes the lending work.

It is the wrong move if

You are refinancing assets to cover trading losses. Releasing cash from your own plant to fund a shortfall converts an owned asset into a monthly commitment and buys a few months, and it is one of the more common steps on the way to a formal insolvency. If that is the situation, our turnaround page is the honest starting point.

What we see that a lender will not tell you

Assets on hire purchase or lease are not yours to sell. Directors regularly forget this, and it surfaces at the worst possible moment: an administrator arrives, and equipment the business has treated as its own for years turns out to belong to a finance company. Once a company is in administration the finance company cannot simply repossess, since it needs the administrator's consent or the court's permission, but the asset is still not the company's to sell. That changes what a business is worth to a buyer, and it changes what a pre-pack administration can actually transfer. Before any insolvency conversation, establish exactly which assets you own outright, which are financed, and what each agreement says on default. It takes an afternoon and it changes the options.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

If the kit is not the problem and the trading is, turning the business around is the work that matters, not another facility. If the issue is the shape of what you already owe, that is restructuring the debt. And if a guarantee on an existing agreement has been called, your own position is a separate question with its own answers.

Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between hire purchase and leasing?

With hire purchase you are buying the asset over time and own it at the end. With a lease you are paying for use, and ownership usually stays with the lender. The distinction affects your accounts, your tax position and, importantly, what happens to the asset if the business fails.

Can I raise money against equipment I already own?

Often yes, if it is unencumbered and has a resale value. It is one of the quicker routes to working capital. Whether it is a good idea depends entirely on what the money is for.

Do you arrange the finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission from lenders. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we tell you first whether borrowing is the right move at all.

What happens to financed assets if the company fails?

They generally belong to the finance company, not to the business. A liquidator cannot sell them. An administrator can, but only with the finance company's agreement or a court order, and the finance company has to be paid the asset's value out of the proceeds. Either way they are not simply yours to transfer. Our administration page explains what that means in practice.

CTA block

Not sure whether to fund the asset or fix the cash flow?

We are not brokers and do not arrange facilities, so we have no reason to talk you into one. One conversation will tell you whether asset finance is the right answer or a symptom of something else.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Commercial Mortgage

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Commercial mortgages

A commercial mortgage is long-term borrowing secured on business premises, either property you trade from yourself or property you hold as an investment. Development schemes are funded differently, and our property finance page covers those. It is the most straightforward form of commercial lending and usually the cheapest, because the lender's security is tangible and its position is strong.

For most owner-managed businesses it is also the largest single financial commitment they will make, and the one whose terms get the least scrutiny, because the headline rate is what everyone reads and the covenants are what actually bite.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What lenders actually look at

Three things, in this order. The property, because that is the security: what it is worth, how specialised it is, and how easily it could be sold to someone else. The income, meaning whether the business or the rent covers the payments with room to spare. And the covenants, which are the conditions you agree to keep to, typically around loan-to-value and interest cover. The covenants are where owner-managed businesses get caught, because a breach can be triggered by a valuation moving rather than by anything the business did.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You are buying premises you will occupy, or refinancing property you already own onto better terms. The income covers the payments with genuine headroom rather than exactly. You expect to hold the property for a period long enough to justify the arrangement costs.

It is the wrong move if

You need the money quickly, in which case this is the wrong instrument and bridging finance is what people use, expensively. Or the business is under strain and the mortgage is being drawn to fund trading, which turns a property asset into a monthly obligation the trade already cannot support.

Enforcement in Scotland works differently

Almost everything written online about commercial mortgage enforcement describes England and Wales, where a lender appoints a receiver under the Law of Property Act 1925. That regime does not exist in Scotland. Security over Scottish property is a standard security, and a lender enforces it under the Conveyancing and Feudal Reform (Scotland) Act 1970 by serving a calling-up notice or a notice of default, then exercising its remedies. Where any part of the property is residential, including a flat above a shop, the lender needs a warrant from the sheriff before it can sell or take possession. If your property is in Scotland, the LPA guidance you will find is describing another country's law, and our LPA receivership page sets out the contrast properly.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

If the property is sound and the business under it is not, the answer is a turnaround plan rather than a larger loan. If the debt itself is the problem, restructuring what you owe is the conversation. And if a guarantee has been called, your own position is dealt with separately from the company's.

Frequently asked questions
How much can I borrow against commercial property?

It depends on the property, the income covering it and the lender, and any figure quoted without a valuation is a guess. What matters more than the maximum is the headroom: borrowing to the limit leaves no room for a valuation to move against you.

What is a covenant breach and why does it matter?

A covenant is a condition in the facility, usually about loan-to-value or interest cover. Breaching one can put the facility in default even if every payment has been made on time, which is why a falling valuation can create a problem out of nothing you did.

Is a Scottish commercial mortgage different?

The lending is the same; the security and the enforcement are not. Scottish property is secured by a standard security and enforced under the 1970 Act, not by the Law of Property Act. Use a lender and a solicitor who deal with Scottish property routinely.

Do you arrange commercial mortgages?

No. We are not brokers and we do not arrange facilities. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we say plainly when borrowing is the wrong answer.

CTA block

Worried about a covenant, or a facility coming up for renewal?

We take no commission from lenders, so the advice is not shaped by a facility completing. One conversation will tell you where you stand and what your lender is likely to do.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Bridging Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Bridging finance

A bridging loan is short-term borrowing secured on property, arranged quickly and priced accordingly. It sits alongside the other options in our finance and funding section. It exists to cover a gap: a purchase that has to complete before a sale, a refinancing that has not landed yet, a development that needs finishing before it can be let or sold.

Used properly it is a useful and entirely legitimate instrument. Used to plug a hole with no clear way out, it is the single most expensive mistake a business under pressure can make, and we see the results of that more often than we see the successes.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

The exit is the whole thing

Every bridge is underwritten on its exit, meaning the specific event that repays it: a sale completing, a term facility drawing down, a development finishing and letting. The rate matters far less than whether that event is real and whether the timescale is honest. A bridge with a credible exit is short-term borrowing. A bridge without one is a deadline you have paid a premium to set for yourself, and when it arrives the usual answer is another bridge at a worse rate.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

There is a defined, evidenced event that repays the loan, and it is close enough that the cost of the bridge is proportionate. A property sale with a buyer, a refinancing with an offer, a development with a contractor and a programme. You have a margin for the exit slipping, because it usually does.

It is the wrong move if

The exit is a hope rather than a plan, or the money is being borrowed to service other debt. Borrowing expensively to keep up payments on cheaper borrowing is the most reliable route we know from a difficult position to an impossible one, and the reason is arithmetic rather than judgement. If that is where you are, debt restructuring is the conversation to have instead.

What we see afterwards

A meaningful share of the businesses that reach us in real distress have a bridge on the balance sheet, taken six or nine months earlier, whose exit did not happen. The pattern is consistent: the bridge was taken to buy time to fix something, the fix took longer than expected, and the bridge's own deadline arrived first. Because it is secured and short, the lender's options are quick, so the bridge frequently sets the timetable for everything that follows, including an administration. If you are considering one, the useful question is not what it costs but what happens on the day it falls due and the exit has not arrived.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

A bridge with no exit is a delay, not a solution. Where the underlying trading needs fixing, that is turnaround work. Where the existing borrowing is the thing that will not work, look at reshaping the borrowing first. And if you have guaranteed any of it personally, personal debt options covers where you stand.

Frequently asked questions
How quickly can a bridge be arranged?

Faster than a term facility, which is the point of it and part of what you pay for. The speed is genuine, and it is also what makes it easy to commit to before thinking the exit through.

Why is bridging so expensive?

It is priced for speed, short duration and the lender's risk of the exit failing. On a genuinely short bridge the cost is proportionate. On one that rolls, it compounds quickly.

What happens if I cannot repay at the end?

The lender will look at an extension, usually at a higher rate, or at enforcing its security. That is why the exit is underwritten at the start, and why a bridge without a real one is dangerous.

Do you arrange bridging finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and on this product in particular we will tell you plainly when the answer should be no.

CTA block

Being offered a bridge, and unsure about the exit?

We are not brokers and do not arrange the facility, whether you take it or not. One conversation will tell you whether the exit stands up and what happens if it slips.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Unsecured Business Loans

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Unsecured business loans

An unsecured business loan is borrowing without a charge over a specific asset. There is no property to enforce against, as there would be with a commercial mortgage, and no equipment pledged, which is why the process is quicker and why the rate is higher than secured lending.

The word unsecured does a lot of work in that sentence, and it is worth being precise about what it actually means, because for an owner-managed business it very rarely means what people assume.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Unsecured almost always means guaranteed

For a company of any size below the corporate mid-market, an unsecured facility is normally conditional on the directors giving a personal guarantee. The loan is unsecured against the company's assets, and secured against yours. That is not a criticism of lenders, it is how the risk is priced, but it changes the decision entirely: what looks like the company borrowing is, in substance, you borrowing. A great many directors sign these without reading them, and discover the terms only when the guarantee is called.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

The business needs working capital or funding for growth, has no suitable asset to secure against, and can service the repayments comfortably from trading. You have read the guarantee, you understand what it covers and for how long, and you are content to stand behind it personally.

It is the wrong move if

The company is already struggling and the loan would fund a shortfall rather than an opportunity. Taking on personally guaranteed borrowing at that point moves the risk from the company, which has limited liability, to you, who do not. It is the mechanism by which a business failure becomes a personal one.

What a guarantee does when the company fails

Liquidating the company does not extinguish your guarantee. The lender's claim against the company disappears into the insolvency, and its claim against you continues, reduced only by whatever the lender recovers in the liquidation, which is why a director can emerge from a creditors' voluntary liquidation owing money personally on borrowing the company took. Guarantees also hide: in bank facilities, equipment leases, commercial property leases and supplier credit applications, sometimes signed years earlier and forgotten. Before any insolvency decision, find out exactly what you have guaranteed, because it frequently changes which route is right. Where a guarantee is called and cannot be met, that becomes a personal debt problem with its own answers, covered in our Debt Help Scotland section.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

If the borrowing is a symptom rather than the problem, turning the business around is the work worth doing. If the existing facilities are unaffordable as they stand, that is reshaping the borrowing. And because these facilities are so often personally guaranteed, personal insolvency in Scotland is worth reading alongside this page.

Frequently asked questions
Is an unsecured business loan really unsecured?

Unsecured against the company's assets, usually. Not against yours, because most lenders require a personal guarantee from the directors. Read what you are signing: the distinction is the whole risk.

What happens to my guarantee if the company is liquidated?

It survives. Limited liability protects you from the company's debts generally; it does not protect you from a promise you personally made to a lender. The lender will look to you for the shortfall.

Can I negotiate the guarantee?

Sometimes, on the cap, the duration, or whether it is joint and several with other directors. It is worth trying before signing and almost impossible afterwards. Take advice on the wording, not just the amount.

Do you arrange this kind of lending?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission from lenders. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we will tell you when borrowing personally guaranteed money is the wrong answer.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › VAT Loans

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

VAT and tax loans

A VAT loan is short-term borrowing that pays a tax bill on your behalf so you can repay it over several months rather than in one payment. The same product exists for corporation tax and for self-assessment liabilities.

It is a straightforward facility and it solves a real problem for businesses whose income is lumpy. It is also, more often than the industry admits, an early warning sign, and this page is mainly about telling the two situations apart.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What it does

It converts a single large payment into a series of smaller ones, usually over three to twelve months, at a cost. For a business with genuinely seasonal or contract-driven income, that smoothing is exactly what it should be used for: the money is there across the year, just not on the day the bill falls due. The lender pays HMRC directly, so the liability is settled and you owe the finance company instead.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

Your income is lumpy for a structural reason and the bill has landed in a trough. The business is profitable and the cash arrives, just not in the right week. You are using it occasionally rather than as a matter of course.

It is the wrong move if

You need one every quarter. At that point the business is not experiencing a timing problem, it is trading beyond its working capital, and each quarter's borrowing makes the next one harder. That is a capital management question, and if the trend is downwards it is a turnaround one.

Why we treat repeat tax funding as a warning

VAT is money the business has already collected on HMRC's behalf. If it is not there when the return falls due, it has been used to fund something else, usually the ordinary shortfall between what the business spends and what it collects. Borrowing to replace it fixes the symptom for a quarter. What we look at instead is why the money was not there, because that answer is the one that decides whether the business has a cash timing issue or a solvency issue. There is also a conduct dimension worth knowing: where a company later fails, an insolvency practitioner has to report on the directors' conduct, and using tax money to pay other creditors is one of the things the Insolvency Service names as unfit conduct. Our creditors' voluntary liquidation page covers that.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Borrowing to pay tax that keeps coming back is a trading problem wearing a funding costume, which makes turnaround work the real answer. Where the wider debt needs reshaping, that is renegotiating the debt. And where you have guaranteed borrowing personally, personal debt options sets out where you stand.

Frequently asked questions
Is a VAT loan a good idea?

For a genuinely seasonal business facing a bill in a trough, often yes. As a regular quarterly habit, it is usually treating a symptom, and the underlying problem gets more expensive each time.

Could I use Time to Pay instead?

Possibly, and it is worth asking HMRC before borrowing. Time to Pay is a real arrangement granted on a realistic proposal, and it usually costs less than commercial borrowing, though HMRC charges interest on the arrears throughout. What it requires is that current taxes are kept up to date throughout.

Does taking a VAT loan look bad to HMRC?

Not if it clears the bill by the due date, because then it is paid in full and on time from HMRC's point of view. Pay late and HMRC's late payment penalties and interest have already started, and borrowing does not undo them. The question the page raises is not about HMRC's view of you, it is about what the need for the loan tells you about the business.

Do you arrange tax funding?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we will say when the honest answer is that the business needs looking at rather than funding.

We are not brokers and do not arrange facilities, so there is no reason for us to recommend one. One conversation will tell you whether this is a timing problem or something that needs addressing.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Property Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Property finance

Property finance covers two quite different things. Development finance funds a build or a conversion, drawn down in stages as the work progresses and repaid when the scheme is sold or refinanced. Investment finance is longer-term borrowing against property held to let, which is closer to a commercial mortgage.

Development is the one that gets businesses into difficulty, and it does so in a specific and predictable way that is worth understanding before you draw the first tranche.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

How development finance works

Unlike the finance and funding products that advance in a single sum, the lender releases development money against a programme. Funds are released in stages as work is completed and signed off, usually by a monitoring surveyor acting for the lender, with interest typically rolled up and repaid at the end out of the sale or refinancing. The whole structure assumes the programme holds: that each stage completes roughly when it was said it would, at roughly the cost stated, and that the exit arrives when planned.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You have a costed scheme, a contractor, a realistic programme and a credible exit, whether that is a sale or a term refinancing. There is contingency in the numbers for the things that always happen, and you can fund a period of overrun without the scheme stopping.

It is the wrong move if

The contingency is thin, the programme is optimistic, or the exit depends on a market rather than on a buyer. Development schemes rarely fail because the buildings were wrong; they fail because time and cost ran past the funding, and the shortest route to that is a programme with no slack in it.

Where schemes actually go wrong

Cost overruns and delays turn into distress faster in development than anywhere else, because the drawdown schedule assumes the programme and the interest keeps rolling up while nothing is being sold. A three-month delay is not a three-month problem: it is three more months of rolled-up interest, a later exit, and often a contractor who now wants paying differently. The lender's security is the site, and the site is worth considerably less half-finished than finished, which shapes how a lender behaves when a scheme stalls. If yours is slipping, the time to talk to the lender is before the next drawdown request, not after it is declined, and our debt restructuring page covers what lenders will and will not agree to.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

A scheme that has slipped rarely recovers on more debt alone. Where the business behind it needs work, that is a turnaround plan. Where the existing facilities need reshaping, renegotiating the debt comes first. And where you have guaranteed any of it, personal debt options covers what that exposes.

Frequently asked questions
How is development finance different from a mortgage?

It is drawn in stages against build progress rather than advanced in one sum, the interest is usually rolled up rather than paid monthly, and it is repaid from a sale or refinancing rather than from income. It is short-term and it is priced accordingly.

What is a monitoring surveyor?

A surveyor appointed by the lender to check that work has actually been done before each stage is released. They act for the lender, not for you, and their view governs the drawdown.

What happens if the build overruns?

Interest continues to roll up, the exit moves later, and further funding may be needed. Lenders will often work with a scheme that is honest with them early. What they respond badly to is discovering an overrun at the drawdown request.

Do you arrange development finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where a scheme is already in difficulty we advise on that rather than on funding it.

CTA block

Is the scheme slipping?

We are not brokers and do not arrange facilities, so we have no reason to recommend more borrowing. One conversation will tell you what your lender is likely to do and what your options are.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Every conversation is 100% confidential, always. That is our Discretion Guarantee.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Engineering Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Engineering and manufacturing finance

Engineering and manufacturing businesses have a funding profile that does not fit standard lending well. Capital equipment is expensive and long-lived, tooling for a specific contract is expensive and often worth nothing to anyone else, and there is usually a long gap between winning work and being paid for it.

The result is a sector that is frequently profitable on paper and short of cash in practice, which is a combination that catches out lenders and owners alike.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What the sector actually needs funding for

Three things, and they behave differently. Capital equipment, which has a resale value and is therefore straightforward to fund through asset finance. Tooling and setup for a specific contract, which is much harder, because it is worth little outside that contract and lenders know it. And working capital across the production cycle, from raw material through work in progress to an invoice that then sits on payment terms, which is where most of the strain actually sits.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You are funding equipment with a genuine second-hand value, or bridging a working capital cycle on contracts you have won and will be paid for. The order book supports the commitment beyond the current contract.

It is the wrong move if

You are funding tooling for a single contract whose margin does not cover it, or borrowing against an order book concentrated in one customer. Both are common and both convert an operational risk into a financial one that outlives the contract.

The pattern we see in engineering failures

Engineering businesses rarely fail because they cannot do the work. They fail because a large contract absorbed working capital faster than it generated cash: materials bought, labour paid, tooling made, and payment arriving months later or in stages that lag the spend. A profitable contract can put a company under, and a growing order book can accelerate it rather than help. That is a capital management question before it is a funding one, and the honest answer is sometimes that the contract should be declined or repriced rather than financed. Where the pattern is already established, our turnaround page is the more useful starting point.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Winning work you cannot fund is a margin problem more often than a lending one, which makes turnaround work the honest first answer. Where the existing facilities are the constraint, look at reshaping the borrowing. And where you have signed personally, personal insolvency in Scotland explains what follows.

Frequently asked questions
Can we finance machinery we already own?

Usually yes, where it is unencumbered and has a resale value. It is one of the faster routes to working capital in this sector. Whether it is the right move depends on what the money is funding.

Can we get funding against an order book?

Sometimes, but lenders discount concentrated order books heavily and are cautious about work in progress that has not been invoiced. Invoice finance against issued invoices is generally more accessible.

Why do profitable contracts cause cash problems?

Because the spending comes first and the payment comes later. The bigger the contract, the bigger the gap, which is why growth in this sector consumes cash rather than generating it in the short term.

Do you arrange this funding?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and we will tell you when the answer is to reprice the work rather than fund it.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Hospitality Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Hospitality and leisure finance

Hospitality is one of the sectors we work in most, and it has a funding profile unlike almost any other: highly seasonal, heavily fixed in its costs, exposed to energy and wage inflation, and frequently operating from leased premises on terms that leave very little room.

That combination means a hospitality business can be trading well and still hit a wall in a specific month, and the businesses that survive are usually the ones that saw that month coming.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What the sector funds

Fit-outs and refurbishment, which are expensive and mostly worthless to a lender as security because they are specific to the site. Equipment, which does have a resale value and is straightforward through asset finance. Acquisitions of a lease or a freehold. And working capital across the season, which is the one that actually decides whether a business gets through the year.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

The trade is sound and the funding covers a known seasonal trough or an investment that will demonstrably increase trade. The lease has enough term left to justify the spend, which is a condition owners frequently overlook when funding a fit-out.

It is the wrong move if

The business is losing money in its good months. Hospitality has a thin margin for error, and funding a loss through a strong season simply means the weak season arrives with the debt already in place. If that is the position, our turnaround page is the honest starting point.

The month that catches hospitality out

Almost every hospitality failure we see has the same shape. Trade is strong through the busy season, the business feels comfortable, and the costs that were deferred through it, the VAT quarter, the rent, the supplier accounts stretched a little, all fall due in the quiet months when the income has gone. January and February do most of the damage in Scotland, and the decisions that determine whether a business survives them are taken the previous autumn. A fit-out funded on the back of a good summer is a decision made at the point of maximum optimism about a business whose cash position will look entirely different in twelve weeks. Where the debt has already built up but the trade is genuinely viable, a company voluntary arrangement can restructure it while the business keeps trading, and that is a conversation to have in October rather than in February.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Borrowing into a quiet season postpones the question rather than answering it. If the trading needs fixing, that is turning the business around. If the debt already in place is the weight, it is restructuring what you owe. And if a guarantee has been called, your own position is a separate matter with its own routes.

Frequently asked questions
Can we get funding on a leased pub or restaurant?

Often, but the lease term matters a great deal. A lender will not fund a fit-out over a period longer than the lease has left, and a tied lease constrains what a business can do to improve its margin, which lenders factor in. Since 2025 a Scottish tied tenant has had a statutory route to a market-rent-only lease under the Scottish Pubs Code, which changes that calculation.

Why is hospitality funding harder than other sectors?

Because the assets are largely site-specific, the income is seasonal, and the margins are thin. Lenders price all three. Equipment with a resale value is the exception and is generally easier to fund.

We are behind on VAT and rent. Is borrowing the answer?

Sometimes, and often not. If the business is profitable across a full year and the arrears are a timing problem, funding can work. If it loses money in the good months, borrowing postpones the decision at a cost. That is worth establishing before you commit.

Do you arrange hospitality finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission from lenders. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and hospitality is a sector where we will often say the problem is not a funding one.

Hospitality and leisure is one of the sectors we know best, and we are not brokers or arrangers of facilities. One conversation will tell you whether funding helps or postpones.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Contractor Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Contractor and construction finance

Construction has a payment cycle that would put most other industries out of business. Work is done, an application for payment is made, a proportion is certified, payment arrives on extended terms, and a slice is held back as retention for a year or more after the job is finished.

A contractor can therefore be busy, profitable and insolvent at the same time, and construction records more insolvencies than any other sector, which reflects exactly that. Construction is one of the sectors we work in most.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

Where the money is tied up

In three places. In work in progress, done but not yet certified. In certified applications waiting out the payment terms. And in retentions, which are the industry's most peculiar feature: money you have earned, held by someone else, sometimes for years, and frequently difficult to recover at the end. Add plant and vehicles, which are funded through asset finance, and the working capital demand on a growing contractor is substantial and constant.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You have certified applications or invoices and the funding bridges the payment terms. The main contractors you work for are financially sound. Growth is funded rather than absorbed, which is the distinction that decides whether a busy year helps or hurts.

It is the wrong move if

You are funding a cash gap caused by disputed work or unrecovered retentions, which is a commercial and contractual problem that money does not fix. Or your exposure is concentrated in one main contractor, in which case the funding does not reduce the risk, it increases what you lose if they fail.

When the main contractor goes under

This is the risk that defines the sector, and it runs downhill fast. When a main contractor fails, subcontractors rank as ordinary unsecured creditors for everything certified and unpaid, for work in progress, and for retentions, and unsecured creditors in an insolvency typically recover very little. The knock-on then takes out subcontractors who were themselves perfectly viable. Practical protection is limited but real: know who you are working for and check them, keep applications and certifications current rather than letting them run, resist the temptation to let one relationship dominate your order book, and take retention recovery seriously rather than treating it as an afterthought. If a main contractor above you has failed, act quickly, because our winding up petition and creditors' voluntary liquidation pages describe timetables that move faster than most subcontractors expect.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Where the contracts are profitable and the cash is simply arriving late, funding may help. Where they are not, turning it around is the real work. Where the borrowing already in place is the constraint, that is restructuring the debt. And if you have guaranteed a facility personally, personal debt options covers your side of it.

Frequently asked questions
Can we finance retentions?

Some lenders will look at retention funding, though it is more specialised and more expensive than invoice finance against certified applications, because the money is harder to collect and the timing is uncertain.

What happens to our money if the main contractor fails?

You become an unsecured creditor for certified work, work in progress and retentions. Recovery for unsecured creditors is usually poor. That is why concentration risk matters more in construction than almost anywhere else.

Is invoice finance available to subcontractors?

Often, but lenders treat construction cautiously because of applications, certification, set-off and retentions. Some specialise in it, and the terms differ from standard invoice finance.

Do you arrange construction finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where the problem is a failing main contractor rather than a funding gap, that is our own work.

CTA block

Exposed to a main contractor you are worried about?

Construction is one of the sectors we know best, and we are not brokers or arrangers of facilities. One conversation will tell you what your exposure actually is and what you can still do about it.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Care Home Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Care home finance

Care home funding sits between a commercial mortgage and trading business lending, and lenders treat it as both. The building is substantial security, but its value depends heavily on continuing to operate as a care home, which depends in turn on the operator holding its registration.

That link between the regulatory position and the value of the asset is what makes this sector different from any other kind of commercial property lending.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What lenders look at

Occupancy first, because it drives everything else in the finance and funding decision. The mix between local authority funded and privately funded residents, since fee rates differ substantially and a home weighted towards local authority rates has thinner margins. Staffing cost and agency dependence, which has been the sector's sharpest pressure. The building itself, including whether the rooms meet current expectations on ensuite provision and size. And the regulatory position, which in Scotland means the Care Inspectorate rather than the Care Quality Commission, a distinction that matters and that English-written guidance gets wrong.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

You are acquiring or refinancing a home with stable occupancy and a defensible fee mix, and the funding is sized against realistic staffing costs rather than best-case ones. Your regulatory grades are sound, because a lender will look at them.

It is the wrong move if

Occupancy is falling, agency dependence is high and rising, or there is an unresolved regulatory issue. In this sector a regulatory problem becomes a financial one very quickly, because it affects admissions, and admissions drive the income that services the debt.

Why regulatory and financial distress arrive together

A care home in financial difficulty tends to reduce spending in ways that show up in inspection: staffing thins, agency use rises, maintenance is deferred. A poorer grade then affects new admissions, occupancy falls, and the financial position worsens. It is a loop, and by the time it is visible in the accounts it has usually been running for a while. It also constrains the options: in practice an insolvency in this sector cannot simply stop trading, because there are residents in the building. The Care Inspectorate has to be told immediately: a care service provider, and any office-holder appointed over it, must notify it of an insolvency event as soon as one happens, and administration, receivership, a creditors' voluntary liquidation and a winding up order all count. Any administration or sale then has to be run with the regulator and the placing local authorities involved from the outset. That is a materially more complex process than an ordinary business sale and it needs more notice, which is the practical reason to take advice early here rather than late.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Occupancy and grades are operational problems before they are funding ones, so fixing the trading position usually comes before any new facility. Where the existing debt is the constraint, renegotiating the debt is the route. And where you have signed personally, personal insolvency in Scotland sets out what that means for you.

Frequently asked questions
Who regulates care homes in Scotland?

The Care Inspectorate. The Care Quality Commission regulates in England only, so guidance written for England names the wrong body and, in places, the wrong requirements.

How do lenders value a care home?

Largely on its trading performance rather than on bricks and mortar, because the value depends on it continuing to operate as a care home. That is why occupancy, fee mix and the regulatory position all feed into the lending decision.

Does a poor inspection grade affect funding?

It can, both on new lending and on existing facilities, because it affects admissions and therefore income. Lenders in this sector follow regulatory grades closely.

Do you arrange care home finance?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where a home is already under pressure we advise on that instead.

CTA block

Occupancy falling, or a regulatory issue affecting the numbers?

We are not brokers and do not arrange facilities, and in this sector the options narrow quickly. One conversation will tell you where you stand and how much time you actually have.

Breadcrumb: Finance & Funding › Sports & Entertainment Finance

Eyebrow: Finance & Funding

Sports and entertainment finance

This part of our finance and funding section covers two related things: funding for clubs, venues and promoters, and funding for individuals in sport and entertainment whose income is large but irregular and whose earning period may be short.

Both are treated cautiously by mainstream lenders, and for the same underlying reason. The income is real but it is lumpy, uncertain and, in the case of individuals, concentrated into a small number of years.

Button: Book a free, confidential call

What the sector funds

For clubs and venues: premises and their improvement, equipment, and working capital across a season whose income arrives in bursts around fixtures, events or a summer. For individuals: property and lifestyle lending underwritten against irregular earnings, which mainstream affordability assessments handle poorly. In both cases the funding challenge is not the total income but its shape.

Who it suits, and who it does not
It may suit you if

There is a demonstrable income pattern over several seasons or years rather than one exceptional period, and the borrowing is sized against a normal year rather than a good one. For a club, there is governance capable of holding to a budget, which lenders in this sector look at closely.

It is the wrong move if

The borrowing is sized against a peak: a promotion, a cup run, a single strong season, a contract that has years left but is not guaranteed. Sport is the sector where optimism most reliably becomes debt, and the commitments made after a good season are the ones that cause the trouble two seasons later.

Why clubs get into difficulty

The pattern is consistent and it is structural rather than a matter of poor management. Costs in sport are competitive: what a club spends is driven by what its rivals spend, because the objective is relative rather than absolute. Income, meanwhile, depends on results, which are uncertain. So costs are committed in advance on the assumption of a level of success that may not arrive, and the gap between the two is filled with debt. Add the fact that a club rarely fails out of public view, because supporters, leagues and sometimes local authorities all have an interest, and you get a sector where insolvency is unusually public and unusually constrained. Where the trade is viable but the historic debt is not, a company voluntary arrangement is the instrument that addresses that, and our company administration page covers the alternative.

How we handle it

We don't try to do everything. Lancefield is an insolvency and restructuring specialist, and that's where our advice carries weight. We take no appointments: where one is needed we bring in a licensed insolvency practitioner we trust. When a client needs commercial finance, we refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well. Not a panel. Not a broker pool. The same integrity-first standard that shapes our advice shapes who we refer to. If we recommend a firm, it's because we'd use them ourselves.

We are not brokers, we do not arrange facilities, and we are not authorised to give regulated credit advice. What we do is tell you whether borrowing is the right move at all, which is a different question from which product to use, and one nobody paid by the lender will answer the same way.

Committed costs against uncertain income is a structural problem, so fixing the trading position usually matters more than the facility. Where the debt itself is the constraint, that is restructuring the debt. And where a guarantee has been called, your own position is dealt with on its own terms.

Frequently asked questions
Why do lenders find sports clubs difficult?

Because income depends on results and results are uncertain, while costs are largely committed in advance. Add asset values that depend on continued operation and governance that varies widely, and mainstream lenders price it cautiously or decline it.

Can individuals with irregular income get funding?

Yes, through lenders who underwrite on the pattern of earnings rather than on a payslip. It is specialist lending and it is priced accordingly. The important discipline is borrowing against a normal year rather than a peak one.

What happens when a club cannot pay its debts?

The same procedures apply as to any company, but the process is more public and more constrained, and league and governing-body rules frequently impose their own consequences. Taking advice early matters more here than in most sectors.

Do you arrange this funding?

No. We are not brokers and take no commission. We refer to a trusted specialist firm we know well, and where a club or an individual is already over-committed we advise on that instead.

CTA block

Committed to costs the income may not cover?

We are not brokers and do not arrange facilities, and in this sector the decisions taken after a good season are the ones that matter. One conversation will tell you where you actually stand.
